items.title: [RFC][NPU] INT8 (C8) KV cache for DSA models (GLM-5.2) on Ascend A2/A3 (910B/910C)
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

This RFC proposes generalizing the existing arch35-only packed FP8 DSA KV cache
to a "packed one-byte quant" path, so that GLM-5.2 (`GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`) and
other DeepSeek-V3.2-style DSA models can run an **INT8 (C8) KV cache on Ascend
A2/A3 (910B/910C)**. Every hardware question the proposal depends on has been
probed on a 910B (CANN 9.0.0, torch_npu 2.10.0); section 4 states measured
verdicts, not predictions.

Sections 1-4 of the full RFC follow. The remaining sections (change-surface
audit, test plan, confidence ledger) exist and can be posted here if useful;
a few forward references to them ("section 5" / "section 6" / "section 7")
remain in the text below -- the "section 7" material is summarized under
**Proposed contribution plan** at the end.

> All `file:line` references are against `sgl-project/sglang` at
> **`06008c170dae333e22caceb51f36224071f9b5b3`** (`[dsv4.1]Optimize FP4 indexer by
> skipping invisible tiles`, #40431), which is an ancestor of `upstream/main` --
> so every citation below is checkable against upstream as-is.
>
> vllm-ascend references are against **`abe8ff18a96bcd5f90d08077d1ccd068b959cab4`**
> and carry a `[va]` prefix, relative to that repo's root.
> ops-transformer references are against `gitcode.com/cann/ops-transformer` at
> **`bcc6304656c9e712b50b1faa22872a158b1e34c5`** (the commit sgl-kernel-npu's CI
> pins; `bcc6304` below) and carry an `[ops-t]` prefix.

## 1. Motivation

SGLang today supports an 8-bit ("C8") KV cache for DSA models on Ascend **only on
arch35 / Ascend 950**, in the FP8-E4M3 packed form added by
`[NPU]Support GLM5.2 and FP8 DSA&Indexer kvcache for 950` (commit `3ff226ba8f`).
On A2/A3 the DSA KV cache is unconditionally BF16.

This matters because the KV cache is the binding constraint on A2-class hardware.
A representative single-node deployment (8x 910B, 64 GB/card, GLM-5.2-W4A8, TP8,
`--mem-fraction-static 0.85`):

| item | per card |
|---|---|
| weights | 49.67 GB |
| KV cache | 1.73 GB -> `max_total_num_tokens = 16768` |
| NPU graphs | 0.75 GB |
| unused | 8.25 GB |

`context_len` is 1 M, but the whole instance holds ~16 K tokens. Raising
`mem-fraction-static` helps, but the ceiling is still set by BF16 KV bytes/token.

Per token, per layer, for GLM-5.2 (`kv_lora_rank=512`, `qk_rope_head_dim=64`,
`index_head_dim=128`):

| component | BF16 | INT8 packed | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| main MLA latent + rope | 1152 B | 656 B (512 int8 + 4x fp32 tile scales + 64x bf16 rope) | **1.76x** |
| indexer K | 256 B | 130 B (128 int8 + 1x fp16 scale) | **1.97x** |
| **total** | **1408 B** | **786 B** | **1.79x** |

The main-KV term dominates, so the expected end-to-end gain is ~1.6-1.8x more
resident tokens at the same memory budget. vllm-ascend reports a **measured
1.62x** for the equivalent change on GLM-5 W8A8 / A3 (75,600 -> 122,309 tokens,
PR #11228 / #11846) -- a second-hand figure from PR prose, but consistent with
the arithmetic above.

---

## 2. What exists today

### 2.1 The arch35 FP8 packed path (the template)

Storage is an **opaque fixed-width record**, one per token per layer, whose width is

```python
# python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/kv_cache_configurator.py, calculate_mla_kv_cache_dim
kv_lora_rank + kv_lora_rank // quant_block_size * 4 + qk_rope_head_dim * rope_storage_dtype.itemsize
# GLM-5.2: 512 + 4*4 + 64*2 = 656 bytes
```

It is produced by `_pack_dsa_fp8_kv_cache`
(`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/memory_pool_npu.py:839`):

```python
quantized, scale = torch_npu.npu_dynamic_quant(latent.reshape(-1, 128), dst_type=self.dtype)
packed = torch.cat((quantized.view(uint8),            # 512 B
                    cache_v.to(bf16).view(uint8),     # 128 B  rope, NOT quantized
                    scale.to(fp32).view(uint8)),      #  16 B  4 per-128-tile scales
                   dim=-1)
```

and consumed by `forward_sparse`
(`python/sglang/srt/hardware_backend/npu/attention/ascend_backend.py:1228`):

```python
torch_npu.npu_kv_quant_sparse_flash_attention(
    query=torch.cat((q_nope, q_pe), -1),   # bf16 [T, H, 576]
    key=packed, value=packed,
    key_quant_mode=2, value_quant_mode=2,
    key_dequant_scale=None, value_dequant_scale=None,   # scales read inline
    quant_scale_repo_mode=1, tile_size=128, rope_head_dim=64,
    layout_query="TND", layout_kv="PA_BSND", sparse_mode=3, attention_mode=2, ...)
```

**Key observation: the record layout is not FP8-specific.** It is "512 one-byte
values + per-128-tile FP32 scales + BF16 rope tail", and INT8 and FP8-E4M3 are
both one byte, so the 656-byte width, the `quant_scale_repo_mode=1` /
`tile_size=128` descriptor, and the `npu_dynamic_quant` call site
(`dst_type=self.dtype` already) carry over structurally. The quantization is
**dynamic** (per-token, per-128-tile, computed online), so no checkpoint
calibration is required.

The scale contract is settled, from two independent implementations: the
**main-KV** per-128-tile scale is **FP32 for INT8 and FP8 alike**, symmetric,
no zero-point (`[va] vllm_ascend/attention/utils.py:87-99` hardcodes an fp32
scale term in the record width regardless of KV dtype;
`[va] vllm_ascend/attention/sfa_v1.py:1991` has the INT8 branch cast the scale
`.to(torch.float32)`). The **indexer** per-token scale is a different buffer
entirely -- FP16 under INT8 on A2/A3, FP32 under FP8 on A5 -- and belongs to
section 2.2, not to this record.

Functional acceptance of this record with an INT8 payload on a 910B is now
**measured** (section 4, V1). Numerical parity against a BF16 reference remains
test item 1 in section 6.

### 2.2 An INT8 indexer already works on pre-A5, in this repo

The DSV4 NPU backend already runs an INT8 lightning indexer on non-arch35 hardware:

```python

items.title: Assertion in TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers: "expected then yield to report fat ptr indices" on a pointer select inside a runtime scf.if
items.author: O1iveira7
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Compiling a legal Triton kernel fails with a C++ assertion in the AMD `TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers` pass. The kernel merges two pointer bases with `tl.where` under a tensor condition inside a runtime `if`; the pass then hits a mixed representation between the two `scf.if` arms and aborts compilation.


**Error log**
```
CanonicalizePointers.cpp:1445: ... ConvertSCFIfOp::matchAndRewrite_(scf::IfOp, OneToNOpAdaptor, ...):
Assertion ifOp.thenYield()->hasAttr(kSCFIfOpYieldFatPtrOffsets) &&
          "expected then yield to report fat ptr indices" failed.
note: Pipeline failed while executing [TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers` on 'tt.func' operation: @kernel]
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed

Failure is in `make_ttgir` (MLIR), before LLVM codegen; exit code 1.
```

The generated TTGIR is:

```
%5 = scf.if %4 -> (tensor<2x!tt.ptr<f32>>) {
  %11 = tt.addptr %10, %0          // base = splat(arg1)
  %12 = arith.select %9, %11, %2   // tensor condition, different bases
  scf.yield %12
} else {
  scf.yield %2                     // base = splat(arg2)
}
%8 = tt.load %5
```
TritonAMDGPUCanonicalizePointers is a 1:N conversion to fat pointers (scalar base, tensor offset). scf.if is only rewritten after both scf.yields are rewritten (tracked via internal then/else-rewritten attributes). ConvertSCFYieldOp sets kSCFIfOpYieldFatPtrOffsets on a yield only when one of its remapped operands is a 2-element fat pointer, while ConvertSCFIfOp unconditionally asserts that the then-yield has that attribute.

Here ConvertArithSelectOp takes its special case for a tensor condition with differing scalar bases and materializes both arms into full tensor pointers instead of a (base, offset) pair. So the then-yield carries a single materialized pointer and gets no fat-pointer index attribute, while the else-yield (a plain tt.addptr) converts to a fat pointer pair and does get the attribute. Both yields are marked rewritten, the scf.if becomes illegal, ConvertSCFIfOp fires, and the assertion fails on the inconsistent arms.

**Reproducer**
```
import os

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(sw, a_ptr, b_ptr, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    p = b_ptr + offs
    if tl.load(sw) == 0:
        p = tl.where(offs >= 0, a_ptr + offs, b_ptr + offs)
    tl.store(a_ptr + offs, tl.load(p))


def _main() -> None:
    device = "cuda"
    N = 2
    a = torch.randn(N, device=device)
    b = torch.randn(N, device=device)
    sw = torch.tensor([0], dtype=torch.int32, device=device)
    print(f"REPRO_START N={N} buffer_ops={os.environ.get('AMDGCN_USE_BUFFER_OPS', 'default')}", flush=True)
    kernel[(1,)](sw, a, b, BLOCK=N, num_warps=1)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print("REPRO_DONE (no crash)", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    _main()
```

### Environment details

- AMD Instinct MI308X (gfx942), ROCm 7.2.3
- triton-rocm 3.8.0, torch 2.14.0+rocm7.2, Python 3.12.13

Hi everyone! 👋

I'm trying to run the model Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 (49.1 GB VRAM) using vllm serve with the --dtype auto option. However, I'm getting the following error:

_`ValueError: The model's max seq len (1010000) is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache (73792). Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization` or decreasing `max_model_len` when initializing the engine.`_

From my understanding:

- The model has ~14B parameters, so in FP16 it should use ~28GB of VRAM (please correct me if that’s inaccurate).
- Running in auto mode (which defaults to FP16), the weights should take ~14GB.
- That leaves ~36GB, which I thought would be enough for the KV cache for a 1M context length. But apparently not?

So I have two questions:

1. Is my assumption about the memory breakdown (weights vs KV cache) correct?
2. How can we estimate the required VRAM for a given number of context tokens? Is there a formula or rule of thumb to calculate the KV cache size needed based on context length and model size?

More broadly, I'd really appreciate if someone could explain how to estimate the total VRAM usage in `vllm serve`, including weights, KV cache, context window, etc.

Thanks in advance!

items.title: [RFC]: Context-Aware KV-Cache Retention API (Prioritized Evictions)
items.author: vMaroon
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

_[tracker doc: [Context-Aware KV-Cache Retention API](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1kRKAZBG7te38tqv9Twxyyc-Pdkk2JZPm7gqHHnNhFpE/edit?usp=sharing) (llm-d)]_

Agentic workloads break prefix caching under concurrent load. Over 90% of tokens in a typical agent turn are prefixes reused verbatim from the previous turn. With prefix caching, this is a hit. But 40–60% of session wall time is spent paused on tool calls, and during those pauses the agent's blocks are unreferenced. Under concurrent load, other agents evict them via LRU. When the session resumes: cache miss, full recomputation of the entire context — which grows to 70K–200K tokens by session end.

Hard pinning doesn't scale. What's needed is a way for the orchestrator to express *which blocks matter more* when eviction is unavoidable. The orchestrator knows this structure — which sessions are live, which tokens are shared prefixes, which are unique tails. LRU sees only recency.

**Evidence that LRU is insufficient:**

- **Production traces confirm skewed reuse.** Alibaba's study of production LLM traffic found 10% of KV blocks account for 77% of reuses. Workload-aware eviction achieved up to 41.9% lower mean response time vs. LRU. [[arXiv:2506.02634](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02634)]
- **Tool-call pauses cause false eviction.** Continuum showed TTL-based retention achieved 1.12–3.66× delay reduction on SWE-Bench and BFCL. [[arXiv:2511.02230](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02230)]
- **Multi-agent interleaving causes mutual eviction.** KVFlow achieved up to 2.19× speedup with workflow-aware scoring. [[arXiv:2507.07400](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07400)]
- **Recomputation cost is invisible to LRU.** MARCONI replaced LRU with cost-aware eviction: up to 34.4× higher token hit rates and 71.1% lower TTFT. [[arXiv:2411.19379](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19379)]

Every system that exploits reuse structure, recomputation cost, or workflow topology beats LRU substantially.

### Proposed Change.

A **token-range retention directive** that lets the orchestrator annotate requests with per-range eviction priorities:

```
RetentionDirective:
    start: int              # token index (inclusive)
    end: int | null         # token index (exclusive); null = end of sequence
    priority: int           # 0 (evict first) to 100 (evict last)
    duration: float | null  # seconds before priority expires; null = persistent
```

A request carries zero or more directives via `extra_body`. Blocks not covered by any directive follow the existing LRU path with zero additional cost.

**Two-structure evictor:**

```
BlockPool
  ├── free_block_queue         [existing, unchanged]
  │     Doubly-linked list. LRU. O(1).
  │     Holds blocks with priority = None.
  │
  ├── priority_eviction_queue  [new]
  │     Min-heap by (effective_priority, last_freed_time).
  │     Holds blocks with priority != None.
  │     Lazy TTL expiry on eviction — no background timers. (TBD)
  │
  ├── Eviction order:
  │     1. Unprioritized blocks (free_block_queue, LRU)
  │     2. Prioritized blocks, lowest priority first
```

Without any directives, the system behaves identically to today.

**Design principles:**

1. **Zero overhead for non-agentic workloads.** No additional allocations, heap ops, or timestamp checks for blocks without priority annotations.
2. **The orchestrator defines policy; vLLM executes it.** The engine understands priority values and TTLs. Intelligence about agent graphs and workflow structure lives outside.
3. **The API is the product.** Specific policies (Continuum-style TTL, KVFlow-style scoring, soft-pinning) are consumers of the API, not the API itself.

**Scoped ownership.** An optional `retention_scope` (opaque string, typically session ID) allows multi-tenant scenarios. Any scope can escalate a block's priority; only the owning scope can downgrade or clear it.

**Example — Continuum-style differential retention:**

```json
{
  "retention_directives": [
    {"start": 0, "end": 4096, "priority": 90},
    {"start": 4096, "end": 12288, "priority": 70},
    {"start": 12288, "end": null, "priority": 50, "duration": 15}
  ],
  "retention_scope": "session-abc"
}
```

**Relationship to request-level priority.** vLLM's existing `SchedulingPolicy.PRIORITY` controls which requests get GPU compute. Block-level priority is orthogonal: request priority determines scheduling order; block priority determines cache eviction order. They compose independently.

**Status.** We have a working implementation, with standard test coverage. Early benchmarking on a multi-turn ReAct workload shows measurable TTFT and session latency improvements under memory pressure. Thorough benchmarking is in progress.

### Feedback Period.

3 weeks.

### CC List.

@robertgshaw2-redhat @njhill @orozery @DarkLight1337 

### Any Other Things.

The story driven here is agentic-inference focused, but this API can be useful for all kinds of workload patterns.

items.title: [RFC]: Qwen3-ASR pseudo-streaming can repeat or miss segments
items.author: shiverking
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

I have been experimenting with Qwen3-ASR pseudo-streaming based on the `response_prefix` / prefix-feedback approach discussed in:

- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/35908
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/36018
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/35894

Thanks to the contributors of these discussions and PRs. They provide a useful path for REST/realtime pseudo-streaming ASR.

In my local tests, this approach works well for English. After normalizing punctuation and whitespace, English content similarity between full-audio transcription and batched pseudo-streaming transcription can reach around `0.99`.

However, for Arabic/Thai and some Chinese cases, pseudo-streaming can enter repeated generation loops or miss transcript segments after repeated rounds are filtered. Based on these experiments, using `response_prefix` as the main mechanism for carrying streaming context does not seem robust enough for production multilingual ASR.

## Observations
The pseudo-streaming loop I tested is:

text
```
1. Split audio into chunks.
2. Send a sliding audio window to /v1/audio/transcriptions.
3. Keep stable transcript text locally.
4. Send stable text back as response_prefix.
5. Merge the new response into the final transcript.
```

For long audio, around 120 seconds, with 10-second chunks and a 30-second sliding window, I observed:

- English: content-normalized result is very close to full-audio transcription.
- Arabic/Thai: some windows can generate thousands of repeated words/tokens.
- Chinese: some windows can enter repeated short-phrase loops.
- Dropping repeated rounds avoids long repetition, but can miss valid transcript segments.
- Word-based prefix/holdback works better for English than for Chinese/Thai.
- Character-based prefix/holdback is more useful for Chinese/Thai.

Example repeated-generation pattern:
```
round=6 latency_ms=204617 ttft_ms=188 response_words=2993
round=7 latency_ms=200947 ttft_ms=132 response_words=2929
round=8 latency_ms=201293 ttft_ms=281 response_words=2929
```
This can reproduce with concurrency=1, so it does not appear to be a concurrency issue. Even if this loop is moved from the client side into a server-side realtime wrapper, the core mechanism is still accumulated/sliding audio plus text-prefix feedback, so the same accuracy risks remain.

I would like to propose adding true Engine-level streaming ASR support, where the engine keeps streaming session state across audio chunks instead of relying on caller-side or server-side pseudo-streaming with `response_prefix`.
This would address two separate issues:
- Accuracy: avoid changing decoding behavior through repeated independent window decoding and text-prefix feedback.
- Efficiency: avoid repeatedly uploading and/or re-encoding overlapping audio windows as the audio grows.

The key idea is Engine-level streaming， which is also mentioned in option B of 35908:

```text
one ASR streaming session
new audio chunks are appended to the same session
the engine preserves model context/cache across chunks
partial/final transcript is generated from the continuous session state
```

### Proposed Change.

I would like to discuss whether vLLM should treat `response_prefix`-based pseudo-streaming as a short-term workaround and move toward true Engine-level streaming ASR with preserved model/cache state.

Although client-side or server-side pseudo-streaming is easier to implement, my experiments suggest that it can introduce significant accuracy risks. Since each chunk/window is still decoded as a separate request and stitched together with prefix feedback, the result can diverge from full-context decoding. For some languages, this can lead to repeated generation, prefix pollution, or missing transcript segments after repetition filtering.

### Feedback Period.

No strict deadline. I am opening this to collect feedback from maintainers and contributors on the intended direction for streaming ASR support in vLLM.

### CC List.

cc @vllm-project/maintainers
Also cc contributors/reviewers from the related discussions if appropriate:
#35908
#36018
#35894

### Any Other Things.

Model: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B
API: /v1/audio/transcriptions
Streaming: SSE enabled
Audio length: around 120 seconds
Chunk size: 10 seconds
Sliding window: 30 seconds

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Feature]: Priority scheduling is not reflected in KV/prefix cache retention under cache pressure
items.author: lcc-star
items.body_excerpt: ### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch I ran a minimal experiment to check whether the `priority` field in vLLM affects only request scheduling, or whether it is also considered by KV/prefix cache management. The result suggests that `priority` works for request scheduling, but does not appear to affect KV/prefix cache retention. Under KV cache pressure, high-priority requests are not protected from losing cached prompt tokens compared with low-priority requests. This may be expected behavior today, but it creates a gap for priority-based serving: high-priority requests can be scheduled earlier while still losing their KV cache benefit under memory pressure. ## Environment - vLLM version: `0.19.0` - Model: `Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` - GPU: NVIDIA A800 80GB - Dataset: MMLU validation split - Prefix caching enabled The KV cache was intentionally limited to create cache pressure: GPU KV cache size: 8,192 tokens ## Experiment Design The experiment has two parts. 1. Scheduling probe I first verified that `priority` affects request scheduling. Setup: - Submit 32 low-priority requests first. - Wait 0.5 seconds. - Submit 8 high-priority requests. - Use streaming completions and record first-token time. - `priority=0` is treated as high priority. - `priority=10` is treated as low priority. Result: high priority first-token range: 1.448s - 1.483s queued low-priority tail first-token range: 2.697s - 2.723s The high-priority requests, despite being submitted later, were scheduled before the tail of the low-priority queue. This confirms that priority scheduling is active. 2. KV/prefix cache retention probe Then I tested whether priority affects cache retention. Each trial has three phases: warm -> pressure -> probe - `warm`: send sentinel prompts A and B to populate prefix/KV cache. - `pressure`: send MMLU filler prompts to create KV cache pressure. - `probe`: send the same sentinel prompts again and inspect `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`. Two sentinel groups are used: - Group A - Group B For each pressure setting, I run two priority assignments: swap_priorities = false: A: high priority B: low priority swap_priorities = true: A: low priority B: high priority If KV cache retention uses request priority, then the group assigned high priority should retain more cached tokens after pressure. ## Observed Results No pressure control:pressure_count = 0 A:high cached_tokens = 1808 B:low cached_tokens = 1828 A:low cached_tokens = 1808 B:high cached_tokens = 1828 With cache pressure:pressure_count = 64 A:high cached_tokens = 1324 A:low cached_tokens = 1324 B:low cached_tokens = 1320 B:high cached_tokens = 1320 The cached token count follows the prompt group, not the assigned priority. Swapping priority between A and B does not change the number of retained cached tokens. ### Alternatives For priority-based serving, it would be useful if request priority could also influence KV/prefix cache retention or eviction. For example, under KV cache pressure, vLLM could optionally prefer retaining KV blocks associated with higher-priority requests, or expose a policy hook such as: --kv-cache-eviction-policy priority-aware or integrate request priority into the existing eviction score. ### Additional context ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: Responses API streaming aborts mid-stream (nameless ResponseFunctionToolCallItem) with Qwen3.8 + qwen3_coder + DFlash speculative decoding
items.author: ruiwarn
items.body_excerpt:
### Current environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev1104` (main branch, 2026-08-22 dev build). Also verified that no released version up to and including v0.28.0 (2026-08-26) contains a fix for this bug.
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (FP8)
- Speculative decoding: DFlash drafter enabled
- `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`
- `--reasoning-parser qwen3`
- Client: `/v1/responses` with `stream: true` (via LiteLLM)

### 🐞 Describe the bug

In agentic (tool-heavy) workloads, the Responses API SSE stream aborts mid-stream with no terminal `response.*` event, leaving the client with an unclassifiable truncated stream. The failure is intermittent but recurrent.

### Error message

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ResponseFunctionToolCallItem
name
  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType]
...
RuntimeError: Caught handled exception, but response already started.
```

### Root cause analysis

The crash occurs when a single engine step spans the end of a tool call and the start of the following reasoning/content segment — speculative decoding makes such multi-boundary steps common.

`split_delta()` decomposes a compound `DeltaMessage` in the fixed order reasoning → content → tool_calls. When the tool-call part of the compound delta is the *argument tail* of an already-open tool call (its first `DeltaToolCall` carries no function name — e.g. the flush emitted by the parser engine at `</tool_call>`), replaying it *after* reasoning/content means the state machine has already transitioned away and closed the call. The tail then forces `SimpleStreamingEventProcessor.open()` to construct `ResponseFunctionToolCallItem(name=None)`, which fails pydantic validation. Because the SSE response has already started, the exception aborts the stream without any terminal event.

### Reproducing the problem

Serve the model with the configuration above, then send an agentic, tool-heavy prompt to `/v1/responses` with `stream: true`. The crash is intermittent (depends on where step boundaries fall relative to tool-call boundaries) but recurs reliably in tool-heavy workloads with speculative decoding enabled.

### Impact and workaround

We cannot use the `/v1/responses` streaming path for this deployment. As a workaround we set `use_chat_completions: true` in LiteLLM to route traffic through `/v1/chat/completions`, which loses the Responses API path for this deployment. There is no release containing a fix, so we are stuck on a dev build with no supported upgrade path.

items.title: [Feature]: Logprobs on parsed path streaming `/derender`
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Streaming `/derender` with a reasoning or tool parser (#50550) doesn't return logprobs. #55029 added streaming logprobs but only on the unparsed path. The parsed path builds its stream choices without them. A client that streams with `logprobs: true` through a parser gets nothing back.

Agreed on #47161 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47161#issuecomment-5893681568): the engine is the reference for logprob token strings. Standalone `/derender`, including the parsed path should use one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens` and `_correct_decoded_token` with parity tests against the engine.

Scope:

- Resolve each chunk's logprobs and attach them to whatever delta the parser emits. `/v1/chat/completions` does the same, with one `logprobs.content` list no matter which field the tokens land in.
- Update `logprob_context_token_ids` on the parsed path, like the plain path does. Keep it starting empty, like the engine.
- Drop logprobs on every chunk when `include_reasoning=false` with a parser, like the engine does.
- Fix batch derender too. `_derender_chat` clears `reasoning` but still returns the logprobs.
- Add parity tests against `/v1/chat/completions` with `include_reasoning` on and off, a chunk the parser swallows (tool-call markup) and a multi-byte char split across chunks.

`DerenderStreamState` stays as is. Chunk logprobs already cover only that chunk's tokens and replay never touches them, so no cursor is needed. #59510 handles streaming stop with a 400, so no pending text field either.

Blocked on #58181 (still open). The shared helper (`decode_token_ids`) and the parity tests depend on it.

@shimib has offered to take this. @hyeongyun0916 will review and help with repros.

### Alternatives

Re-resolving token strings separately in the parsed path. We ruled this out on #47161 because the paths already disagree (see #59241).

### Additional context

- #47161: RFC thread where this was agreed
- #55029: streaming logprobs for the unparsed path
- #50550: parser aware streaming derender
- #58181 / #57574: `GenerateLogProbs` with integer token IDs
- #59241 / #59252: SentencePiece leading space dropped in derender logprob strings
- #57052 / #59510: stop handling on derender. #59510 makes streaming `/derender` return 400 on `stop` and notes that logprobs aren't trimmed to the cut text.

items.author: the-Shallow

### Your current environment
The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.30.0 (the latest release) and 0.28.0, CPU, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug `xLAMToolParser.extract_tool_calls_streaming` extracts each call's `arguments` object with a regular expression that allows only one inner level of braces and ignores string literals. items.title: [Bug]: stream_interval is ignored for RequestOutputKind.CUMULATIVE (the SamplingParams default)
items.author: Justee21
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Pure-Python logic in `vllm/v1/engine/output_processor.py`; reproducible on CPU on `main` (checked at 4ac0179), no GPU or model needed.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`stream_interval` (engine `--stream-interval` or per-request `SamplingParams.stream_interval`) is ignored when `output_kind` is `RequestOutputKind.CUMULATIVE`, which is the `SamplingParams` default. Every generated token produces a `RequestOutput`, as if `stream_interval=1`. DELTA mode batches correctly.

```python
from vllm.sampling_params import SamplingParams, RequestOutputKind
from vllm.v1.engine import EngineCoreRequest, EngineCoreOutput, FinishReason
from vllm.v1.engine.output_processor import OutputProcessor

for kind in [RequestOutputKind.DELTA, RequestOutputKind.CUMULATIVE]:
    op = OutputProcessor(None, log_stats=False, stream_interval=4)
    op.add_request(EngineCoreRequest(
        request_id="r", external_req_id="e", prompt_token_ids=[1, 2, 3],
        mm_features=None, pooling_params=None, arrival_time=0.0,
        lora_request=None, cache_salt=None, data_parallel_rank=None,
        sampling_params=SamplingParams(detokenize=False, output_kind=kind, max_tokens=10),
    ), None)
    emitted = 0
    for i in range(10):
        fr = FinishReason.LENGTH if i == 9 else None
        emitted += len(op.process_outputs([EngineCoreOutput("r", [100 + i], finish_reason=fr)]).request_outputs)
    print(kind.name, emitted)
```

```text
DELTA 4
CUMULATIVE 10
```

Cause: in `RequestState.make_request_output`, `sent_tokens_offset` is only updated inside the `if self.output_kind == RequestOutputKind.DELTA:` branch. In CUMULATIVE mode it stays `0`, so the "first token" condition (`self.sent_tokens_offset == 0`) is true on every step and nothing is held back.

The OpenAI-compatible server always uses DELTA for streaming, so this mainly affects direct `AsyncLLM` users who keep the default `output_kind`. CUMULATIVE support was intended when the feature was added (#27869 review discussion); the offset update just ended up inside the DELTA-only branch.

I have a fix ready and will open a PR.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug][MP] Stale CUDA IPC mappings block vLLM restart after an abnormal worker exit
items.author: ertcmm
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

In multiprocess mode, LMCache currently performs the server-side CUDA IPC KV-cache registration from `register_kv_caches()` before vLLM finishes model warmup and CUDA Graph capture.

This creates a failure window:

1. vLLM allocates its KV cache.
2. LMCache imports the KV cache through CUDA IPC.
3. vLLM is still running warmup or CUDA Graph capture.
4. The vLLM worker crashes before it sends `UNREGISTER_KV_CACHE`.
5. LMCache keeps the imported CUDA IPC mappings.
6. A restarted vLLM worker may fail to start because of retained GPU memory, or may encounter `CUDA error: CUDA-capable device(s) is/are busy or unavailable`.

The current `worker_registration_grace_seconds` default is very large, so LMCache may keep the old CUDA resources for a long time. Restarting the LMCache server is currently the most reliable way to release them.

This issue is related to [PR #2798](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/2798), [PR #2943](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/2943), [Issue #4014](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/4014).

## Background

PR #2798 changed the heartbeat behavior so that the heartbeat starts after KV-cache registration. PR #2943 later changed it again so that the heartbeat starts only when the first `STORE` or `RETRIEVE` request arrives.

The reason for the lazy heartbeat was that vLLM may still be performing warmup and CUDA Graph capture after KV-cache registration, and the heartbeat thread may become blocked or may incorrectly cause health-state transitions during this period.

The maintainer @maobaolong confirmed that this behavior was observed in a real deployment.

However, delaying only the heartbeat does not prevent LMCache from already importing and retaining the vLLM CUDA IPC resources. If the worker crashes between KV-cache registration and the first request, there may be no heartbeat and no unregister request. The server therefore keeps the CUDA resources until the registration grace timeout expires.

## Root cause

The current flow is approximately:

```text
vLLM register_kv_caches()
  -> LMCacheMPConnector.register_kv_caches()
  -> LMCacheMPWorkerAdapter.register_kv_caches()
  -> create_transfer_context()
  -> transfer_ctx.register()
  -> REGISTER_KV_CACHE
  -> LMCache imports the CUDA IPC tensors
```

Once the server has imported the CUDA IPC tensors, the resources remain referenced by the server-side `GPUCacheContext` until one of the following happens:

- the worker sends `UNREGISTER_KV_CACHE`;
- the server reaps the worker after a heartbeat timeout;
- the LMCache server itself is restarted.

The current worker `instance_id` is generated randomly using `uuid.uuid4()`. A restarted worker therefore receives a new ID, so the server cannot reliably determine which old worker it replaces.

Using `model_name`, rank, world size, or CUDA device as a deterministic identity is not generally sufficient, because multiple independent vLLM instances can have identical model and parallel configuration, and may even use the same rank and GPU.

## Proposed solution

The preferred solution is to defer the actual server-side CUDA IPC registration until vLLM has completed warmup and a real transfer operation is needed.

The vLLM connector callback can still be invoked at the existing time, but LMCache would treat it as a pending registration:

```
vLLM register_kv_caches()
  -> save KV-cache tensors and layout metadata locally
  -> do not create the CUDA transfer context
  -> do not send REGISTER_KV_CACHE
  -> return successfully

First real STORE or RETRIEVE operation
  -> ensure registration has completed
  -> create the transfer context
  -> send REGISTER_KV_CACHE
  -> start the heartbeat
  -> continue with the STORE or RETRIEVE operation
```

This would prevent a vLLM crash during warmup or CUDA Graph capture from leaving an imported CUDA IPC context in LMCache, because no CUDA IPC registration would have occurred yet.

## Expected behavior after the fix

The following cases should work:

```
vLLM register_kv_caches() callback
  -> LMCache records pending registration only
vLLM crashes during warmup
  -> LMCache has no imported CUDA IPC mapping
  -> no GPU memory is retained by LMCache
```

## Trade-offs and compatibility considerations

This changes the meaning of the client-side `register_kv_caches()` call: it would acknowledge the KV-cache metadata locally, while the server-side CUDA IPC registration would happen lazily.

Potential trade-offs include:

- The first STORE or RETRIEVE request will pay the registration cost.
- The first request may need to handle registration failure.

An alternative would be to add an explicit vLLM callback after warmup and CUDA Graph capture, but that would require vLLM-side changes.

Another possible mitigation is a manual HTTP endpoint to trigger worker reaping. This would be useful as an operational fallback, but it would not automatically solve the failure.

## Questions

1. Is lazy server-side CUDA IPC registration from the first STORE/RETRIEVE path acceptable for MP mode?
2. Should LMCache also provide a manual HTTP endpoint to trigger worker reaping as an operational fallback?

items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)
or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌


**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as sub-issues are filed.

items.title: [Bug][MP] Failed prefetch cleanup can publish invalid L1 data
items.author: ae86zhizhi
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`

**Describe the bug**

In MP mode, `PrefetchController` cleans up the L1 destination of an L2 load that failed (the adapter reported the key as not loaded) with two calls in this order:

```python
l1_mgr.finish_write(failed_keys)
l1_mgr.delete(failed_keys)
```

(`lmcache/v1/distributed/storage_controllers/prefetch_controller.py`, "Clean up failed keys" in the load-completion handler; the same pair runs in `_cleanup_in_flight_requests` on `stop()` for every request still in its load phase.)

`finish_write` makes the destination readable and notifies the write-finished listeners even though the load has not been confirmed successful; its contents may be incomplete or uninitialized. `StoreController`'s listener enqueues the key and its loop calls `reserve_read` on it, which now succeeds. If the store controller acquires and still holds that read lock when the `delete` runs, the `delete` returns `KEY_IS_LOCKED` and the entry stays; the destination is then stored to the policy-selected L2 adapters under a valid key, and a later lookup returns it as a hit.

The shutdown path has the same shape without needing a failed load: every in-flight request's `write_reserved_keys` goes through the same two calls while the store controller's loop is still running.

Even when the `delete` wins the race, the key is announced to every `L1ManagerListener` as write-finished, and `finish_write` publishes `L1_WRITE_FINISHED`, so metrics and coordinator cache events report an unconfirmed destination as a completed write.

**To Reproduce**

With the regression test of the linked pull request (`tests/v1/distributed/test_prefetch_failed_load_cleanup.py`), against `dev`:

1. Store one key in a `MockL2Adapter` and wrap it in `FaultInjectL2Adapter(gap_indices=(0,))`, so the key is present at lookup and its load is reported as failed.
2. Register an `L1ManagerListener` that records `on_l1_keys_write_finished`, and start a `StoreController` with a second, empty `MockL2Adapter` as its target.
3. Submit a prefetch for the key and wait for its result (0 retained keys).
4. The recording listener has received the failed key as write-finished (`assert key not in listener.write_finished_keys()` fails). Depending on scheduling, the empty adapter may also receive a store of the destination.

The second test checks L1 absence and listener silence when `stop()` interrupts an unfinished load (an adapter that accepts a load which then stays pending); it fails on `dev` for the same reason.

**Expected behavior**

A reservation whose load failed or was cancelled is removed while it is still write-locked. The key never becomes readable, is never announced to the write-finished listeners, and no store task is created for it. `reserve_read` on the key returns `KEY_NOT_EXIST`.

`L1Manager.delete(keys, force=True)` already does this; the fix is to call it instead of the `finish_write` + `delete` pair at both sites. A pull request with the change and the two tests follows.

**Environment**

- LMCache `dev` at 45e019df (2026-09-08); the same two call sites are in v0.5.4.
- Linux x86_64, Python 3.12, torch 2.13.0. The tests use the pinned-memory L1 and no model.

### Motivation

We noticed that in the `_get_logits` function of vllm, `gather` instead of `all_gather` will be used under certain conditions (the main condition is that for non-tpu devices):
Code link:

- [logits = tensor_model_parallel_gather(logits)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e1fc61f0fb90c37f0d4a1a8f76235a6e4e1103c/vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py#L101C22-L101C50)

The change from using `all_gather` to `gather` is initially added in this PR for your reference: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/2221.

While in SGLang, we see currently `all_gather` is always used:
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e868d0b60eb2d435c5599165f787bca06bdc9c3d/python/sglang/srt/layers/logits_processor.py#L246

items.title: [Performance] NVFP4 KV cache regresses Qwen4Exp decode ~29% on DGX Spark (SM121) vs fp8_e4m3 — consider arch-gating the default
items.author: leego
items.body_excerpt:
# [Performance] NVFP4 KV cache regresses Qwen4Exp decode ~29% on DGX Spark (SM121) vs fp8_e4m3

## Summary
`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4` (the new default, `NVFP4_KV_CACHE=1`) costs **~29% single-stream
decode throughput** for Qwen4Exp-style models (QSA sparse attention) on GB10/SM121,
versus fp8_e4m3 KV. The FP4 packed-KV path's gather-side dequant is expensive on this
silicon; on datacenter parts the tradeoff may differ, but on Spark the pool-size win
is pointless (262K native context already fits with fp8) and the decode cost is real.

## Data (2× DGX Spark TP=2, NEXTN 3/1/4, decode CUDA graphs on, n=7-10 median)
| KV dtype | single-stream decode | notes |
|---|---|---|
| nvfp4 (default since the NVFP4-KV change) | 44.0 tok/s | also occasional deep dips |
| **fp8_e4m3** (`NVFP4_KV_CACHE=0`) | **56.8-58.6 tok/s** | stable |
| bf16 | 54-59 (more variance) | |

Same cluster, same weights (RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4), same bench
(`completion_tokens`-based streaming, 400-token runs).

## Suggestion
- Gate `NVFP4_KV_CACHE` default by arch: keep 1 on SM100+, default 0 on SM120/121 for
  QSA models (or autotune at first capture).
- Alternatively add a fused gather+dequant path for FP4 KV in the QSA Triton varlen
  fallback kernel (`qsa_fa_fallback.py` pattern used on SM121).

## Environment
Image lmsysorg/sglang:qwen38flashnext (+SM121 QSA fallback), 2×GB10, RoCEv2 TP2.
Full methodology: MiaAI-Lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-Dual-DGX-Sparks → OPTIMIZATION-2026-08-28.md.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache backup thread dies on any storage backend exception; queued backups and their host memory are never released
items.author: qidaye
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`HiCacheController.backup_thread_func` (and the `HybridCacheController` override) only catches `queue.Empty`:

```python
while not self.storage_stop_event.is_set():
    try:
        operation = self.backup_queue.get(block=True, timeout=1)
        if operation is None:
            continue
        if not self.backup_skip:
            self._page_backup(operation)
        self.ack_backup_queue.put(operation)
    except Empty:
        continue
```

Any exception raised by the storage backend while writing a page (I/O error, timeout, malformed response from a remote store such as Mooncake / NIXL / 3FS / HF3FS / file backends) escapes the loop and kills the daemon thread. From that point on:

- every backup operation stays in `backup_queue` forever and is never written to L3;
- `ack_backup_queue` never drains, so `HiRadixCache` / `UnifiedRadixCache` never release the host memory held by those operations (`entry.release_host()` in the backup drain path);
- the only visible symptom is host pool exhaustion much later. There is no log line pointing at the dead backup thread, and `hicache_*` metrics keep reporting as if backups were in flight.

A backend that returns `False` from `batch_set` already stops the current operation, but the acked `StorageOperation` carries no information about the failure, so the ack consumer cannot distinguish a partial or failed write from a complete one.

Expected: a failing backup should be logged, the operation should still be acked (so host memory is released and the queue keeps draining), and the ack should say what went wrong.

### Reproduction

Drives the production `backup_thread_func` with a controller stub whose backend raises once. No GPU or model needed.

```python
import threading
from queue import Empty, Queue
from unittest import mock

import torch

from sglang.srt.managers.cache_controller import HiCacheController, StorageOperation

controller = mock.MagicMock()
controller.storage_stop_event = threading.Event()
controller.backup_skip = False
controller.page_size = 16
controller.backup_queue = Queue()
controller.ack_backup_queue = Queue()

calls = [0]
def page_backup(operation):
    calls[0] += 1
    if calls[0] == 1:
        raise RuntimeError("storage backend I/O error")  # e.g. remote store timeout
    operation.completed_tokens = 16 * len(operation.hash_value)
controller._page_backup = page_backup

def make_op(n):
    return StorageOperation(torch.zeros(n * 16), list(range(n * 16)), hash_value=[f"h{i}" for i in range(n)])

controller.backup_queue.put(make_op(4))
controller.backup_queue.put(make_op(2))

t = threading.Thread(target=HiCacheController.backup_thread_func, args=(controller,), daemon=True)
t.start()
t.join(timeout=3)
print("backup thread alive:", t.is_alive())
acked = []
try:
    while True:
        acked.append(controller.ack_backup_queue.get(timeout=1).id)
except Empty:
    pass
print("acked operations:", acked, "(2 expected)")
print("still queued:", controller.backup_queue.qsize())
```

Output on `main` (2358916d5a):

```
Exception in thread Thread-1 (backup_thread_func):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../sglang/srt/managers/cache_controller.py", line 1289, in backup_thread_func
    self._page_backup(operation)
RuntimeError: storage backend I/O error
backup thread alive: False
acked operations: [] (2 expected)
still queued: 1
```

The same happens in a real deployment whenever the L3 backend raises during `batch_set` (observed with a remote storage backend timing out under load): the backup thread disappears and host memory is never reclaimed.

In a server the trigger is any exception from the configured `--hicache-storage-backend` during a write; e.g. `--enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-storage-backend <backend>` with a backend that becomes unreachable.

### Environment

Reproduction above is CPU-only and does not depend on the accelerator.

```
sglang: main @ 2358916d5a (editable install from source)
python: 3.12.13
torch: 2.13.0+cpu
OS: Ubuntu 24.04, Linux 7.0.0-30-generic
```

`python3 -m sglang.check_env` currently fails on a CPU-only host with `NameError: name 'env' is not defined` (no branch in `check_env.py` for the CPU case), so the versions above were collected manually.

A fix is in #38427.

items.title: [Bug] HiCache write_through does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction
items.author: donghyq
items.body_excerpt:
# [SGLang] HiCache `write_through` does not fully persist first-seen prefixes before eviction

## Summary

When `--hicache-write-policy write_through` is used with Mooncake Store, a first-seen prefix can be evicted from L1/L2 before all of its KV is backed up to storage. Replaying that prefix after eviction restores only part of it from L3; the rest is recomputed.

Using `--hicache-write-policy write_back --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete` on the same workload restores the full prefix from Mooncake Store, so the storage backend and restore path are functional.

## Environment

- SGLang commit: `bdf8886ad3`
- Branch: `main`
- Model: Qwen3-4B
- GPU: 1 × NVIDIA H20-3e
- Attention backend: Triton
- HiCache:
  - `--enable-hierarchical-cache`
  - `--hicache-size 4`
  - `--hicache-write-policy write_through`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend mooncake`
  - `--hicache-storage-backend-extra-config '{"standalone_storage": true, "client_server_address": "127.0.0.1:50300", "enable_group_semantics": false}'`
- Mooncake Store:
  - master/client started independently
  - `root_fs_dir` and `cluster_id` configured
  - global segment size: 16 GiB
- Prompt: 5 distinct 16,011-token prefixes, `max_new_tokens=1`
- L1 capacity: 42,763 tokens
- L2 capacity: 27,127 tokens

## Reproduction

1. Start SGLang with the `write_through` configuration above.
2. Flush the cache.
3. Send five distinct 16,011-token prefixes sequentially.
4. Replay prefix A after prefixes B–E have displaced it from L1/L2.

## Expected

Prefix A should be restored from Mooncake Store with roughly:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Actual

Prefix A restores only part of the KV from storage:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 2551,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 2551,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

A second replay then reports a full device hit:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16009,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 16009,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 0,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

## Control experiment

The same workload with:

```text
--hicache-write-policy write_back
--hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete
```

returns:

```json
{
  "cached_tokens": 16010,
  "cached_tokens_details": {
    "device": 0,
    "host": 0,
    "storage": 16010,
    "storage_backend": "MooncakeStore"
  }
}
```

This indicates that Mooncake Store can persist and restore the full prefix when the write path is forced.

## Possible cause

In `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/hiradix_cache.py`:

- `_inc_hit_count()` at line 926 skips chunked requests.
- `write_backup()` at line 856 is only called after `hit_count` reaches `write_through_threshold`.
- For a first-seen prefix, the leaf node may therefore not be backed up before eviction.
- `write_backup()` also requires the parent node to already be backed up, so a long first-seen prefix may only be partially persisted.
- `_evict_write_back()` at line 1105 shows the working control path: it stages the node to host, waits for the backup, and then writes storage.

## Suggested fix

One of the following would make the behavior clearer:

1. Add a true “write-through on insert” mode that persists the full prefix chain when a request finishes.
2. Document that `write_through` means “second-hit persistence” rather than “insert-time persistence”.
3. Keep the current optimization, but add a warning when a first-seen prefix is evicted before its backup completes.

## Impact

This affects long first-seen prompts that are evicted before a second request arrives. It can silently reduce L3 hit rate and make shared-cache routing less effective.

items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

items.title: MP client: unanswered STORE/RETRIEVE RPCs cause unbounded client-side memory leak after GPU context loss
items.author: wuwanxu
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

In a 3P1D deployment using vLLM + LMCacheMPConnector + per-node LMCache sidecars, a sidecar can lose a worker GPU context while the client remains active. Subsequent STORE and RETRIEVE blocking handlers raise a missing-GPU-context ValueError. The server logs the exception but does not return a response to the DEALER client.

The primary impact is an unbounded client-side memory leak, not only a server-side error. A MessageQueueClient pending future is removed only after a response arrives. When the response is omitted, the future permanently retains its request payload, including token IDs. The vLLM worker adapter also waits for that future to complete before removing per-request store/retrieve futures and CUDA IPC events. Every later failed request therefore leaks future, request-key/token payload, and event state; memory grows linearly with request rate until the worker container approaches its memory limit.

## Observed evidence

Three sidecar logs were inspected. p1 and p2 show the same persistent fault; p3 does not.

| Sidecar log | Blocking-handler errors | Missing instance GPU context | Missing model GPU context during lookup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| p1 | 5,932 | 11,864 | 17,260 |
| p2 | 5,976 | 11,952 | 17,625 |
| p3 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Representative p1 sequence:

1. 2026-09-18 08:25:39.639: lookup reports no GPU context for the model/world-size pair.
2. 2026-09-18 08:25:39.749: mq.py _notify_response logs Error in blocking handler.
3. The handler ends with ValueError: No GPU context registered for instance ID.
4. The failures repeat continuously; Session not found, skipping touch warnings also appear.

The logs show that the sidecar runs a 30-second worker reaper. They prove the missing-context and silent-RPC-failure pattern, but do not by themselves prove the exact reaper decision that removed a particular context.

## Expected behavior

A failed blocking RPC must always resolve its client future with an explicit failure. Independently, clients need bounded cleanup for every unanswered request. A failed async retrieve must surface its failed block IDs so the serving engine recomputes rather than consuming unloaded KV.

## Proposed direction

1. Add TTL-based cleanup for unanswered MessageQueueClient pending requests; expire them with a dedicated exception and remove pending state.
2. Make device-aware futures propagate the expiry without attempting CUDA event import.
3. Make the vLLM worker adapter treat expiry as a completed failed STORE/RETRIEVE, remove per-request futures/events, and report failed retrieve block IDs.
4. Follow up with server-side error responses and worker re-registration or health signaling so this failure is immediate rather than TTL-delayed.

## Reproduction outline

1. Start an MP sidecar and a vLLM worker.
2. Cause the server to lose or reap the worker GPU context while the client stays alive.
3. Submit STORE or RETRIEVE for the stale instance ID.
4. Observe repeated missing-context errors on the server and unanswered client RPCs; inspect client pending future and worker per-request collections for growth.

items.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
items.author: mrBenBern
items.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.

items.title: [RFC]: CPU backend support for the vLLM connector + Mooncake Store L2 for multi-instance CPU serving
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes upstreaming two related contributions that enable **LMCache on the vLLM CPU backend** and make **cross-instance KV reuse** work for CPU serving:

1. **A CPU GPU-connector** (`VLLMCPUConnector`): a pure-torch gather/scatter path between vLLM's paged CPU KV cache and an LMCache `MemoryObj`, handling vLLM's 4D fused K/V CPU layout. This is the missing piece that lets LMCache run at all on `device=cpu`.
2. **Fixes to the Mooncake Store L2 connector** so it works on the CPU backend and shares KV **across instances** (fork-safe per-process client init, a correct `exists()`/lookup path, and a config-key alias).

Together these let multiple vLLM CPU instances behind a load balancer share one KV cache (SHM on a single box, or Mooncake Store over TCP across a cluster), instead of each instance recomputing the same prefixes.

Note that the CPU connector (contribution 1) is **backend-agnostic**: it is the shared foundation that unlocks the *entire* LMCache backend ecosystem on CPU (local DRAM L1, the shared SHM server, pickle, and remote L2s). Contribution 2 is one representative distributed L2 (Mooncake). We enable and validate **both** the default (SHM) and Mooncake paths because they target different deployment scopes (see §3.4).

We propose **two stacked PRs** (CPU connector, then Mooncake-on-CPU) plus this RFC to tie them together.

## 2. Motivation

- **CPU inference is growing** (cost, availability, disaggregated/CPU-tier deployments), and vLLM has a maturing CPU backend.
- **Multi-instance CPU serving needs *shared* KV.** vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is **per-instance**: behind a load balancer, instance B cannot reuse instance A's prefix KV, so shared system prompts / few-shot / documents are recomputed on every instance.
- **LMCache already solves cross-instance reuse**, but had **no CPU connector**, so it could not run on vLLM CPU at all; and the **Mooncake Store L2** path did not work on CPU or across instances (fork-safety + lookup bugs).
- **Measured impact** (Section 5): on a single-socket AMD EPYC, an external shared KV cache gives **+27-31% aggregate throughput at 3 instances** and **-28%/-34% p95/p99 tail latency** vs APC.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Topology

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LB[NGINX load balancer] --> V1[vLLM CPU inst 1]
    LB --> V2[vLLM CPU inst 2]
    LB --> V3[vLLM CPU inst 3]
    V1 <-->|store / load KV| L[(LMCache)]
    V2 <-->|store / load KV| L
    V3 <-->|store / load KV| L
    L <-->|put / get| S{{Shared KV: SHM  or  Mooncake Store L2 / TCP}}
```

### 3.2 CPU connector (`VLLMCPUConnector`)

**Why a CPU connector is needed.** Every existing GPU connector relies on CUDA custom ops (`c_ops`) and CUDA streams and assumes the GPU KV memory layout. None of that exists on CPU, so LMCache previously could not run on vLLM's CPU backend at all. `VLLMCPUConnector` fills that gap.

**What it implements.** The same connector interface, using **plain PyTorch tensor operations** (indexing + copy) with no CUDA kernels or streams:

- `from_gpu(...)` (**STORE / gather**): copy the KV for tokens `[start, end)` out of vLLM's paged CPU buffer into a contiguous `MemoryObj`.
- `to_gpu(...)` (**LOAD / scatter**): copy KV from a `MemoryObj` back into vLLM's paged buffer, placing each token's K/V into the slot given by vLLM's slot mapping.
- `batched_from_gpu(...)` / `batched_to_gpu(...)`: batched variants that handle several token ranges in one call.

**Handling vLLM's CPU KV layout.** vLLM's CPU backend stores each layer's cache as a single **4D fused K/V tensor** (K and V packed together), which is laid out differently from the GPU cache. For each layer the connector derives logical views shaped `[num_blocks, block_size, num_heads, head_size]` for K and for V (`_kv_token_views`), then uses the request's block/slot offsets to move exactly the right rows. This keeps gather/scatter correct without copying the whole buffer.

**Selection.** The connector is picked automatically when the device is CPU (`torch_device_type == "cpu"` in `CreateGPUConnector`), so no user config change is required.

**Plugging in as a `GPUConnectorInterface`.** So the CPU connector can subclass `GPUConnectorInterface` without importing the CUDA-heavy `gpu_connectors`/`utils` modules (which import `c_ops`, absent in NO_GPU_EXT builds), the interface ABC is extracted into a small `c_ops`-free `interface.py` that `gpu_connectors.py` re-exports. Existing GPU connectors are unaffected.

### 3.3 Mooncake Store L2 on CPU

The Mooncake client (Go runtime + multithreaded C++) is **not fork-safe**, and vLLM forks its scheduler/worker processes. Fixes:

- **Fork-safe, lazy per-process init**: the store/lookup client is created inside each process on first use (`_ensure_store()`), never inherited across a fork.
- **Correct lookup path**: `exists()`/`exists_sync()` now call `_ensure_store()` first (the contains/lookup path can run before any put/get on an instance) and compare `is_exist() == 1` (it returns `1/0/-1`) so an error never reads as a cache hit. Without this, cross-instance lookups were swallowed as misses and the instance recomputed.
- **Config-key alias**: accept `master_server_address` as an alias for `master_server_addr` in dict-based setup.

**Cross-instance key consistency (usage requirement, not connector code):** for a prefix computed on instance A to be found by instance B, the KV keys must hash identically across processes. Python's default randomized hashing breaks this; deployments must use a stable algorithm (e.g. `LMCACHE_PRE_CACHING_HASH_ALGORITHM=sha256` with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`). This will be documented.

### 3.4 Why enable both paths (default SHM and Mooncake L2)

The CPU connector is transport/backend-agnostic, so a natural question is *why validate two L2 paths instead of one*. Because they are **complementary, not competing**: the right choice is dictated by deployment topology, and we want CPU users to be able to pick either without changing the connecto
