items.title: OTel tracing overhead cliffs at c=50 on TP=2 deployments — level/flush tuning has no effect
items.author: wangxf1987
items.body_excerpt:
## Title

OTel trace overhead benchmark on a production-style K8s deployment (TP=2, 2 replicas): throughput loss of 20-33% at c>=50, trace level and flush threshold have negligible effect

## Summary

We benchmarked `--enable-trace` overhead on a production-shaped K8s deployment (RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, not docker-compose), Qwen3.6-27B-CHO on sglang v0.5.18, TP=2 per replica x 2 replicas (4 GPUs total, not an exclusive full node). This complements the larger-scale results already discussed elsewhere for TP=8 exclusive-node setups, and shows the overhead shape is very different at smaller TP.

Full report (charts + tables): attached PDF (`report-en.pdf`). Raw data (`result.csv`, GPU/CPU logs) available on request.

## Environment

- sglang `v0.5.18` (community image), `SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC=1`
- Deployment: K8s RBG + LeaderWorkerSet, TP=2 per replica, 2 replicas, 4x H20 GPUs
- Trace path: sglang engine -> local OTel Agent (DaemonSet, node-local endpoint) -> Gateway -> backend, i.e. a two-hop agent-gw architecture, not a direct hardcoded Gateway connection
- 4 configs compared:
  | Group | trace level | async | flush threshold |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | G1 baseline | disabled | - | - |
  | G2 | 2 | 1 | default |
  | G3 | 3 | 1 | default |
  | G4 | 2 | 1 | 50 |
- Load generator: fixed-prompt benchmark client, concurrency swept across 1/10/50/100/200, 3 repeats per level (median)

## Findings

1. **Overhead is mild at low concurrency (c<=10)**: ttft_p99 +6~71%, throughput loss only 3~4%.
2. **c=50 is a clear inflection point**: ttft_p99 jumps 4.6x (172ms -> 965ms) going from G1 to G2 — roughly equivalent to the G1 baseline's own c=100 latency level being pulled forward to c=50. In other words, enabling trace shifts the whole latency-saturation curve left by one concurrency tier.
3. **From c>=50 onward, throughput loss is stable at 20~33%**, and grows with concurrency (-20.3% at c=50, up to -33.1% at c=200).
4. **Trace level 2 -> 3 produced no measurable incremental overhead** at c>=10 (all deltas within noise, ±2%).
5. **`SGLANG_TRACE_ASYNC_FLUSH_THRESHOLD=50` vs. default also produced no measurable benefit** at c>=50 (within ±16%, mostly ±2%; one anomalous +132.9% ttft_p99 spike at c=10 looked like a transient one-off, not reproduced at other levels).
6. **Root cause for (4) and (5): CPU was never the bottleneck in this setup.** Host CPU utilization on the GPU node stayed at 2~3% across all 4 groups (vs. GPU sm% rising from 14.8% baseline to 16~19% with trace enabled). Both trace-level and flush-threshold tuning target CPU-side span processing cost — with only 2 TP ranks, span volume is low enough that CPU headroom is never exhausted, so those knobs have nothing to bite on at this scale.
7. This is a **much smaller overhead** than what we see at TP=8 on an exclusive full node (throughput loss there was 75~79%, itl_p99 spiking ~28x, with CPU pegged at 99% — happy to share that data too if useful). The magnitude gap tracks roughly linearly with TP rank count, since span generation scales with the number of ranks, and the TP=8 test used synchronous export while this one used async by default.

## Why we're filing this

- The community advice we've seen elsewhere ("lower `SGLANG_TRACE_LEVEL` to reduce overhead", "tune the async flush threshold") holds at high TP / high CPU pressure, but **doesn't transfer to smaller TP configs** — those knobs are simply inert until CPU saturates. Worth calling out in docs/guidance so users at TP<=2-4 don't spend time tuning a lever with no effect.
- The **c=50 inflection point** (throughput loss going from ~4% to ~20% within one concurrency step) suggests there may be a queueing/lock-contention effect on the trace export path that kicks in once concurrent in-flight spans cross some threshold, rather than a smooth linear cost per request. Might be worth profiling `trace_async.py`'s buffer/flush path under concurrent load to see if there's a lock or queue that serializes once request volume rises (in our TP=8 investigation, we found `trace_req_finish()`/`abort()` and `__getstate__` all trigger unconditional flushes regardless of the configured threshold, and `trace_req_start()`'s `tracer.start_span()` + `propagate.inject()` calls are synchronous OTel API calls on the request path — happy to dig further if maintainers think that's a productive direction).
- Production guidance: for small/mid TP deployments (TP<=2-4), default trace config (level=2, async on) is fine as-is. For TP=8-class deployments, overhead is materially higher and level-tuning is the effective lever — but this should probably be stated explicitly since it's not obvious from the trace docs which regime a given deployment falls into.

## Attachments

- `report-en.pdf` — full benchmark report with charts (ttft_p99 / itl_p99 / e2e_p50 / throughput vs. concurrency, delta% overview, GPU/CPU resource usage)
[Uploading report-en.pdf…]()

items.title: [Bug] Potential hybrid GDN Radix-cache selected-logprob drift on repeated branch scoring
items.author: furedericca-lab
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues and did not find an existing report that fully covers this request shape.
- [ ] I have not re-run this on today's latest main; the reproduction was observed on pinned main commit `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a` (2026-09-25).
- [x] Environment details and a standalone `/generate` reproducer are included below.
- [x] This is a possible correctness issue rather than a general usage question.
- [x] Report is in English.

## Describe the bug

With a hybrid GDN Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 checkpoint, repeated selected-token logprob scoring is stable when Radix Cache is disabled, but the first Radix-enabled branch scoring pass differs substantially from subsequent identical passes.

The observation is:

| Cache configuration | Max repeated selected-logprob delta | Pattern |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Unified Radix Cache enabled | `2.551527976989746` | run 1 differs; runs 2 and 3 match exactly |
| Radix Cache disabled | `0.0` | runs 1, 2 and 3 match exactly |

The prefix is explicitly warmed before the repeated branch batches. With Radix enabled, the server log reports `#cached-token: 0` for the first branch batch and `#cached-token: 128` for later identical branch batches. With Radix disabled, the three repeated branch batches are bit-stable.

This strongly correlates the drift with the cache-hit execution path, but I do **not** want to over-attribute the root cause: the current evidence does not prove that a specific GDN recurrent-state checkpoint, restore, split, or other hybrid-cache internal operation is responsible.

This was found while gating a decision workload that consumes candidate-token logprobs directly, so cache-hit equivalence matters even when the top-1 decision itself does not change.

Related work:

- #22935 — Mamba Radix cache prefix/split behavior
- #34899 — bit-exact correctness coverage for Unified Radix Cache
- #38625 — interior/no-buffer checkpoint work

I am not assuming that #22935 or #38625 has the same root cause or fully covers this request shape. In particular, I would like to know whether a shared prefix followed by divergent option branches is expected to preserve selected-token logprobs under deterministic inference when the later identical branch requests hit the hybrid cache.

## Environment

Tested environment:

- SGLang source: `2f5c9ac43d76eef11e8561c89c55a79db7db715a`
- SGLang package: `0.5.21.dev612+g2f5c9ac43`
- Model: `ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4`
- Model revision: `332d277a083ca395aa2f822842b82f5f2f3913a2`
- Architecture: `Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration`, hybrid GDN / full attention
- Quantization: ModelOpt mixed FP8/NVFP4
- GPUs: 2 × NVIDIA RTX 5090 (SM120), TP=2
- NVIDIA driver: `610.57.04`
- Kernel: `7.0.0-34-generic`
- Python: `3.13.11`
- PyTorch: `2.14.0a0.post20260925` (CUDA 13.4)
- Triton: `3.7.0`
- `sglang-kernel==0.4.7`
- `flash-attn-4==4.0.0b19`
- Attention backend: Triton
- Deterministic inference: enabled
- Prefill CUDA Graph: disabled
- Decode CUDA Graph: retained
- Unified Radix Cache: enabled for the failing case
- Observed Mamba strategy: `extra_buffer`
- Comparison case: identical server settings plus only `--disable-radix-cache`

A literal `python3 -m sglang.check_env` dump was not retained for this run; the exact pinned runtime versions above are from the same project environment used for the reproduction.

## Reproduction

Launch the candidate server with Radix Cache enabled:

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /path/to/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27b-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30001 \
  --trust-remote-code --tp-size 2 \
  --attention-backend triton \
  --enable-deterministic-inference \
  --disable-prefill-cuda-graph
```

Then run this standalone script. It does **not** import Reflex. It warms the exact shared prefix using native `/generate`, then submits the same two divergent branch items three times and compares the selected A/B/C token logprobs.

<details>
<summary>Standalone /generate reproducer</summary>

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import json
import math
import urllib.request
from uuid import uuid4

SYSTEM_PROMPT = (
    "You are a System One decision model. You read the State and answer each Question "
    "by choosing exactly one of the listed options. You never explain. You answer with "
    "the single option label only."
)
STATE = "An apple was picked from the orchard."
INSTRUCTIONS = "Which listed item is the fruit mentioned in the state?"
OPTIONS = {
    "apple": "the fruit picked from the orchard",
    "stone": "a mineral rock",
    "river": "flowing water",
}
ORDERS = (("apple", "stone", "river"), ("river", "stone", "apple"))
LABELS = ("A", "B", "C")

def prefix_text():
    return (
        f"<|im_start|>system\n{SYSTEM_PROMPT}<|im_end|>\n"
        "<|im_start|>user\n# Evidence\n"
        f"{STATE}\n\n"
    )

def branch_text(order):
    option_lines = [
        f"{label}. {key}: {OPTIONS[key]}"
        for label, key in zip(LABELS, order, strict=True)
    ]
    body = "\n".join([
        f"# Criterion\n{INSTRUCTIONS}\n",
        "# Options",
        *option_lines,
        "\nRespond with only the letter of the best option.\n",
    ])
    return f"{body}<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>assistant\n<think>\n\n</think>\n\n"

def post(url, payload):
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"{url.rstrip('/')}/generate",
        data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),

items.title: [Bug] Hybrid-SWA + radix cache: admission livelock when the SWA prefix lock pins a finished request's untrimmed last chunk
items.author: bill-h-lin
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

With a hybrid-SWA model, the radix cache on and a tight SWA pool, the scheduler can stop admitting a request forever: 1 waiting, 0 running, GPU idle, no log line. We hit it on MiMo-V2.6-Flash (sliding window 128, page size 1) and traced it to `SWAComponent.acquire_component_lock` pinning a whole tree node that holds a finished request's untrimmed last chunk of SWA, instead of one window.

**Sequence** (`--chunked-prefill-size 8192`, `--swa-full-tokens-ratio 0.06448` → SWA pool 8,451, `--context-length 131072`, `--max-running-requests 1`, overlap scheduler on):

1. A 32,768-token request with `max_new_tokens=1` (it finishes at its first token).
2. A request with the same 32,768 tokens, a different next token, then 4,999 more (37,768 in all).

Request 2 matches 32,768 cached tokens, needs 5,001 SWA slots and never runs. `/v1/loads` stayed at 1 waiting, 0 running for 43 minutes. The same sequence runs fine with `--chunked-prefill-size 4096` or with a 16,643-token SWA pool.

### Root cause (line numbers on `main` @ 6624999385)

1. Under the overlap scheduler, a request that finishes at its first token still gets one decode step prepared before its prefill result is processed: `alloc_for_decode` (`allocation.py:587`) commits one more token, and `release_kv_cache` → `insert_req(req, up_to=req.owned_kv_len())` keys `(origin_input_ids + output_ids)[:kv_committed_len]`. So it is cached with 32,769 tokens, its output token included.
2. `cleanup_after_caching_req` (`swa.py:1011`, the `not is_finished` guard at `:1023`) frees out-of-window SWA only for unfinished requests. So the request's final 8,192-token chunk keeps its SWA live. In the tree that is a node `[24,576, 32,641)` holding 8,065 live SWA slots, then the 128-token window leaf that `_maybe_split_leaf_for_swa_lock` (`swa.py:555`) capped "so locking it pins only one window".
3. Request 2 diverges at position 32,768, so its match splits the window leaf into 127 + 1. `acquire_component_lock` (`swa.py:811`) pins whole nodes until it has covered 128 tokens: the 127-token node, then the whole 8,065-token parent. **8,192 slots pinned** for a 128-token window.
4. `SWAPrefillBudget.check_prefill` (`prefill_budget.py:213`) sees 5,001 needed and 259 available. Since 5,001 fits an empty pool, it is not a permanent shortfall ("Transient pressure waits"), so the request waits for running requests to free slots. None exist.

The bound: only an untrimmed final chunk holds more than about one window of live SWA, so the lock over-pins by at most one chunk, while a request needs at most one chunk + 1. A pool of 2 × chunk + window + slack therefore always leaves enough (by 258 slots here), and one of chunk + window + slack, as above, can deadlock whenever a request reuses the path of one that finished at its first token (`max_tokens=1`, an immediate EOS or stop) and diverges inside its last window.

### Reproduction

- End to end: on a GPU (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) with SGLang at 542a043, reproduced with the sequence above. That build carries local changes (an MoE expert-offload tier, and #41263's chunked-prefill SWA free order); none of them changes the radix tree, the SWA lock or `check_prefill` (#41263 only moves when a chunked request's out-of-window SWA is freed).
- On CPU, on the same build: the same four steps, with the scheduler's own `UnifiedRadixCache`, SWA allocator and `PrefillAdder` plus the orphan decode step, give 259 / 5,001 available / needed (not admitted) at chunk 8,192 / pool 8,451, and admit at chunk 4,096 (4,355 / 4,097) and at pool 16,643 (8,451 / 5,001).
- On `main`: the unit test in the linked PR builds a live parent + capped window leaf, matches a key that diverges on the last page and locks it; the lock pins the whole parent. Links 1, 2 and 4 are unchanged in the code on `main`; we have not run the end-to-end sequence on `main`.

### Proposed fix

In the lock walk, split a live, unlocked device-SWA node that is longer than what the window still needs, so only the in-window tail is pinned (the same idea as the leaf cap, applied to whatever node the walk reaches). PR: #41580.

Related: #27210 caps compute locks by splitting the lock's endpoint node. It does not cover this case: at page size 1 the match ends inside the capped leaf, the endpoint is shorter than a window, and the over-pin comes from its parent. #32379 fixed a different SWA admission livelock (decode headroom double-counted for cached resumes).

### Environment

SGLang 542a043 (end to end) and `main` 6624999385 (unit test), CUDA 13.0, torch cu130, one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm120), `--tp-size 1`, radix cache on, overlap scheduler on.

items.title: [Bug][KV Cache] nvfp4 KV silently reuses the checkpoint's fp8-calibrated k/v_scale as NVFP4 global scale → deterministic long-context corruption (single-variable proof, sm_120)
items.author: chengye75-star
items.body_excerpt:
## TL;DR

Serving an NVFP4 KV cache (`--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) on a checkpoint whose `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme` says `num_bits: 8` (e.g. unsloth's NVFP4 quants, which ship fp8-calibrated `k_scale`/`v_scale`) silently corrupts the KV cache: 32 tiny `[1]` bf16 scalars are loaded verbatim and consumed as the NVFP4 **global scale**. Removing exactly those 64 **bytes** flips long-context needle from 1/4 to 4/4 on an otherwise bit-identical 22.5 GB checkpoint. No log line ever mentions scales. Related but distinct: [#36121](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/36121) (fp4 scales not traveling through HiCache host transfers; footnote has our hybrid-path measurement), [#39942](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/39942) (fp8 KV scales silently *dropped* — opposite failure, same blind spot: nothing validates KV scale provenance).

## Setup

SGLang 0.5.21 (official PyPI wheel), torch 2.13.0+cu130, 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (sm_120, TP2), driver 595.91.07. Model: `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` (hybrid 16 full-attention + 48 GDN layers, head_dim 256, compressed-tensors). Flags: `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4 --prefill-attention-backend flashinfer --decode-attention-backend trtllm_mha --disable-prefill-cuda-graph --context-length 195000 --page-size 64`, greedy, chat format. (Same rig as my [#36010 evidence post](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/36010#issuecomment-5788493111); this bug is **independent of spec decode** — it hits the plain no-spec nvfp4 path.)

## Symptom

With scales as shipped, long-context retrieval collapses: needle **1/4 (d50) / 0/4 (d500)**; answers degenerate into question-echoing after a short thinking block. Everything else looks healthy — boot logs clean, short prompts / tool calls / vision normal. Deterministic: completion tokens reproduce byte-for-byte across boots and repeats.

## Root cause (source walk; mechanism marked as inference)

1. The checkpoint carries 32 per-layer `*.self_attn.{k,v}_scale` tensors — `[1]` bf16 scalars calibrated for **fp8** KV (`config.json → kv_cache_scheme: {num_bits: 8, static_minmax, symmetric}`).
2. *(inference, from source)* At load, `weight_utils.maybe_remap_kv_scale_name()` attaches them to the attention modules unconditionally; the fp4 path (`layers/attention/kvfp4_tensor.py`, comment: *"The KV cache path passes preloaded per-layer scales already on device"*) consumes them as the NVFP4 `global_scale` in `x_fp4 * block_scale * global_scale`.
3. *(inference)* Nothing validates the checkpoint's KV scheme against the runtime `--kv-cache-dtype`. An fp8-geometry scalar (amax/448 family) applied under NVFP4 geometry (amax/6 family) is off by ~75× → every stored K/V is systematically mis-scaled.

## Single-variable proof (same box, same day, same prompts)

| config (one variable per row) | needle d50 | needle d500 |
|---|---|---|
| unsloth + nvfp4, scales as shipped | 1/4 | 0/4 |
| **unsloth + nvfp4, 32 scale tensors stripped (64 bytes total), `kv_cache_scheme=null`** | **4/4** | **4/4** |
| unsloth + fp8_e4m3 (scale geometry matches dtype) | 4/4 | 2/4 |
| `sakamakismile/Qwen3.8-27B-MTP-NVFP4` + nvfp4 (checkpoint ships no scales) | 4/4 | 1/4 |

The stripped copy is a hardlink farm with only `model.safetensors` rewritten (header offsets recomputed; post-check: 0 leftover scale tensors) — the rest of the ~22.5 GB is byte-identical. Same-checkpoint before/after is the control: 64 bytes of metadata move the score by three needle questions.

## Why this is not an edge case

The filename pairing (`…-NVFP4` weights + `--kv-cache-dtype nvfp4`) is the natural reading, and unsloth's NVFP4 releases ship fp8-calibrated KV scales as a matter of their recipe. Everyone doing that pairing gets silently wrong KV with zero log evidence; needle-style evals are the only thing that notices, and most people don't run those. Checkpoints without shipped scales (dynamic path, row 4) are unaffected — which is presumably why this hasn't surfaced loudly.

## Asks

1. **Validate at load**: if the checkpoint carries `k_scale`/`v_scale` and `kv_cache_scheme.num_bits` disagrees with `server_args.kv_cache_dtype`, warn loudly and skip them (fall back to dynamic scales) instead of reinterpreting an fp8 scalar as an fp4 global scale.
2. Checkpoints whose scheme says `num_bits: 4` (e.g. NVIDIA/ModelOpt NVFP4-KV exports) *should* consume their scales — the bug is specifically the mismatched pair, not scale loading per se.
3. Optional `--load-kv-scales {auto,never}` for quick A/B without safetensors surgery (our workaround rewrites a 22 GB file's header — works in 3 minutes, but terrifying to recommend).

## Verified workaround & production numbers

Drop the 32 `*.self_attn.[kv]_scale` tensors from `model.safetensors`, rewrite header offsets, set `quantization_config.kv_cache_scheme = null`. The healthy config now serves our production: 185K-token cold prefill ~176 s, decode ~25 tok/s; with HiCache L2 (20 GB host, `write_through`, `page_first`, slru) a post-eviction 185K re-ask lands in **2.4–5.5 s** (vs 178 s cold) with the secret code word intact across the L2 round-trip (2/2 rounds, backup counters confirm real transfers); needle 4/4+4/4; tool-calls live. sm_120 hybrid-attention reference points are thin here — happy to post logs/transcripts.

Footnote re #36121: its fail-fast covers paths our hybrid assembly doesn't traverse (UnifiedRadixCache picks host pools in `hybrid_pool_assembler`), and in our exact combo (nvfp4 + HiCache + page_first + write_through) the fp4 block scales evidently *do* survive L2 as measured above — so the guard as drafted wouldn't cover this configuration either way. Full hybrid-path measurements posted as a review note on that PR.

items.title: [Bug] DFlash2/DSpark + prefix caching corrupt output after a cache hit on Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (compressed-tensors) on 0.30/0.31; 0.29, FP8 target and MTP are fine
items.author: sinmkd
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

- vLLM 0.31.0 (also reproduced on 0.30.0). vLLM 0.29.0 passes the same test.
- torch 2.13.0+cu130, flashinfer-python/cubin 0.7.0.post1 (0.6.18.post1 on 0.30.0), CUDA 13.3, driver 610.57.04
- 1× RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell 48 GB (sm_120), Ubuntu 24.04, kernel 7.0.0-34
- Target: `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B` NVFP4 checkpoint, compressed-tensors mixed precision (NVFP4 on the MLP projections, FP8 W8A8 on attention / GDN projections / lm_head, `linear_attn.{in_proj_a,in_proj_b,norm}` and `mtp.*` unquantized via `ignore`)
- Drafter: `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` (`DFlash2DraftModel`, sliding_window 2048), `num_speculative_tokens: 7`

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Since 0.30.0, serving Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 with the DFlash2 drafter and prefix caching enabled produces garbage after a prefix-cache hit. The first requests of a conversation are fine. From the third request on, once the prompt resumes from cached blocks, the model emits a single repeated token (`duct`, over and over) with no coherent content, and the drafter accepts nothing (`SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted: 0 tokens`). The same five requests against 0.29.0 come back coherent every time. I have run the comparison twice on each version.

The test is a replay of a real agent conversation: five consecutive chat-completions requests from one session (31,776 / 45,606 / 52,737 / 65,364 / 67,502 prompt tokens, 25 tool schemas, seed 17), sent in order to a fresh engine so each request hits the previous one's prefix. The conversation itself is private, but I can build a synthetic equivalent if that helps.

Serve command (production flags):

```
vllm serve /models/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 --max-model-len 250000 --kv-cache-memory-bytes 17379961324 \
  --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","model":"/models/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2","num_speculative_tokens":7}' \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder --reasoning-parser qwen3 \
  --override-generation-config '{"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":20,"min_p":0.0}' --scheduling-policy priority
```

env: `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=0 VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING=false`. Prefix caching on (default), `mamba_cache_mode` resolves to `align`.

### What I tried, to narrow it down

All on 0.31.0, same five requests, fresh engine each time:

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| nothing (command above) | fails at request 3 |
| PR #57128 applied (the `MambaManager.find_longest_cache_hit` / `drop_eagle_block` fix) | fails |
| `--gdn-prefill-backend triton` instead of FlashInfer | fails |
| `--linear-backend cutlass` (in-tree CUTLASS NVFP4 GEMM) | fails |
| `--linear-backend marlin` (weight-only W4A16, no activation quant) | fails |
| smaller KV pool / 180K window / util 0.94 (copied from my FP8 route) | fails |
| `"disable_eagle_block_drop": true` in the speculative config | worse: garbage from request 1, even cold |
| **no speculative config at all** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}` (checkpoint's own MTP head)** | **passes 5/5** |
| **`{"method":"dspark","model":"RedHatAI/Qwen3.8-27B-speculator.dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7}`** | **fails at request 3** |
| **FP8 target (`Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8`, `quant_method: fp8`) with the same DFlash2 config** | **passes 5/5, twice** |

A unique `cache_salt` per request on 0.30.0 also makes requests 3–5 pass, so the failure needs an actual cache hit.

So the NVFP4 GEMM kernels are not involved (three different kernels, including weight-only, all fail), the GDN prefill kernel is not involved, and the KV pool size is not involved. What it needs is: a hidden-state drafter (DFlash2 or DSpark; MTP is fine) + a prefix-cache hit + this compressed-tensors NVFP4 target, on 0.30 or later. The FP8 checkpoint with the identical drafter config is fine. Turning off the EAGLE trailing-block drop makes it strictly worse, which reads to me like the drafter is leaving bad Mamba/GDN state in the cached tail block and the drop normally hides it inside a request but not across requests.

The compressed-tensors checkpoint is the obvious difference from the FP8 one: it has an `ignore` list covering `linear_attn` sub-modules (the bf16 `in_proj_a` / `in_proj_b` / `norm`) alongside `config_groups` that target `linear_attn.{in_proj_qkv,in_proj_z,out_proj}` at FP8. If the drafter path resolves those layers differently from the plain `fp8` loader, that would be where I'd look first, but I haven't gone further than the table above.

Related: #53912 and #55766 describe neighbouring hybrid-GDN prefix-cache corruption with speculative decoding.

### What I can provide

Per-request replay output (prompt token counts, finish reasons, draft metrics), engine logs for every ablation above, and a synthetic reproducer on request.

items.title: [Feature] L1/L2/L3 cache hit rate observability — Prometheus metrics, OTel spans & per-request JSONL trace
items.author: grissomsh
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation

LMCache's current `PrometheusLogger` provides basic metrics (`time_to_retrieve`, `num_retrieve_requests`), but is missing:

1. **Per-tier cache hit rate** — no way to distinguish whether a hit came from L2 (CPU RAM), L3 (NVMe Disk), or a remote backend.
2. **TTFT decomposition** — `frontend_latency` (API server → engine core) and per-request `kv_lookup_time` / `kv_retrieve_time` are not surfaced.
3. **Per-request tracing** — no way to correlate cache-hit details to an individual request for debugging latency spikes.

These gaps make it hard to answer operational questions like: *"Why did TTFT spike — was it a slow disk read, CPU cache contention, or GPU prefix cache eviction?"*

---

### Design Goals

1. **Three-layer observability model**: throughput → latency → cache hit rate
2. **Minimally invasive**: extend existing `LMCStatsMonitor`, `PrometheusLogger`, and `cache_engine` — no breaking API changes
3. **TP-aware**: cross-process bridge via `/dev/shm` for Worker ↔ EngineCore per-request data relay when TP > 1
4. **Self-verifying**: every trace carries token identity equations for automated correctness validation

---

### Proposed Design

#### Layer 1 — Throughput: Token Source Decomposition

```
Tokens/s = local_compute + L1_hit + L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit
```

**Approach**: Extend `cache_engine.py`'s `retrieve()` / `retrieve_layer()` to classify hit tokens by storage backend. Add a `_BACKEND_NAME_TO_HIT_TIER` mapping:

| Backend | Tier |
|---------|------|
| `LocalCPUBackend` | L2 |
| `LocalDiskBackend` / `GdsBackend` | L3 |
| `RemoteBackend` | Remote |

**New Prometheus metrics** (6 total):

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

#### Layer 2 — Latency: TTFT Decomposition

```
TTFT = frontend_latency + queue_time + prefill_time
prefill_time ⊃ kv_lookup_time + kv_retrieve_time
```

**Approach**: Add `LMCacheKVConnectorStats` (extending vLLM's `KVConnectorStats`) on the vLLM side, and expose per-request timing through `vllm_v1_adapter.py`'s `request_finished()` via `EngineCoreOutput.kv_transfer_params`.

**New Prometheus metrics** (9 bridge metrics + 1 framework metric):

| Metric | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram | KV lookup latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram | KV retrieve latency |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: process_tokens phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram | Retrieve: CPU→GPU DMA phase |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L2 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side L3 bridge |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter | vLLM-side remote bridge |
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram | API server → engine core latency |

#### Layer 3 — Cache Hit Rate & Per-Request Trace

One JSONL `[trace]` line emitted per request at completion:

```json
{
  "ts": 1782023561.679,
  "rid": "chatcmpl-xxx",
  "prompt_tokens": 3934,
  "output_tokens": 32,
  "TTFT_ms": 169.2,
  "queue_ms": 0.04,
  "prefill_ms": 130.1,
  "decode_ms": 144.6,
  "e2e_ms": 314.3,
  "frontend_ms": 39.0,
  "input_tokens_cache_hit": 3840,
  "L1_hit": 0,
  "external_kv_hit": 3840,
  "L2_hit": 0,
  "L3_hit": 3840,
  "remote_hit": 0,
  "input_tokens_no_cache_hit": 94,
  "kv_transfer_mode": "non_layerwise",
  "kv_lookup_ms": 1.2,
  "kv_retrieve_ms": 101.5
}
```

**Token identity equations** (verifiable by automated scripts at runtime):

```
prompt_tokens = input_tokens_cache_hit + input_tokens_no_cache_hit
input_tokens_cache_hit = L1_hit + external_kv_hit
external_kv_hit ≈ L2_hit + L3_hit + remote_hit   (≈ due to chunk_size=256 granularity)
```

#### Cross-Process Bridge (TP > 1)

When TP > 1, `retrieve()` runs on Worker_TP0 while `request_finished()` runs on the EngineCore/scheduler process. Per-request data is relayed via file-based bridge in `/dev/shm/lmcache_bridge/` (tmpfs, memory-backed):

- Per-tier counters: file + `fcntl.flock` for atomic cross-process updates
- Timing data: `write-tmp + os.replace` for atomic JSON
- Cleanup: throttled periodic sweep + retry limit (3) to prevent `/dev/shm` exhaustion

#### OTel Span Attributes

8 attributes on the `"llm_request"` span:

| Attribute | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_frontend` | API → engine |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_lookup` | KV lookup |
| `gen_ai.latency.time_in_kv_transfer` | KV retrieve |
| `gen_ai.usage.l1_hit_tokens` | L1 (GPU prefix cache) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l2_hit_tokens` | L2 (CPU RAM) |
| `gen_ai.usage.l3_hit_tokens` | L3 (NVMe/SSD) |
| `gen_ai.usage.remote_hit_tokens` | Remote backend |
| `gen_ai.latency.kv_transfer_mode` | layerwise / non_layerwise |

---

### Metrics Summary (16 new Prometheus metrics)

**LMCache side (6):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `lmcache:l2_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l2_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:l3_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_l3_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |
| `lmcache:remote_hit_tokens` / `lmcache:num_remote_hit_tokens` | Histogram + Counter |

**vLLM bridge (9):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_lookup_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_retrieve_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_process_tokens_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_retrieve_to_gpu_seconds` | Histogram |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l2_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_l3_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_num_remote_hit_tokens` | Counter |
| `vllm:lmcache_kv_transfer_mode` | Info |

**vLLM framework (1):**

| Metric | Type |
|--------|------|
| `vllm:request_frontend_latency_seconds` | Histogram |

---

### Verification

The design has been validated end

items.title: [Bug][MP] lmcache_mp.l1_read counts released read reservations even when no GPU retrieve occurs
items.author: 0andy
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

`lmcache_mp.l1_read` is documented as "Number of chunks read from L1"
(`docs/source/mp/observability/metrics.rst`).

However, the counter also increments when L1 read reservations are only
released and no LMCache-driven CPU→GPU retrieve is submitted.

With the vLLM connector, this can happen when the requested prefix is already
available in vLLM's local GPU prefix cache.

LMCache lookup/prefetch finds the matching chunks and retains/read-locks them.
Later, `update_state_after_alloc()` determines that no external retrieve is
needed and calls `free_lookup_locks()`.

That path eventually reaches `L1Manager.finish_read()`, which publishes
`L1_READ_FINISHED`. The `lmcache_mp.l1_read` metric therefore increases even
though no LMCache-driven retrieve was submitted.

In my repro:

- 5 retained L1 keys with no retrieve caused `l1_read` to increase by 5.
- Another 6 retained L1 keys with no retrieve caused it to increase by 6.
- After restarting vLLM, the same 6 retained keys were actually retrieved from
  L1, and `l1_read` again increased by 6.

So `lmcache_mp.l1_read` increases by the number of retained/released keys in
both cases and does not distinguish a real retrieve from a lookup reservation
that is later released unused.

---

**To Reproduce**

Environment:

- LMCache dev @ `1ca53a8a` (`0.5.6rc3.dev31`)
- vLLM `0.30.0`
- MP mode
- ZMQ transport
- `lmcache_driven` transfer
- `--chunk-size 16`
- 1x A100

Steps:

1. Start the LMCache MP server with `--chunk-size 16`.
2. Start one vLLM instance using `LMCacheMPConnector`.
3. Send prompt P (85 tokens) once to populate the cache.
4. Send P plus a short suffix (97 tokens) twice using the same vLLM process.
5. Observe the LMCache logs and `/metrics`.
6. Restart only vLLM, leaving the LMCache server running.
7. Send the same P + suffix request again from the fresh vLLM process.
8. Compare `lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total` with the actual retrieve metrics.

Observed before restarting vLLM:

```text
=== 1: P, cold ===
Stored 80 tokens
Stored 16 tokens
lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 6.0
(no l1_read)
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)

=== 2: P + suffix, same vLLM process ===
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 5/6 retained keys (5 L1, 0 L2) in 1.2 ms
Stored 16 tokens
Stored 16 tokens
(no "Retrieved" line)

lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 8.0
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 5.0
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)

=== 3: same request again, same vLLM process ===
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 6/6 retained keys (6 L1, 0 L2) in 0.9 ms
Stored 16 tokens
(no "Retrieved" line)

lmcache_mp_l1_write_chunks_total 9.0
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 11.0
(no num_submitted_retrieves / num_finished_retrieves)
```

The `l1_read` counter increased:

```text
0 -> 5    (+5)
5 -> 11   (+6)
```

exactly matching the number of retained keys, while no GPU retrieve was
submitted.

The extra `Stored 16 tokens` in step 3 is unrelated to this issue. The two
requests produced different completions, so the final chunk containing
generated tokens differed.

As a control, I then restarted vLLM while keeping the same LMCache server
running. This removes vLLM's local GPU prefix cache, so the cached prefix has
to be retrieved from LMCache.

The same request then produced:

```text
Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 6/6 retained keys (6 L1, 0 L2) in 1.7 ms
Retrieved 96 tokens in 0.001 seconds

lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 17.0
lmcache_mp_num_submitted_retrieves_total{device="cuda:0"} 1.0
lmcache_mp_num_finished_retrieves_total{device="cuda:0"} 1.0
```

The previous reading, taken after step 3, was:

```text
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total 11.0
```

No other requests were sent in between, so the real retrieve also increased
`l1_read` by exactly 6:

```text
11 -> 17   (+6)
```

This gives the following A/B comparison:

```text
Case A: 6/6 retained, no retrieve
l1_read +6
num_submitted_retrieves +0
num_finished_retrieves +0

Case B: 6/6 retained, real CPU->GPU retrieve
l1_read +6
num_submitted_retrieves +1
num_finished_retrieves +1
```

`lmcache_mp.l1_read` therefore grows by the same amount in both cases. Only the
`num_*_retrieves` metrics distinguish whether a real retrieve occurred.

Relevant code path at `1ca53a8a`:

- `lmcache/v1/mp_observability/subscribers/metrics/l1.py:49`

  `L1MetricsSubscriber` subscribes to `L1_READ_FINISHED`.

- `lmcache/v1/distributed/l1_manager.py:433`

  `finish_read()` publishes one `L1_READ_FINISHED` event containing the keys
  whose read locks were released; the metric subscriber counts those keys.

- `lmcache/integration/vllm/lmcache_mp_connector.py:1381` →
  `lmcache/v1/multiprocess/modules/lookup.py:481`

  `free_lookup_locks()` → `finish_read_prefetched()` → `finish_read()`,
  without a data-transfer request on the no-retrieve path.

---

**Expected behavior**

The metric semantics and documentation should be consistent.

If `lmcache_mp.l1_read` is intended to represent chunks actually read from L1,
it should not increase for the `free_lookup_locks()` path when no retrieve was
submitted.

If it is intentionally a read-reservation lifecycle counter, its description
should make that clear and documentation should not use it as proof that a
retrieve occurred.

This is especially relevant because the SGLang quickstart
(`docs/source/getting_started/quickstart.rst`) currently tells users they can
"confirm the retrieve" by checking:

```text
lmcache_mp_l1_read_chunks_total
```

The repro above shows that this counter can increase even when no
LMCache-driven retrieve was submitted.

I reproduced the no-retrieve behavior with the vLLM connector. I have not
tested whether the same no-retrieve path is reachable through SGLang.

---

**Screenshots**

Not required for reproduction. The relevant LMCache server logs and metric
values are included above.

---

**Desktop (please complete the following information):**

- OS: Ubuntu 24.04
- Browser: N/A
- LMCache: `1ca53a8a` (`0.5.6rc3.dev31`)
-

items.title: Unauthenticated fleet control plane on LMCache MP Coordinator (default 0.0.0.0:9300)
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

The LMCache MP Coordinator — the fleet-level cache control plane — starts by default on 0.0.0.0:9300 with no authentication on any endpoint. A network peer registers fake cache instances, deregisters real ones (removing them from scheduling), rewrites tenant quotas, injects fabricated cache events, and enumerates the fleet's key directory. Runtime-confirmed on lmcache 0.5.5 (latest PyPI release); the companion controller API server (`lmcache.v1.api_server`, default 0.0.0.0:9000) exposes the same unauthenticated /lookup, /clear and /pin surface. Suggested severity: High, CVSS 8.8.

### Details

`lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator.config` hardcodes `host: str = "0.0.0.0", port: int = 9300`. The coordinator's FastAPI app (`lmcache/v1/mp_coordinator/app.py`) mounts routers with no authentication middleware anywhere in the package (a full-source scan for api_key/auth/token primitives returns zero hits):

- `POST /instances` / `PUT /instances/{id}/heartbeat` / `DELETE /instances/{id}` — anyone registers, keeps alive, or removes fleet instances; deletion removes the instance's reported placements from scheduling.
- `PUT /quota/config` and `PUT /quota/{cache_salt}` — fleet and per-tenant quota tampering.
- `POST /cache/pins`, `DELETE /cache/pins`, `POST /events` — pin manipulation and fabricated cache events that feed the coordinator's placement/eviction views.
- `GET /directory/keys` (paged), `POST /directory/lookup`, `POST /directory/blend-lookup` — full key directory with token-id lists and per-instance placements.

The controller API server (`lmcache/v1/api_server/__main__.py`, `--host` default 0.0.0.0, port 9000) adds `POST /lookup` (token-to-placement layout), `POST /clear` and `POST /pin` for any instance_id, likewise with no authentication.

### PoC

Environment: Linux, `pip install lmcache==0.5.5`, `python -m lmcache.v1.mp_coordinator --host 0.0.0.0 --port 9300` (`ss -ltnp` confirms 0.0.0.0:9300). From any peer:

```bash
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/healthz                       # 200
# register a fake instance (schemas read from the installed package's pydantic models)
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @fake_instance.json   # 200/201
curl -s http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances                      # fake instance listed
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-aaa/heartbeat -d @hb.json      # 200
# remove an instance from the fleet
curl -s -X DELETE http://192.168.105.123:9300/instances/attacker-mp-bbb                          # 200
# quota tampering and event injection
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/config -d @quota.json                           # 200
curl -s -X PUT http://192.168.105.123:9300/quota/default -d '{"...": 0}'                         # 200
curl -s -X POST http://192.168.105.123:9300/events -d @fake_events.json                          # 200
# fleet key directory
curl -s "http://192.168.105.123:9300/directory/keys?limit=100"                                   # keys+placements
```

Observed on 0.5.5: every call above succeeded without any credential; the fake instance appeared in `GET /instances`, the DELETE removed an instance, quota writes were accepted, `/events` accepted a fabricated batch, and `/directory/keys` returned the directory enumeration surface. The api_server on 0.0.0.0:9000 likewise answered unauthenticated `/lookup` (200 with layout structure) and accepted `/clear` and `/pin` requests. Expected secure behavior: a fleet control plane authenticates callers and authorizes instance/quota mutations.

### Impact

Any network peer that can reach the coordinator port (fixed, documented default 9300, bound on all interfaces) corrupts the fleet's shared cache state: deregistered workers disappear from placement (requests lose their cache or fail over), fake instances redirect placement decisions, quota tampering starves or floods tenants, injected events poison placement and eviction views, and the key directory discloses which prefixes (token id lists) are cached where across the fleet. Confidentiality (directory/placement disclosure), integrity (fleet membership, quotas, events), availability (instance removal, quota starvation). Suggested CVSS:3.1 vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:H (8.8), CWE-306. Affected: lmcache <= 0.5.5 (latest release), deployments running the MP coordinator / controller API server; no patched version yet.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.author: NeedForSpeed73
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

llama-server --version
version: 0.3.0-dev (build 10731, commit 0eadefebd)
built with GNU 15.2.0 for Linux x86_64

[repro_test.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31701373/repro_test.py)

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server --model Qwen3-Coder-Next-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf --ctx-size 65536 --gpu-layers 999 --split-mode layer --tensor-split 4,1 --n-cpu-moe 34 --flash-attn on --parallel 1 --jinja --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With --tensor-split active, on sessions with growing multi-turn context, the model intermittently degenerates into repetitive/mechanical output instead of following the actual content. Failure modes observed:

A single response ballooning to ~14 MB / 15+ minutes (vs. 6-45 KB / 7-70s for normal responses in the same session).
A consolidated list repeating the same claim ~55 times with only line numbers incrementing, referencing line numbers up to 3281 in a 543-line source file — the model is extending a numeric pattern rather than reading the file.
Milder cases: citing the same line reference twice in a row with vague trailing qualifiers ("ecc.") as if running out of distinct content to report.

Crucially, this reproduces independently of the client. Initially observed via an agentic coding client (Cline, over the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with tool calls). To rule out client-specific causes (prompt structure, tool-call formatting), I wrote a minimal Python script that sends the same codebase directly via /v1/chat/completions, one file per turn, maintaining conversation history, followed by a final consolidation request — no tool calls, no agent framework, plain multi-turn text. Result: 1 of 2 runs was clean, 1 showed the same degeneration pattern (case 3 above). This matches the intermittent nature also seen with Cline (3 collapsed / 2 clean over Cline sessions).

This does NOT occur on short tasks (1-3 calls) with the same --tensor-split config, nor across multiple long-context runs with the identical command minus --tensor-split (0 collapses observed there).

Additional observation

Even where --tensor-split doesn't cause degeneration, it barely rebalances actual per-GPU compute load: MoE experts stay almost entirely on one device regardless of the split ratio tried; only non-MoE tensors seem affected by the split value. --main-gpu had no effect on the imbalance either.

Question for maintainers: does this look like a numerical-stability edge case in how --tensor-split interacts with --n-cpu-moe on MoE models at long context, or something else worth narrowing down further?

items.title: [RFC]: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference（CCF 赛题四）
items.author: Pinoeer-kingxi
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

<!-- GitHub-safe plain Markdown. Copy from the raw .md text, not from Word or a rich-text preview. -->

# RFC: EPD Disaggregation and Cooperative Scheduling for Agentic Multimodal Inference

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| RFC | RFC-EPD-Agent-Multimodal-2026 |
| Status | Draft |
| Date | 2026-07-05 |
| Target Project | Mooncake / Mooncake Transfer Engine / MooncakeStore |
| Target Integrations | vLLM, SGLang, Qwen-VL/Qwen3-VL-style multimodal models |
| Scope | Encoder-Prefill-Decode disaggregation, Agent state cloning, cross-step KV reuse, evaluation protocol |
| Primary Audience | Mooncake maintainers, serving-system contributors, vLLM/SGLang integration reviewers |
| Implementation Horizon | One-month prototype milestone, followed by staged hardening |
| Compatibility Target | Preserve existing PD and colocated serving paths; new features must be gated by configuration |

---

## Summary

This RFC proposes an extension to Mooncake for **agentic multimodal inference**. The core idea is to generalize Mooncake's KVCache-centric disaggregated serving capability from a two-stage Prefill-Decode model into a broader **Encoder-Prefill-Decode (EPD)** architecture, while also supporting:

- **Agent state cloning** for multi-branch reasoning;
- **visual feature caching** for repeated image/document contexts;
- **cross-step KV reuse** for repeated workflow prefixes;
- **tool-call offload/restore** to release GPU memory during blocking I/O;
- **A2A handoff** for state transfer among planner, executor, verifier, and domain agents;
- **coordinated scheduling** across Encoder, Prefill, Decode, and storage resources.

The proposal introduces a unified `MultimodalState` abstraction that represents visual feature bundles, textual/multimodal KV pages, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, TTL, and ownership.

The design intentionally avoids a single global strongly-consistent KV registry. Instead, it uses:

1. **KV Directory** for eventually consistent metadata lookup;
2. **Workflow Shards** for per-workflow strong consistency, refcount, CAS, fork, release, and CoW;
3. **Decentralized Scheduler** for admission control, priority scheduling, offload/restore, and A2A-aware routing.

For KV reuse correctness, the RFC uses a conservative default:

> **Exact Prefix Reuse by default; Approximate Reuse only behind validation gates and feature flags.**

Approximate reuse is never required for correctness. If any validation step fails, the system falls back to exact prefix reuse or full Prefill.

---

## Motivation

### Multimodal inference is naturally EPD-shaped

Multimodal inference contains three computationally different stages:

1. **Encoder**: image/video/audio features are produced by a modality encoder.
2. **Prefill**: the language model processes the full multimodal prompt and builds KV cache.
3. **Decode**: autoregressive generation produces output tokens.

Traditional PD disaggregation couples Encoder with Prefill. This becomes inefficient when the same multimodal context appears repeatedly across turns, agent steps, or branch candidates. Separating Encoder from Prefill enables:

- independent scaling of visual encoder workers;
- reuse of visual features across turns and workflows;
- lower repeated prefill cost for multimodal prompts;
- more flexible routing for prefill-heavy versus decode-heavy workloads.

### Agent workflows require persistent state

Agent workloads are not simple one-shot requests. They involve:

- multi-turn conversations;
- external tool calls and long I/O waits;
- multi-branch reasoning such as Tree-of-Thought, beam search, and verifier branches;
- A2A handoff between planner, executor, retriever, tool agent, and verifier;
- repeated prefixes across workflow steps.

These patterns make KV state a first-class runtime object rather than a temporary per-request artifact.

### Mooncake is well positioned for this extension

Mooncake already focuses on disaggregated KVCache management and high-performance transfer. Extending it to EPD and agentic workflows is a natural next step because the same core primitives are needed:

- cross-node tensor transfer;
- distributed KVCache pooling;
- offload and restore;
- memory ownership;
- scheduling across heterogeneous workers;
- efficient movement of large intermediate states.

This RFC defines a practical architecture that can be implemented incrementally and reviewed in stages.

---

## Goals

This RFC has the following goals.

### G1. Support EPD disaggregation

- Separate Vision Encoder, Prefill, and Decode into independently schedulable workers.
- Transfer Encoder outputs to Prefill and Prefill KV pages to Decode through Mooncake Transfer Engine.
- Preserve fallback paths to normal colocated or PD-only execution.

### G2. Introduce a unified multimodal state abstraction

- Represent FeatureBundle, KVPage, workflow metadata, state versions, fork branches, leases, and TTL.
- Support snapshot-based state reads, page-level refcount, and Copy-on-Write.
- Provide clear lifecycle transitions for active, shared, offloaded, restored, released, and aborted states.

### G3. Support Agent State Cloning

- Enable low-cost fork for multi-branch reasoning.
- Avoid deep-copying full KV state for each branch.
- Make branch writes safe through page-level CoW.
- Make refcount correctness testable and observable.

### G4. Support cross-step KV reuse

- Use exact prefix reuse as the safe default.
- Add approximate or non-contiguous reuse behind validation gates and feature flags.
- Always preserve fallback to full Prefill.

### G5. Reduce control-plane bottlenecks

- Avoid a globally locked GDKR-style metadata service.
- Move refcount and CAS to workflow-local shards.
- Keep cross-workflow metadata eventually consistent with bounded staleness.
- Prevent a single hot workflow or global registry from throttling unrelated workflows.

### G6. Provide a reproducible evaluation protocol

- Define datasets, workload construction, ba

items.title: [Bug][TE] TCP transport: first transfer after an idle gap fails with queue-full rejections; PD decode hangs until timeout
items.author: CAICAIIs
items.body_excerpt:
## environment

- mooncake-transfer-engine **0.3.13.post1** (PyPI wheel); also reproduced on the **0.3.14rc1** release wheel
- vLLM 0.29.0 (built-in `MooncakeConnector`), 1 node, disaggregated prefill/decode (1P1D) on one host
- 2× NVIDIA H20 96GB (one GPU per instance), TCP transport (`mooncake_protocol: "tcp"`, `MC_FORCE_TCP=1`; RDMA path not usable on this host)
- Qwen/Qwen3-8B

## 🐛 Describe the bug

With the TCP transport, the **first KV transfer between two engine instances succeeds, but a transfer submitted after a short idle gap (~5 s) fails**: on the producer, every slice of the batch is rejected by the TCP lane queue (`TCP lane queue-full rejection count: 1 → 2 → 4 → ... → 512+` within milliseconds), `batch_transfer_sync_write` returns -1, and the error is relayed to the consumer (`pulling kv_caches for [...] failed: Mooncake transfer engine returned -1`).

The consumer request then stays in `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` (`Deferred: 1`) and the client hangs until its own timeout. A request sent **~90 s later succeeds**, so deployments observe either 60-90 s TTFT spikes after every idle period or outright request failures, depending on client timeout.

## How to reproduce

1. Start P and D with the built-in vLLM `MooncakeConnector` over TCP (single host; any router that fires the prefill and decode requests concurrently works, e.g. `examples/disaggregated/mooncake_connector/mooncake_connector_proxy.py`):

```bash
# prefill (GPU 0)
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B --port 8111 --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
  --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 4 --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.60 --no-enable-prefix-caching \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MooncakeConnector","kv_role":"kv_producer","kv_connector_extra_config":{"mooncake_protocol":"tcp"}}'
# decode (GPU 1)
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B --port 8112 --tensor-parallel-size 1 ... \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"MooncakeConnector","kv_role":"kv_consumer","kv_connector_extra_config":{"mooncake_protocol":"tcp"}}'
```

2. Send a completion request through the router → **succeeds** (P logs `Sending to ... done, took 0.18 s`).
3. Wait ~5 s. Send it again → **hangs until client timeout**. P side:

```
W tcp_transport_lane_impl.h:1330] TCP lane queue-full rejection count: 1
W tcp_transport_lane_impl.h:1330] TCP lane queue-full rejection count: 2
... doubling up to 512+ within one millisecond ...
E mooncake_connector.py:1877] pulling kv_caches for ['cmpl-...'] failed: Mooncake transfer engine returned -1
```

4. Send it again ~90 s after step 3 → **succeeds again**.

Consistently reproduced on two machines (H20 and A100), multiple runs. Also reproduced with `MC_TCP_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT_MS=60000` (failure shape changes: the batch is not hard-rejected but still never transfers).

## Analysis

After a transfer completes and the peer connection group goes idle, the group is **retired** — all lanes are closed and `group->state` is set to `CLOSED` (`tcp_transport_lane_impl.h`, retirement block). A submission that arrives shortly after finds the group via `state->groups.find(key)`, sees `group->state != GroupState::OPEN`, and is **hard-rejected with `SHUTDOWN`** (`enqueuePooledTransfer`) instead of re-creating the group and its connections. The retired group is not removed from `state->groups` in the retirement path, so submissions keep failing until something re-creates the group — which matches the observed ~90 s self-heal.

Evidence summary:

- First transfer after engine start always succeeds; the failure only appears after an idle gap
- During the hang the four lane connections are `ESTABLISHED` with empty kernel queues → the stall is in TE user space (lane queue / admission), not the kernel
- Failure depends on the admission timeout (default 1 s fails immediately; 60 s still hangs) but recovery time (~90 s) is unchanged — consistent with a stale `CLOSED` group rather than a transient queue backlog

Suggested fix: in `enqueuePooledTransfer`, drop a non-`OPEN` group and re-create it (or remove retired groups from `state->groups` atomically when retiring) instead of rejecting the work.

## Workaround

Retry the request after ~90 s (self-healed), or keep the peer continuously busy (impractical). No configuration knob we found avoids it.

items.title: [Bug]: Unauthenticated object deletion via client-controlled force flag in Mooncake Store Master
items.author: yyymk
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

Mooncake Store Master serves `Remove`, `RemoveByRegex`, `RemoveAll` and `BatchRemove` on its unauthenticated RPC port (default 0.0.0.0:50051) without any caller ownership or tenant validation. The only protection for an object is its lease, and the `force` flag that bypasses the lease is a client-supplied field of the RPC request. A network peer that can reach the master deletes any object with `force=true`, wipes objects matching an arbitrary regex across all tenants, or clears the whole cluster with `RemoveAll(force=true)`. Runtime-confirmed on the master binary shipped in the 0.3.13.post1 wheel (latest release); no fix available. Suggested severity: Critical, CVSS 9.1.

### Details

In `MasterService::Remove` (mooncake-store/src/master_service.cpp) the complete validation of a delete is:

```cpp
if (!force && !metadata.IsLeaseExpired()) {
    return tl::make_unexpected(ErrorCode::OBJECT_HAS_LEASE);
}
```

The lookup goes by key across all metadata shards. There is no client identity, no object ownership check, and no tenant isolation: the RPC wrapper (`WrappedMasterService::Remove(key, force)` in rpc_service.cpp) forwards both fields straight from the request, and the request carries no authentication at all. With `force=true` (one byte in the request body) the lease check is skipped entirely; only sanity checks remain (all replicas completed, no replication task).

`RemoveByRegex(pattern, force)` applies the same logic with an attacker-supplied regex over every shard of every tenant, and `RemoveAll(force)` erases every completed object in the cluster. `BatchRemove(keys, force)` loops the same path.

Three facts show this is not an intended trust decision. First, the sibling method `BatchReplicaClear` in the same file performs an explicit ownership check (`// Security check: Ensure the requesting client owns the object`, comparing `metadata.client_id`), so the codebase both knows how to validate ownership and stores the field needed for it. Second, the request path treats the lease as a real protection (a `force=false` delete of an object with an active lease is rejected with OBJECT_HAS_LEASE, verified at runtime), which the force flag silently voids for anyone. Third, clients are not isolated from each other: a forged request carrying no identity at all deleted objects put by a different client (verified at runtime on 0.3.13.post1), and although the 0.3.13 RPC signature carries a `tenant_id` parameter, `enable_multi_tenants` defaults to false (source default), so the parameter provides no isolation in the default configuration.

This is distinct from CVE-2026-96762 (unauthenticated `UnmountSegment` deletes another client's segment): different asset (object metadata vs segment registration), different method with a different missing check, and the additional client-controlled `force` bypass of the lease defense.

### PoC

Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.11. The master binary ships in the wheel: `pip install mooncake-transfer-engine==0.3.13.post1`, then start it:

```bash
<path>/env/bin/mooncake_master --rpc_address=0.0.0.0 --rpc_port=50051 \
  --metrics_port=9003 --default_kv_lease_ttl=20000 --logtostderr=1
```

Victim (separate process, its own auto-generated client_id) puts objects using the Python store client:

```python
from mooncake.store import MooncakeDistributedStore
store = MooncakeDistributedStore(...)
store.setup("192.168.105.123", "P2PHANDSHAKE", "seg_victim", 64 << 20, 16 << 20,
            "tcp", "", "192.168.105.123:50051", tenant_id="default")
for i in range(1, 4):
    assert store.put("victim_key_%05d" % i, b"V1CANARY_REG_AAA" + b"A" * 4078) == 0
# then poll: is_exist + get for each key, logging state every 5 s
```

Attacker: the Python client cannot send `force`, so the frame is forged. The master RPC is coro_rpc: a 20-byte header (magic=21, version=0, serialize_type=0, msg_type=0, u32le seq/function_id/length/attach_length) followed by a struct_pack body. Run the attacker's own store client through a tee proxy (a plain TCP forwarder that hex-dumps both directions) so one legit `remove("atk_key_0001")` call yields the exact frame template, then replay it with the key bytes replaced by an equal-length victim key and the `force` byte (the single byte after the length-prefixed key string) flipped from 0 to 1:

```python
# template = captured Remove frame (function_id observed as 4054882164)
body = bytearray(template_body)
# replace the 12 key payload bytes with the equal-length victim key,
# then set the force byte right after the length-prefixed key to 1
frame = header(seq=2, func=4054882164, body=bytes(body))
send(frame)   # -> success (tl::expected ok body ends fa010001)

items.title: GSP: grammar-conditioned sparse LM-head projection - replication and SGLang integration feedback wanted
items.author: StealthEyeLLC
items.body_excerpt:
I am sharing an open research artifact that may be relevant to SGLang's structured-generation path.

GSP (Grammar-Conditioned Sparse Projection) consumes a packed grammar legality mask before/during the target-model LM-head projection instead of computing the full vocabulary projection and masking afterward.

The current artifact includes:
- packed-mask row-sparse Triton projection for latency-oriented decoding
- batched block-GEMM that skips grammar-inactive vocabulary tiles
- density-aware dense fallback for permissive/mixed states
- support/top-1 correctness checks
- raw paired end-to-end Qwen3.5-2B results

On the reference RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, 30 paired AB/BA trials gave median end-to-end ratios of 1.0756x (enum JSON), 1.0642x (tool-call JSON), and 1.0842x (nested-array JSON). The free-string control is not claimed as a reliable mean speedup.

This is not claiming first invention of batch-1 grammar-aware LM-head filtering; the contribution boundary is the packed-mask batched execution, heterogeneous routing, and controlled target-model evaluation.

I would especially value:
- SGLang integration feedback
- datacenter GPU replication
- heterogeneous-batch measurements
- negative results / dense-winning crossover cases

Release, verified preprint, source, raw evidence:

items.title: Questions on Triton basic concepts
items.author: peastman
items.body_excerpt:
I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

comments.author: Arthur031221
comments.body:
Some of this is in the tutorials, though spread out: [01 vector add](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/01-vector-add.html) explains the `meta` grid, and [08 grouped GEMM](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/08-grouped-gemm.html) and [09 persistent matmul](https://triton-lang.org/main/getting-started/tutorials/09-persistent-matmul.html) between them use both kinds of tensor descriptor (08 builds them in the kernel, 09 uses both). I checked each answer below with triton 3.8.0 and torch 2.14 on an RTX 5090 (compute capability 12.0). The script and its output are at the bottom.

**What can be passed to a kernel?** torch tensors, ints, floats, bools, `None`, tuples (I tried `(2, 3.0)`), and `TensorDescriptor` objects. A `str`, `list`, `dict` or `torch.float32` passed as a normal argument fails with `TypeError: failed to specialize argument of type: ...`. A `tl.constexpr` parameter is more permissive: it took `tl.float32` and the string `"double"`.

**What is `meta`?** A dict of the launch arguments keyed by parameter name, constexprs included. For `add[grid](x, y, o, x.numel(), BLOCK=256)` its keys were `BLOCK, n, out, x, y`. That lets the grid depend on a constexpr such as the block size: `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(meta["n"], meta["BLOCK"]),)`.

**How do I get one element?** Inside the kernel, a tensor argument is a pointer, and `tl.load` gives you a block. Blocks have no element indexing at all: `av[i]` with a runtime `i` fails with a confusing message (`Did you forget to add @triton.jit ?`), and `av[I]` with a constexpr `I` fails with `unsupported tensor index: constexpr[5]`. Load the element from the pointer instead:

```python
s = tl.load(a + i)
tl.store(out + offs, s * tl.load(b + offs))
```

If the values are already in a block, `tl.sum(tl.where(offs == i, av, 0.0), axis=0)` pulls out one element. Both give `a[i] * b` in the script.

**`tensor_descriptor` vs `TensorDescriptor`?** Both describe an array by base pointer, shape, strides and a block shape, and both are used through `desc.load([row, col])` and `desc.store([row, col], value)`. The difference is where they are made. `triton.tools.tensor_descriptor.TensorDescriptor` is built on the host, e.g. `TensorDescriptor.from_tensor(x, [BM, BN])`, and passed in as a kernel argument; inside the kernel it has the type `tl.tensor_descriptor`. `tl.make_tensor_descriptor(ptr, shape=..., strides=..., block_shape=...)` builds one inside the kernel, which is what you want when the pointer or shape is only known inside the kernel, as in the grouped GEMM tutorial. On my card the in-kernel version needed `triton.set_allocator(...)` first; without it the launch failed with `Kernel requires a runtime memory allocation, but no allocator was set`. On GPUs older than Hopper (compute capability below 9) the NVIDIA backend rewrites descriptor loads and stores into ordinary pointer loads (`make_ttir` in `backends/nvidia/compiler.py`).

**`tl.constexpr`?** The value is baked into the compiled kernel, and yes, each new value compiles a new variant: `K = 1, 2, 2, 3` gave 3 variants. Some things require a constexpr: `tl.arange(0, B)` with a plain int `B` fails with `arange's arguments must be of type tl.constexpr`, and `tl.static_range` bounds have the same requirement. Plain int arguments are specialized too, on whether the value is 1 and whether it is divisible by 16: in the script 7, 9 and 13 shared one variant, 16 added a second (32 and 48 reused it), and 1 added a third. `@triton.jit(do_not_specialize=[...])` turns that off for the arguments you list.

**`tl.const`?** In 3.8.0 it is a compile-time check. Storing through a `tl.const` pointer fails with `Cannot store to a constant pointer`, and on this NVIDIA card a small kernel compiled with and without `tl.const` on its input gave the same PTX once the kernel name and debug lines were removed. On main it does more on AMD: #11294 (merged 2026-08-21) puts `tl.const` pointer arguments in the AMDGPU constant

items.title: [RFC]: Agent-Aware KV Cache Affinity Scheduling and Lifecycle Management
items.author: daisyEliot
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix has established a production-grade distributed KV cache architecture with L1 DRAM offloading, L2 shared cache clusters, prefix-aware routing, and P&D (Prefill/Decode) disaggregation, delivering significant efficiency gains for general inference workloads. As agent-based traffic becomes dominant in production clusters, the current cache stack lacks semantic awareness of agent task properties, leading to suboptimal cache reuse, avoidable eviction of high-value prefixes, and misalignment between cache lifetime and agent execution cycles.

This RFC proposes extending the AIBrix stack with agent-native cache management capabilities built on top of standard `agent_hints` fields. The changes span the API gateway routing layer, KV cache runtime, event synchronization protocol, and P&D scheduler — all while preserving full backward compatibility with existing engines, cache backends, and routing policies. The proposal introduces program-level cache affinity, context-weighted eviction, session-aligned cache pinning, and intent-driven speculative prefill, optimized specifically for AIBrix's layered cache and disaggregated architecture.

### Motivation

Agent workloads now account for 40%–60% of production inference traffic in AIBrix deployments, and exhibit fundamentally different cache behavior compared to one-shot requests. The current AIBrix cache stack was designed for generic prompt-based traffic and faces four structural gaps when handling agent workloads:

### 1. Prefix routing lacks program-level semantic affinity

AIBrix's existing `prefix-cache` routing plugin matches requests purely by recursive token block hashes, with no awareness of agent program identity. Requests from different sessions of the same agent program — which share identical system prompts, tool definitions, and role instructions that can span thousands of tokens — are treated as unrelated prefixes. This results in:

- Redundant prefills of the same program prefix across multiple Serving Units
- Wasted L2 cache capacity from duplicate copies of identical program-level prefix blocks
- No ability to intentionally colocate same-program workloads for maximum cache sharing

In multi-tenant agent clusters, this limits global prefix cache reuse rate to roughly 30%, even when most workloads share common agent program templates.

### 2. Cache eviction is blind to context value and task priority

AIBrix's current scan-resistant eviction policy ranks KV blocks only by access frequency and recency, uniformly across all block types. In agent scenarios, cache value varies by orders of magnitude:

- `system_prompt` and `tool_def` blocks are reused across the entire session and have the highest durable value
- `conversation` history blocks accumulate incrementally and have moderate value
- `reasoning` intermediate blocks are single-use and have near-zero reuse value

Without semantic differentiation, high-value permanent prefixes are frequently evicted to make room for low-value temporary reasoning state. Additionally, there is no priority differentiation between production-critical agent tasks and background batch workloads, so low-priority traffic can evict high-priority session cache and cause SLA violations.

### 3. Cache lifetime is decoupled from agent task execution cycles

Agent workloads alternate between inference generation and external tool/API calls, with idle windows ranging from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of seconds. Under AIBrix's default LRU-based eviction, session cache becomes eligible for eviction during tool call idle periods. When the agent resumes execution:

- The full context must be re-prefilled, increasing end-to-end latency by 2–5x
- GPU cycles are wasted recomputing previously computed cache
- In P&D disaggregation mode, the session must be re-mapped to a Prefill GPU, adding scheduling overhead

The existing `session-affinity` routing only maintains pod stickiness but does not protect cache from eviction during idle periods.

### 4. KV event protocol carries no agent semantic metadata

The AIBrix KVCache v1 Connector and event synchronization protocol only transmits block-level physical attributes (block hashes, token IDs, size, medium) to the L2 cache cluster and gateway. Without agent semantic fields in events:

- The L2 cache cannot implement tiered storage policies based on priority or context type
- The gateway cannot make routing decisions informed by agent program identity
- Observability stacks cannot break down cache metrics by agent program or priority tier

### 5. No proactive prefill orchestration for multi-turn agent conversations

AIBrix's P&D disaggregation architecture separates compute-heavy prefills from decode-heavy generation, but prefill operations are still triggered only by incoming requests. For multi-turn agent dialogues, the next turn's prefix (conversation history + latest assistant reply) is highly predictable. Without an intent-driven prefill mechanism, every agent turn incurs full cold-start prefill latency, leaving first-token latency suboptimal for interactive agent use cases.

### Proposed Change

All proposed changes are additive and backward-compatible. Existing workloads without `agent_hints` continue to behave exactly as today. The proposal is structured around five targeted extensions to the AIBrix stack:

### 1. Standardized `agent_hints` Field and End-to-End Propagation

Define a standard set of agent semantic fields propagated from the API gateway through to the KV cache runtime and event protocol:

- `program_id`: string identifier for the agent program, used for affinity scheduling
- `priority`: integer task priority level, used for tiered eviction and storage
- `context_type`: enumerated value (`system_prompt`, `tool_def`, `conversation`, `reasoning`)
- `speculative_prefill`: boolean flag enabling proactive next-turn prefill
- `session_ttl_hint`: suggested cache lifetime for the session

**Integration points in AIBrix**:

- The Envoy-based

comments.author: hengguangcui11-cyber
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed RFC. A few questions, mostly on the routing / P&D parts:

1. **Program affinity vs. existing prefix routing.** The gateway already builds the prefix-match text as system prompt + canonicalized `tools` JSON + messages (`combinePrefixText` / `canonicalToolsText`, `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_INCLUDE_TOOLS` defaults to on), and hashes it as chained content blocks from the start. So requests from different sessions that share an identical system prompt and tool definitions already produce the same leading block hashes and are routed toward the same pods. Is the gap that prompts/templates differ across sessions of the same program, or the affinity-vs-load trade-off? Some data on this would help scope Part 2.
2. **Overlap with #2742.** `x-aibrix-session-key` (set by the caller from the first request, Redis-backed across gateway replicas) already covers part of Parts 2 and 4. Would `program_id` / session pinning build on that key rather than add a parallel mechanism?
3. **KV event fields.** `BlockStored` / `BlockRemoved` are emitted by the engine (AIBrix decodes vLLM's msgpack format), so the new fields would need engine-side changes. How would `context_type` / `priority` be defined for a block that spans a boundary (e.g. end of system prompt, start of conversation), or for a prefix block shared by requests with different hints?
4. **Speculative prefill.** In P&D, the decode pod already holds the KV for history + reply when decode finishes. Would offloading that KV to L2 be cheaper than recomputing it on a prefill GPU? Also, the 5s default TTL seems short given the tool-call idle windows (up to tens of seconds) in the motivation.

Given the scope, splitting this into phases (e.g. gateway-side affinity first, evaluated with the agent session workload generator from #2483) might make it easier to review.

items.title: [RFC]: Support ViT Full CUDA Graph (Tracker)
items.author: shen-shanshan
items.body_excerpt:
### Motivation.

Multimodal large language models (e.g., Qwen3-VL, Qwen3.5, GLM-V, Kimi K2.5) rely on a Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder to process visual inputs before feeding them into the language model backbone. In production serving scenarios, the ViT forward pass involves launching a large number of small CUDA kernels — including patch embedding, layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, and MLP projections — each of which incurs non-trivial kernel launch overhead on the host side.

Currently, vLLM supports CUDA graph capture for the decoder (LLM) portion of the model, which has proven effective at reducing kernel launch costs and improving throughput. However, the ViT encoder is still executed eagerly, meaning every forward pass re-launches all kernels from scratch. Extending full CUDA graph support to the ViT encoder would allow the entire encoder forward pass to be captured and replayed as a single graph, eliminating per-kernel launch overhead and enabling more consistent, low-latency inference for multimodal models.
