items.title: Loop-carry detection skips `prev = cur` when both start as the same value, silently keeping the pre-loop value instead of carrying it
items.author: Hughshine
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug


**TL;DR.** `CodeGenerator._find_carries` decides which variables of a `for` or `while` loop become `iter_args` by comparing IR values after one dry run of the body, instead of asking whether a value can differ between iterations. If `prev` and `cur` are the same IR value before the loop and the loop runs `prev = cur`, `prev` looks unchanged and is not carried, so it keeps its pre-loop value in every iteration and after the loop. Regression from #7200, first in 3.5.0 (3.4.0 is right). Possible fix: also carry every name that is assigned in the loop (as 3.4.0 did), or only those that share their initial IR value with another name.

**Why one dry run misses it.** `_find_carries` ([L485-L524](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L485-L524), the comparison is [L513](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L513)) runs the body once with every name bound to its pre-loop value. When `prev = cur` runs there, `cur` is still at its pre-loop value, so `prev` is bound to the value it already had. In the real body `cur` is a block argument, so `prev = cur` is a different value in every iteration. Seeing that takes a second pass that already knows `cur` is carried.

The smallest example. `prev` is `cur`'s value at the start of each iteration; `SAME=False` is the control, where `prev` is equal to `cur` but a different IR value:

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def kernel(out_ptr, n, SAME: tl.constexpr):
    cur = 0
    if SAME:
        prev = cur          # prev and cur are the same IR value
    else:
        prev = cur + 0      # control: equal to cur, but a different IR value
    for i in range(n):
        prev = cur          # prev is cur's value at the start of the iteration
        cur = cur + 1
    tl.store(out_ptr, prev)      # expected n - 1
    tl.store(out_ptr + 1, cur)   # expected n


n = 5
for same in (True, False):
    out = torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda")
    k = kernel[(1, )](out, n, same)
    print(f"SAME={same!s:5} prev, cur = {out.tolist()}, expected {[n - 1, n]}")
    print("   ", [l.strip() for l in k.asm["ttir"].splitlines() if "scf.for" in l][0].split(" : ")[0])
```
```
SAME=True  prev, cur = [0, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %cur = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32)
SAME=False prev, cur = [4, 5], expected [4, 5]
    %prev:2 = scf.for %i = %c0_i32 to %n step %c1_i32 iter_args(%cur = %c0_i32, %prev_0 = %c0_i32) -> (i32, i32)
```
With `SAME=True` only `cur` is an `iter_arg`. 3.4.0 has two `iter_args` in both cases and returns `[4, 5]`. Without an `iter_arg`, `prev` is still bound to its pre-loop value when the body starts, and `enter_sub_region` restores that binding when the loop ends ([L146](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/6fe3348e6e907584e07e593ab19a35caee95c37a/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L146)).

**Why since 3.5.0.** Up to 3.4.0 every name that is assigned in the loop and live before it was carried ([visit_For](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1114-L1115), [visit_While](https://github.com/triton-lang/triton/blob/d4432f6b89ef554007a53ef90f2499d90792d7e7/python/triton/compiler/code_generator.py#L1153-L1154)). #7200 (2025-06-23, "Improve detection of loop carries", for builtins that modify their arguments) replaced that with the comparison of IR values; v3.5.0 is the first tag that contains it. The existing tests for shared initial values (`test_loop_carry_shared_initial_value` and its while and tuple variants in test_frontend.py, #11369) update the aliased variables independently (`a = a + 1`, `b = b + 2`), so none has a copy between them.

**Possible fix.** Two variants, both tested as source patches on main @6fe3348e6.

items.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

items.title: [Performance] Measure Transformers backend startup time vs native
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
This comes from an old comment and was never backed by measurements, so the first
task is to establish whether the effect is real at all. It may not be.

Runtime throughput was brought in line with native implementations in #47187, but
nobody has measured startup time either before or since.

### Step 1: is there a difference?

Time engine init for a model that has both implementations, e.g.:

    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl transformers
    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl vllm

Compare time-to-ready across a few runs and a couple of model sizes. Warm vs cold
HF cache matters, so control for it.

If there is no meaningful difference, say so and close this issue. That is a
perfectly good outcome and still worth having measured.

### Step 2: only if a delta shows up

The backend does some work at load time that native implementations do not, so
these are plausible starting points rather than known causes:

- `fuser.py` — `get_fuser` traces each module class with `fx` to match it against
  the available fusers. Cached per class, but tracing is not free.
- `base.py` — `recursive_replace` walks the module tree applying fusers per instance.
- Config resolution and `auto_map` handling for remote-code models.

A profile of init (py-spy or cProfile) will be more informative than guessing from
this list.

### Done when

Either the startup delta is quantified and explained, or it is shown that there
isn't a meaningful one and this is closed.

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: [RFC]: Add KVCacheStore as a shared capacity backend for Mooncake Store
items.author: zxpdemonio
items.body_excerpt:
## Changes proposed

This RFC proposes an optional KVCacheStore Low Level adapter for Mooncake Store. The adapter uses the existing distributed-storage integration point, keeps Mooncake Master authoritative for logical object lifecycle, and accesses KVCacheStore through the node-local EFC data plane.

The first community change covers the publicly documented Low Level API. A prototype also exists for KVCacheStore Standard, but Standard is not part of the first landing because its control-plane contract and end-to-end query deadline are not yet documented well enough for a maintainable open-source integration.

The design requires explicit configuration and remains buildable when the KVCacheStore SDK is absent. It does not start EFC, infer enablement from a Unix socket, or copy provider placement state into Mooncake metadata.

## Why this needs an RFC

Mooncake's [contribution guide](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) asks architectural changes larger than 500 lines to start with a GitHub RFC. This change affects storage metadata, request routing, failure handling, and the distributed-storage abstraction. It also overlaps with two existing proposals:

- [#1957: Mooncake Store NVMe KV Backend](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/1957)
- [#2993: Distributed KV Storage Backend for Mooncake Store](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/issues/2993)

The driver itself is not the hard part. This RFC asks where a shared, provider-managed cache should attach to Mooncake and which parts of the lifecycle Mooncake should own.

## Motivation

Mooncake already moves KV cache data between memory and external capacity tiers. KVCacheStore adds a provider-managed G3.5 capacity tier with a user-space KV interface. Its public deployment model places an EFC process beside the application; the SDK talks to EFC over a Unix socket and shared memory, while EFC handles the remote storage data path. The storage service can be attached to another compute node without copying data into that node first.

That model is useful for disaggregated inference, but it does not fit perfectly into Mooncake's current OSS offload path. The current [OSS offload design](https://kvcache-ai.github.io/Mooncake/deployment/oss-offload.html) treats the external object as a `LOCAL_DISK` replica owned by a real Mooncake client. Readers contact that owner, and the owner accesses OSS through `FileStorage` and `DistributedStorageBackend`.

KVCacheStore is different in one important respect: every correctly configured compute node has a local EFC endpoint for the same attached storage pool. Sending a read through the original writer adds an unnecessary owner hop and makes the writer part of the read availability path. The proposed adapter lets the requesting Mooncake client read the shared provider directly, after Mooncake Master has confirmed that the logical replica is valid.

The integration must preserve a clear metadata boundary:

- Mooncake decides whether a logical object exists and whether its replica is committed.
- KVCacheStore and EFC decide where provider records live and may reclaim them under capacity pressure.
- The adapter translates between those two views without turning transient provider details into durable Mooncake metadata.

## Goals

- Add an optional KVCacheStore Low Level backend without changing existing deployments.
- Reuse Mooncake's existing distributed-storage and object-adapter path where practical.
- Keep Mooncake Master authoritative for logical object state and commit ordering.
- Allow any configured Mooncake client to read the shared provider through its local EFC.
- Define a portable, versioned layout for objects larger than one KVCacheStore value.
- Treat provider eviction as a cache miss, never as valid data.
- Bound Low Level provider operations and make partial outcomes explicit.
- Preserve tenant separation in provider keys.
- Keep the SDK optional at build time.
- Split the implementation into reviewable pull requests with SDK-free tests.

## Non-goals

- Starting, supervising, or reconfiguring EFC from Mooncake.
- Reimplementing provider capacity management, watermarks, compaction, or device GC.
- Storing EFC mountpoints, device identities, or provider placement in Mooncake Master.
- Adding Mooncake-side replication or migration between Low Level targets in the first release.
- Making delete or upsert atomic across Mooncake Master and KVCacheStore.
- Supporting multiple writers that bypass the Mooncake Master lifecycle.
- Landing KVCacheStore Standard in the first community PR.
- Changing the separate Mooncake Store RS cold-tier implementation.

## Public KVCacheStore architecture

The following diagram is limited to behavior described in the public KVCacheStore documentation. It does not assume an internal control-plane topology.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Node[Compute node]
        App[Inference process]
        SDK[KVCacheStore Low Level SDK]
        EFC[kvcs-efc data-plane proxy]
        SHM[Shared-memory rings]

        App --> SDK
        SDK -->|Unix socket| EFC
        SDK <--> SHM
        EFC <--> SHM
    end

    EFC -->|record operations| G35[Attached KVCacheStore G3.5 tier]
    G35 --> Capacity[Provider-managed capacity and LRU]
```

The public [integration guide](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/kvcachestore/best-practices-for-integrating-the-kvcachestore-sdk) establishes the constraints that matter to Mooncake:

- the application and `kvcs-efc` run on the same node and under the same OS user;
- the SDK connects to `/var/run/kvcs/efc-grpc.sock` by default;
- data transfer uses shared-memory rings sized from value size, batch size, and worker counts;
- Low Level provides batch put, query, get, and delete operations;
- LRU eviction is part of the service and cannot be disabled;
- applications own key-prefix isolation and must handle a miss by recomputing or fetching data elsewhere.

The broader [product overview](https://www.alibabac

items.author: holtwood
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

Contributes to #3244.

The existing multi-node example expands `$SLURM_NODEID` in the batch shell, before `srun` creates its per-task environments. Both launches can therefore receive the same node rank. The existing readiness loop also checks only whether a TCP port is open.

This PR covers basic multi-node serving, single-node serving, and offline batch inference. #29991 has a separate scope around PD disaggregation and Apptainer.

## Changes

- Evaluate `$SLURM_PROCID` inside each `srun` task and use Slurm `%n` patterns for per-node logs.
- Use configurable HTTP and distributed-init ports, a bounded `/health` check, and early process-exit detection.
- Add a single-node serving job with cleanup and an SSH forwarding hint.
- Add an offline job that writes a real Python file with a `__main__` guard, as required by the Engine multiprocessing setup.
- Document the log-directory prerequisite and cluster-specific scheduler, network, port, and model-cache settings.

## Validation

- `bash -n` on all three batch scripts.
- `mint validate`.
- `mint broken-links`.
- Parsed and mock-executed the offline Python example, including Engine context cleanup.
- Checked task-side rank expansion with `SLURM_PROCID=0` and `SLURM_PROCID=1`.
- Cross-checked the Engine `spawn` setup, context-manager support, `/health` behavior, and referenced server arguments against the PR base revision.

I did not run these examples end to end on a Slurm GPU cluster. The `#SBATCH` resource values, partition name, network interfaces, and port availability remain site-specific.

items.title: [Feature]: Share non-streaming chat message assembly between `OpenAIServingChat` and batch derender
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Tracking issue for the "Unify (not mirror) the assembly path" item in #42729, raised by @sagearc in the #48617 review (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48617#pullrequestreview-4695988048).

#### Why

Batch chat derender (`OnlineDerenderer._derender_chat`) builds the assistant message itself instead of  sharing the code in `OpenAIServingChat.chat_completion_full_generator`. Both run the same `Parser.parse()` over the same tokens. They differ in what happens after:

- which `tool_choice` branch applies
- `content or ""` for named / required tool choice
- tool call IDs
- the `finish_reason` rewrite to `tool_calls`

The two have already drifted three times:

- `null` vs `""` content, fixed in #48617
- `finish_reason`: batch derender passes through the generate side's `stop` for tool calls (fix in open PR #47931)
- tool call IDs: batch derender builds `ToolCall(id=random_uuid())` and drops the parser's ID, while coupled chat uses `tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`. Batch IDs lose the `chatcmpl-tool-` prefix, and Kimi K2 `functions.<name>:<idx>` IDs are lost. A fix will follow once #47931 merges, since both change the same block of `_derender_chat`.

The round trip parity test (`test_derender_parity.py`) missed the last two. It compares only tool names and arguments, and it feeds the coupled response's `finish_reason` into derender instead of the engine's.

#### Proposal

Pull the post parse message assembly out of `chat_completion_full_generator` into a helper that both paths call. It takes the parser output (`reasoning`, `content`, `tool_calls`), the request and the tool config and returns the `ChatMessage` fields and the final `finish_reason`. It owns:

- the `tool_choice` branches (none / named / required / auto)
- tool call IDs (`tc.id or make_tool_call_id()`)
- `content or ""` for named / required
- `auto_tools_called` and the `finish_reason` rewrite

Constraints:

- **Subclass hooks stay.** `_create_chat_message` and `_finalize_response_message` are overridden by the Cohere v2 handler (`cohere/serving.py`). The helper returns fields and serving still builds the message through the hooks. Derender doesn't subclass `OpenAIServingChat`.
- **No behavior change for `/v1/chat/completions`.** This is the hot non-streaming path.
- **Batch only.** Streaming is #57572.

#56851 `derender` level reuses `OnlineDerenderer.derender_chat`, so it picks this up without adding a third copy.

#### Done when

- [ ] Helper extracted from `chat_completion_full_generator`. Existing chat completion and tool / reasoning parser tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] `_derender_chat` uses it.
- [ ] #47931 and the tool call ID fix have landed first, so the refactor changes no behavior on either path. The tool call ID fix also makes `test_derender_parity.py` feed the engine's `finish_reason` and check tool call ID format.

### Alternatives

- **Rely on the parity test.** Cheaper  and it should be tightened anyway. But it runs one model with one parser configuration and it has already missed two of three drifts.
- **Fold this into #57572.** Both touch `OpenAIServingChat` but the streaming step works on deltas and this one builds a whole message. Keeping them apart keeps each serving change reviewable on its own. If the helpers end up sharing code (the `finish_reason` rewrite, tool call IDs), that can happen in whichever lands second.

### Additional context

- RFC #42729, "Unify (not mirror) the parse/assembly path"
- #48617 (parity test), #47931 (`finish_reason` fix, open). The tool call ID fix follows after #47931.
- #57572: streaming counterpart
- #56851: reuses `derender_chat` for its `derender` level

cc @sagearc @chaunceyjiang

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: `kv_cache_dtype="fp8"` auto-selects the FLASHINFER attention backend without a usable FlashInfer JIT and crashes instead of falling back to TRITON_ATTN
items.author: fede-kamel
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment
vLLM nightly `0.30.1rc1.dev740+gaad4579bb` installed from the wheel, torch 2.13.0+cu132, RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell (sm_120), driver 610.57. No CUDA toolkit and no `flashinfer-cubin`.

### 🐛 Describe the bug
```python
# VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 avoids the separate sampler crash (#49497)
from vllm import LLM
LLM("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", kv_cache_dtype="fp8", max_model_len=2048)
```
```
WARNING [flashinfer.py:123] FlashInfer kernels are disabled: flashinfer-cubin is not installed and nvcc (CUDA_HOME, CUDA_PATH, PATH or /usr/local/cuda) or ninja (PATH) is missing. ...
INFO [cuda.py:526] Using FLASHINFER attention backend out of potential backends: ['FLASHINFER', 'TRITON_ATTN'].
...
RuntimeError: Could not find nvcc and default cuda_home='/usr/local/cuda' doesn't exist
```

vLLM itself reports that FlashInfer is disabled, then selects the FLASHINFER attention backend a few lines later.

Passing `attention_backend="TRITON_ATTN"` makes it work. On this GPU, FlashAttention rejects fp8 KV, so FLASHINFER is the next candidate. But the FlashInfer attention backend is never checked for availability: `supports_compute_capability` only checks the capability range, and the configuration validation never consults `has_flashinfer()`.

A related gap: `has_flashinfer()` (`vllm/utils/flashinfer.py`) returns True as soon as `flashinfer-cubin` is installed. That package only ships trtllm-gen cubins, while attention, sampling, CUTLASS MoE and the mxfp8 GEMM are JIT modules that still need nvcc or `flashinfer-jit-cache`. So on SM120 the same crash also happens with `flashinfer-cubin` installed.

Suggested fix: treat FLASHINFER as invalid during auto-selection when FlashInfer can't JIT (no nvcc+ninja and no jit-cache), so selection falls through to TRITON_ATTN. Have `has_flashinfer()` reflect whether the JIT modules can actually be built, not just whether cubins exist.

Related: #49497 (sampler), PRs #49314 and #51741 (sampler only). PR #58360 notes that "FlashInfer attention is not gated by has_flashinfer()".

items.title: [RFC] Apple Silicon serving redesign: Torch-owned SRT path with an exported whole-model MLX region (roadmap)
items.author: noob-se7en
items.body_excerpt: **Jump to:** [Roadmap](#user-content-roadmap) · [Design](#user-content-design) · [Evidence](#user-content-evidence) · Implementation PR: #36164 This updates the original proposal (can be found in previous edited version) after the Torch/MLX interoperability work in [#32984](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/32984). The stub problem remains, but zero-copy access to Torch MPS storage gives us a smaller solution: keep one standard SRT serving path and use MLX or Metal only for computation. The architecture below has been implemented and validated behind a default-off flag in the accompanying draft PR, [noob-se7en/sglang#2](https://github.com/noob-se7en/sglang/pull/2) (branch `rfc-whole-region-mlx-clean`, stacked on the #32984 bridge): none of it is upstream yet; measured results are in the Evidence section. **Implementation.** The core stack of this RFC — capture → lowering → serving — is under review upstream as sgl-project/sglang#36164 (three commits on current `main`, off by default behind `SGLANG_ENABLE_MLX_WHOLE_REGION`). The full RFC branch with every measurement quoted below is [noob-se7en/sglang#2](https://github.com/noob-se7en/sglang/pull/2); [noob-se7en/sglang#3](https://github.com/noob-se7en/sglang/pull/3) is the extraction that became #36164. Follow-up items and their PRs are tracked in the [Roadmap](#user-content-roadmap). ## Why this matters MLX compatibility bugs have repeatedly reached users through startup failures, request-time attribute errors, incomplete feature paths, lifecycle leaks, and configuration drift. Examples include #26882, #29681, #30181, #30389, #30547, #32115, #32445, #32446 and #32447. The same split also creates review burden. A scheduler or `ModelRunner` change may not mention MLX, but an MLX reviewer still has to check whether the new path reaches the stub, whether the required field was initialized, whether the MLX worker intercepts the operation, and whether copied framework calculations still match core. In #30547, for example, MLX silently ignored the configured `max_running_requests` because its stub maintained a separate calculation. #32115 then had to update that copied behavior again. As long as SGLang has two owners for serving state, fixes in the standard path can continue to drift from MLX. ## Current flow Today Apple Silicon serving has two execution paths selected at the backend level: ```text Scheduler | +-- Standard Torch path | TpModelWorker | Torch ModelRunner | Torch model | Torch request tables and KV cache | +-- Native MLX path MlxTpModelWorker MlxModelRunnerStub: Torch-shaped bookkeeping MlxModelRunner: model execution mlx-lm model separate request and KV lifecycle ``` `MlxModelRunnerStub` exists because generic serving code still expects a Torch-shaped `ModelRunner`, while the actual model is loaded and executed by a separate MLX runner. The arrangement is safe only for fields and paths that have already been mirrored and reviewed. The problem is not simply that the stub is incomplete. The framework has two implementations of model loading, request state, KV ownership, feature handling, and lifecycle behavior. ## Proposed flow Apple Silicon should use the standard Scheduler, worker, and Torch `ModelRunner` as the only owners of serving state: ```text Standard Scheduler Standard TpModelWorker Torch ModelRunner Torch-owned model, weights, requests and KV cache +-- eager Torch MPS forward (always available; also serves any | batch the region rejects before launch) +-- direct Metal AOT/JIT operators (existing fused-op dispatch) +-- exported whole-model MLX region (standard graph-runner slot; eligibility and export checked per batch before any device work) ``` Torch owns the model and storage. Metal and MLX are computation backends behind the two dispatch points SGLang already has: the fused-operation dispatch for individual operators, and the graph-runner slots for the exported region. They may read or update Torch-owned buffers through an explicit contract, but they do not load a second model or own another scheduler, request table, KV pool, sampler, or weight-update lifecycle. Models the region cannot serve continue to use the complete Torch MPS path. ## Design ### One owner for serving state | Concern | Authoritative owner | | --- | --- | | Scheduling, batching, request lifecycle and Radix cache | Standard SGLang Scheduler | | Model loading, parameters, request tables and KV allocation | Torch `ModelRunner` | | Logits, sampling, logprobs, grammar, LoRA and weight updates | Existing standard SRT components | | Operator dispatch and region selection | Existing fused-op dispatch and the standard graph-runner slot | | Accelerated computation | Torch MPS, Metal AOT/JIT or MLX | Neither dispatch point introduces a second copy of framework state. New Scheduler and `ModelRunner` behavior is inherited automatically because Apple Silicon uses the standard implementations. ### Direct Metal for small operations Model-independent operations such as RMSNorm, fused add and RMSNorm, and SiLU-and-multiply should use the existing fused-operation dispatch mechanism: ```text SGLang operation +-- supported Metal AOT/JIT kernel +-- otherwise Torch implementation ``` These kernels operate directly on Torch MPS buffers and do not cross into MLX. A separate model registry is not needed for this level. ### Capture-and-lower MLX region MLX becomes useful when a sufficiently broad region can remain in MLX long enough to amortize framework dispatch and synchronization. The region is not assembled from per

items.title: [Bug] GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 at TP4 loops in reasoning with no final answer on B200/B300
items.author: dhruvrnaik
items.body_excerpt:
GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 at **TP4** responds with repetitive reasoning until the token limit and no final assistant content on both 4x B200 and 4x B300.

## Environment

- Date: 2026-09-30; Modal, single node with 4 GPUs, 16 CPU cores and 128 GiB RAM.
- Model: RadixArk/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4, exact revision `f46cf340d35a22d0d83d0c1dac8957cf2b1bcd35`.
- Linux amd64 image: `lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4`.
- SGLang image build `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e` (0.5.20), Torch 2.13.0+cu130.

## Reproduction

Download the pinned public model revision, replace the local `/weights/...` path below with that snapshot directory, and run inside the pinned image. Exact measured launch command:

```bash
/opt/sglang/bin/python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path /weights/RadixArk--GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4/f46cf340d35a22d0d83d0c1dac8957cf2b1bcd35 --quantization modelopt_fp4 --tp-size 4 --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_cutlass --speculative-algorithm EAGLE --speculative-num-steps 5 --speculative-eagle-topk 1 --speculative-num-draft-tokens 6 --mem-fraction-static 0.85 --cuda-graph-max-bs-decode 32 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3 --dsa-prefill-backend trtllm --dsa-decode-backend trtllm --reasoning-parser auto --tool-call-parser auto --served-model-name RadixArk/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4
```

Request sent through curl to `/v1/chat/completions`:

```json
{
  "model": "RadixArk/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "What is 15 percent of 240? State the answer clearly."
    }
  ],
  "max_tokens": 2048,
  "temperature": 0,
  "chat_template_kwargs": {
    "enable_thinking": false,
    "thinking": false
  },
  "reasoning_effort": "low"
}
```

Expected: a short answer of 36 with final assistant content and normal stop.

Observed: `content` is empty, `finish_reason` is `length` at the 2048-token request budget, and `reasoning_content` repeats:

```text
15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240
```

The server reached READY. A prompt about sunrise also returned no final assistant content.

## Variants observed

The symptom was also observed with BF16 KV / TileLang DSA instead of FP8 KV / TRTLLM DSA. The B300 high-throughput configuration without EAGLE also reproduced missing final content. All variants below kept TP4:

```json
[
  {
    "config": "glm-b200-tp4-low-latency-fp8-trtllm",
    "final_content_length": 0,
    "finish_reason": "length",
    "reasoning_prefix": "15% of 240 = 36. Also 15% of 2400 = 360? No, just answer 36. Wait, 0.15\u00d7240=36. Yes. But the question might be 15% of 2400? No. Answer: 36. Hmm, but \""
  },
  {
    "config": "glm-b200-tp4-low-latency-bf16-tilelang",
    "final_content_length": 0,
    "finish_reason": "length",
    "reasoning_prefix": "15% of 240 = 36. Also 15% of 2400 = 360? No, just answer 36. Wait, 15% of 240 = 0.15\u00d7240 = 36. But the question might be 15% of 2400? No. Answer: 36. "
  },
  {
    "config": "glm-b200-tp4-high-throughput-fp8-trtllm",
    "final_content_length": 0,
    "finish_reason": "length",
    "reasoning_prefix": "15% of 240 = 36. Also 15% of 2400 = 360? User asked 240. Answer 36. Maybe mention 2400? No. Just 36. Could note if they meant 2400, it's 360. Keep sim"
  },
  {
    "config": "glm-b300-tp4-low-latency-fp8-trtllm",
    "final_content_length": 0,
    "finish_reason": "length",
    "reasoning_prefix": "15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 3"
  },
  {
    "config": "glm-b300-tp4-low-latency-bf16-tilelang",
    "final_content_length": 0,
    "finish_reason": "length",
    "reasoning_prefix": "15% of 240 = 36. Also show work briefly. Also note \"15 percent\" vs \"15 percentage points\"? Just answer. Note: 15% of 240 = 36. Also mention if they me"
  },
  {
    "config": "glm-b300-tp4-high-throughput-fp8-trtllm",
    "final_content_length": 0,
    "finish_reason": "length",
    "reasoning_prefix": "15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 36. 15% of 240 = 3"
  },
  {
    "config": "glm-b300-tp4-high-throughput-bf16-tilelang",
    "final_content_length": 0,
    "finish_reason": "length",
    "reasoning_prefix": "15% of 240 = 36. Also 15% of 2400 = 360. The question: 240 \u2192 36. But wait, \"15 percent of 240\" \u2014 36. Hmm, but maybe they meant 2400? No, answer 36. Ac"
  }
]
```

The full GSM8K evaluator completed 1319 questions for five configurations but scored 0 because the final assistant content was empty (the HTML reports show extracted-answer sentinel -9999999). These runs failed the response checks and are excluded from the benchmark records. Server logs, requests, responses, and evaluator HTML/JSON are saved.

The root cause is undetermined; TP4, the checkpoint, and the runtime have not been isolated.

items.title: [Bug] `--enable-deterministic-inference` does not make gpt-oss-20b deterministic: `test_deterministic --test-mode prefix` returns several outputs for one prompt
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

With `--enable-deterministic-inference`, `openai/gpt-oss-20b` fails SGLang's own prefix-mode determinism test. The same prompt, batched with other requests that share a prefix with it, comes back as several different greedy outputs. Two other models on the same node and build pass the same test every time: dense Qwen3-8B and MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8.

The server accepts the flag for gpt-oss without any warning. The only related log line is `Sampling backend is set to pytorch for deterministic inference.`

Used claude to run some unique outputs per prompt in `--test-mode prefix --n-start 1 --n-trials 30`, two runs per configuration, H100 80GB, v0.5.21 (1 = deterministic). Each prompt got 91 to 146 samples per run:

| model | MoE runner | attention | prefix 1 | prefix 511 | prefix 2048 | prefix 4097 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-oss-20b | triton_kernel (default) | triton | 1, 1 | 2, 3 | 5, 6 | 4, 4 |
| gpt-oss-20b | triton_kernel (default) | fa3 | 1, 1 | 4, 5 | 6, 6 | 6, 6 |
| gpt-oss-20b | triton | triton | 1, 1 | 4, 4 | 5, 5 | 4, 4 |
| gpt-oss-20b | marlin | triton | 1, 1 | 50, 57 | 103, 95 | 45, 42 |
| Qwen3-8B | - | triton | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 |
| Qwen3-8B | - | fa3 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 | default | triton | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 |
| Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 | default | fa3 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 | 1, 1 |

- No MoE runner and no attention backend somehow makes gpt-oss deterministic. With `marlin`, almost every sample differs.
- Only the prompt with a 1-token prefix stays deterministic, so the failure appears when requests in a batch share a prefix.
- On an RTX 4090 (triton attention), the same test gave 2 unique outputs for the 2048-token prefix in 3 of 3 runs, and 1 for the other prefixes.
- `--test-mode single` (30 batch sizes) and `--test-mode radix_cache` pass for gpt-oss on the 4090.

We first saw this as a greedy request answering differently on a prefix-cache hit and a miss under `--enable-deterministic-inference`. That happened in 9 of 9 checks over two runs on gpt-oss-20b, and in 0 of 5 on a hybrid-Mamba model with the same flags.

### Reproduction

```bash
python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path openai/gpt-oss-20b --port 30000 \
    --context-length 8192 --mem-fraction-static 0.80 --max-running-requests 256 \
    --enable-deterministic-inference --attention-backend triton
# optional: --moe-runner-backend marlin   (much worse) / triton / triton_kernel (the default for gpt-oss)

python -m sglang.test.test_deterministic --port 30000 --test-mode prefix --n-start 1 --n-trials 30
```

items.title: cuBLASLt GEMM runners: tactic is an index into a per-exact-M algorithm list, which does not survive M bucketing
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
Code references are FlashInfer main as of 2026-10-06. The mechanism was reproduced on an SM107 (Rubin) GPU through the CuTe-DSL bf16 path's cuBLASLt fallback; the GB300 `mm_bf16 auto` failure is inferred from the same code path.

## How the runners work today
`include/flashinfer/gemm/mm_bf16_cublaslt.cuh::get_algorithms` calls `cublasLtMatmulAlgoGetHeuristic`
for the exact problem (M, N, K, dtypes, bias alignment, workspace limit) and copies up to 100 returned
`cublasLtMatmulAlgo_t` (64 bytes each) into a buffer. The Python runner's tactic is an **index** into
that buffer (`get_valid_tactics` = `range(count)`); `run_with_algo` memcpy's entry `algo_idx` and calls
`cublasLtMatmul` without `cublasLtMatmulAlgoCheck`. `bmm_fp8`'s cuBLASLt runner uses the same scheme.

The heuristic returns a *ranked shortlist for that exact problem*, not a fixed catalogue: membership and
order depend on M (tile count / waves, split-K benefit and its M*N workspace, alignment applicability).
So index i means "the i-th best predicted config for this M" and differs between M values.

## Two bugs from that
1. **`CublasltBf16GemmRunner` (mm_bf16):** `get_cache_key_extras` returns `(M, N, K, ...)`, violating the
   autotuner's rule that extras be synthesis-invariant (`TunableRunner.get_cache_key_extras` docstring).
   Winners are stored under the bucket's synthetic M and looked up with the real M, so they never hit:
   every call in tuning mode re-profiles (24 tactics per call on Rubin at M=512), which raises
   `AutoTuner profiling cannot begin during an active outer CUDA Graph capture` inside graph capture
   (6 failures of `mm_bf16 --backends auto --autotune`, M>=512, on GB300). Outside tuning mode the tuned
   tactic is silently not used.
2. **`CublasFp8GemmRunner` (bmm_fp8):** #3437 fixed the key (extras = dtypes only), but `forward` still
   enumerates the list at the *actual* M and replays the tuned index against it. An in-range index then
   runs whichever algorithm sits at that position for this M -- possibly not the one that won tuning;
   out of range falls back to the heuristic default.

## Proposed fix (both runners)
- Enumerate candidates at the **bucketed M** (the cuDNN runners in the same file already build their
  plans at `self._m_bucket_mapper(actual_m)`), and keep M out of the cache-key extras.
- Make the tactic the **algorithm descriptor** (the 64-byte `cublasLtMatmulAlgo_t`, e.g. as a tuple of 8
  uint64) rather than a list index, so it means the same thing at every M in the bucket and across runs.
- At run time, validate the descriptor once per exact problem with `cublasLtMatmulAlgoCheck` (memoized;
  it also reports the workspace needed, which grows with M for split-K) and fall back to the heuristic's
  top result if it does not apply.
- Persisted tactics are cuBLASLt-version specific: tie them to the cuBLASLt version in the cache
  fingerprint, and rely on the AlgoCheck fallback for anything stale.

Trade-off: a config tuned at the bucket's M may not be the best at every M in the bucket -- the same
trade-off every other bucketed runner already makes.

I am preparing a PR along these lines.

comments.body:
Re. the UI stuff, as explained on [this comment](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/12700#discussioncomment-13141818), I think frontend development in llama.cpp is no longer a beginner-friendly task as it used to be. The problem is that frontend development can be very hard to get it right (too many approaches to do the same thing.) Nowadays, I only accept PRs that follow modern web dev practices, especially practices on ReactJS and Typescript.

However, I think tutorial to document "llama.cpp-specific" setups, like how to build and bundle it with the binary, can be useful, as this is not common frontend dev knowledge.

comments.author: no4ni
comments.body:
**Документация: Работа с `llama.cpp` b6286 (август 2025)**

**1. Изменения в архитектуре и API**

*   **Изменение публичного API:** Прямой доступ к внутренним библиотекам `ggml` и `gguf` через их заголовочные файлы (`ggml/ggml.h`, `ggml/gguf.h`) **больше не является публичным или рекомендуемым**. Функции вроде `gguf_init_from_file`, `gguf_get_n_tensors` и т.д. скрыты.
*   **Унификация API:** Всё взаимодействие с моделью, её метаданными и тензорами теперь должно происходить **только** через унифицированный API, предоставляемый в **`include/llama.h`** (и `include/llama-cpp.h` для C++).
*   **Изменение структуры `include`:** Публичные заголовки теперь находятся непосредственно в `include/`. Внутренние заголовки `ggml` перемещены в `ggml/include/`.

**2. Создание собственного примера/приложения (например, `qedit`)**

*   **Расположение:** Поместите исходный код примера (например, `qedit.cpp`) и его `CMakeLists.txt` в подкаталог `examples/<имя_примера>/` внутри корня проекта `llama.cpp`. Например: `llama.cpp/examples/qedit/`.
*   **`CMakeLists.txt` примера:**
    ```cmake
    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
    project(<имя_примера> CXX) # Замените <имя_примера> на имя вашего проекта

    set(TARGET <имя_примера>)
    add_executable(${TARGET} <имя_файла>.cpp) # Замените <имя_файла>.cpp на имя вашего .cpp файла

    target_compile_features(${TARGET} PRIVATE cxx_std_17)

    # Указываем include-путь к llama.h
    target_include_directories(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include    # папка с llama.h
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/common   # Если используете заголовки из common
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/ggml/include # Только если требуется прямой доступ к внутренним ggml (не рекомендуется)
    )

    # Линкуем необходимые библиотеки
    target_link_libraries(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        # common     # Если используете утилиты из common
        llama        # ОСНОВНАЯ библиотека, предоставляющая API из llama.h
        # ggml       # Обычно не нужно явно указывать, так как llama зависит от ggml.
                     # Но можно оставить для ясности.
        # ggml-cuda  # НЕ НУЖНО. Отдельная цель ggml-cuda НЕ СОЗДАЕТСЯ.
                     # Функциональность CUDA интегрирована в основную библиотеку ggml.
        ${CMAKE_THREAD_LIBS_INIT} # Если требуется
    )
    ```
*   **Использование API:** В коде вашего примера используйте только функции, объявленные в `include/llama.h`. Примеры функций:
    *   `llama_backend_init()`, `llama_backend_free()`: Инициализация/деинициализация бэкенда.
    *   `llama_model_default_params()`: Получение параметров модели по умолчанию.
    *   `llama_load_model_from_file()`: Загрузка модели.
    *   `llama_model_meta_count()`, `llama_model_meta_key_by_index()`, `llama_model_meta_val_str_by_index()`: Доступ к метаданным модели.
    *   `llama_model_n_embd()`, `llama_model_n_ctx_train()`, `llama_model_n_params()`: Получение информации о модели (некоторые могут требовать активного контекста).
    *   `llama_free_model()`: Освобождение модели.

**3. Сборка проекта `llama.cpp`**

*   **Конфигурация CMake:**
    *   Используйте CMake для генерации проекта сборки.
    *   Для включения поддержки CUDA используйте опцию `-DGGML_CUDA=ON` (устаревшая `LLAMA_CUBLAS=ON` больше не поддерживается).
    *   Пример команды для Visual Studio 2022:
        ```bash
        cmake .. -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_COMMON=ON -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON
        ```
*   **Сборка библиотек:**
    *   При включении `GGML_CUDA=ON` и `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` (по умолчанию для MSVC):
        *   Исходники CUDA (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/*`) добавляются в сборку основной библиотеки `ggml`.
        *   Создаются файлы `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.dll` (содержит и CPU, и CUDA код) и `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.lib` (библиотека импорта для этой DLL).
    *   Основная библиотека `llama.lib` зависит от `ggml.lib`. Линковка с `llama.lib` предоставляет доступ ко всей функциональности, включая CU

items.title: Misc. bug: Blackwell GGML-CUDA SOFT_MAX Crash
items.author: giveen
items.body_excerpt:
# Blackwell GGML-CUDA SOFT_MAX Crash Fix

**Author:** Not a programmer — just a security guy who asked DeepSeek-v4 to
write the patches.
**Date:** 2026-06-26
**Target:** llama.cpp ggml-cuda on Blackwell RTX 5090 (SM 12.0), CUDA 13.3,
Driver 580.17

---

## What Went Wrong

Running large models (35B MoE) on an RTX 5090 caused an immediate crash:

```
ggml_cuda_compute_forward: SOFT_MAX failed
```

Under the hood: `cudaErrorInvalidValue` on `cudaLaunchKernel` for the softmax
kernel. The driver said **"Requested 1152 bytes of shared memory, but max is
0 bytes."**

## Root Cause

Two separate bugs:

### Bug 1: The driver handed us a nonsense number

At startup, llama.cpp reads `sharedMemPerBlockOptin` from the GPU to know how
much shared memory it can request. On this RTX 5090 with CUDA 13.3, that value
came back as **4294967297** (= 0x100000001) instead of the correct **101376**.

Why? Unknown. Could be a CUDA 13.3 driver bug on Blackwell, or a struct layout
mismatch in the old CUDA headers the code was compiled with. Either way, the
software then fed that garbage number to `cudaFuncSetAttribute`, which
silently rejected it and left the limit at 0 — meaning any kernel asking for
shared memory was dead on arrival.

**Fix:** Validate the value before using it. If it's below the guaranteed
default or above 256 KB (no GPU has ever had more), use the safe default
instead. This is generic across all architectures, not a Blackwell hack.

### Bug 2: The cache missed every call after the first

The code used a macro `CUDA_SET_SHARED_MEMORY_LIMIT` that only called
`cudaFuncSetAttribute` once per GPU, then cached the result. But softmax
kernels are template instantiations — the same line of source code produces
multiple actual kernel functions at compile time (`soft_max_f32<true, 256,
256>`, `soft_max_f32<true, 512, 256>`, etc.). The cache only saved the flag
for the *first* one it saw, leaving every other instantiation with no shared
memory limit set.

**Fix:** Track kernel function pointers in an array instead of a boolean.
Each unique kernel address gets its own entry. No more missed calls.

## Files Changed

| File | Lines | What |
|------|-------|------|
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/common.cuh` | +15/-4 | Fixed `CUDA_SET_SHARED_MEMORY_LIMIT` to track per-kernel (not per-device) |
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu` | +11/-1 | Added bounds validation on `sharedMemPerBlockOptin` |
| `ggml/src/ggml-cuda/softmax.cu` | +0/-1 | Removed blank line (debug artifact) |

**Total: 21 insertions, 6 deletions**

## Verified On

- **GPU:** NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (32 GB VRAM)
- **Model:** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_XL
- **Benchmark:** pp128=4231 t/s, tg256=262 t/s
- **Errors:** Zero

## Patch

See attached `ggml-cuda-blackwell-fix.patch`.

---

*This fix was written entirely by an AI agent at my direction. I cannot audit
CUDA code. If you are smarter than me (likely), please review and upstream a
better version.*

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

  0.03.207.415 E /mnt/storage/Projects/llama-cpp-exp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:104: CUDA error                                                                                                                                                          
     ggml_cuda_compute_forward: SOFT_MAX failed                                                                                                                                                                                                                  
     0.03.207.421 E CUDA error: invalid argument                                                                                                                                                                                                                 
     0.03.207.423 E   current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_compute_forward at /mnt/storage/Projects/llama-cpp-exp/ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:3128                                                                                                       
     0.03.207.423 E   err                

[ggml-cuda-blackwell-fix.patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29391973/ggml-cuda-blackwell-fix.patch)

items.title: server: pinning a request to an empty slot via id_slot skips the prompt cache
items.author: yitizi
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

master 9723942ad. The same code path is present in d7a207411 (b10644); this logic is byte-identical between the two.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m tinygemma3.gguf --parallel 2 --cache-ram 4096 --slots
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

When a request is pinned to a slot via `id_slot` and that slot is currently **empty**, the prompt cache is never consulted. The request pays a full prefill even when the cache holds an exact match. Slots that already hold tokens are not affected.

**Steps to reproduce**

Setup: 2 slots, `--cache-ram 4096`, tinygemma3.

1. request A with `id_slot=0` — fills slot 0
2. request B with `id_slot=0` — A is moved into the prompt cache; slot 1 has never been used
3. request A again, three variants

Results from step 3:

| pinned to | `cache_n` | `prompt_n` |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| not pinned | 285 | 5 |
| **`id_slot=1` (empty slot)** | **0** | **290** |
| `id_slot=0` (holds B) | 285 | 5 |

**Expected:** pinning to an empty slot should hit the cache. An empty slot has no context that could be destroyed, so it is the safest case for reuse.

**Actual:** the cache is skipped entirely and all 290 tokens are re-processed.

**Root cause**

`tools/server/server-context.cpp:1587`

```cpp
const float f_keep = (f_sim_best*task.tokens.size()) / ret->prompt.tokens.size();
...
// if we are about to lose a large portion of the existing context - save it in the prompt cache
if (f_keep < 0.5f) {
    update_cache = true;
}
```

When the pinned slot is empty, `ret->prompt.tokens.size()` is 0, and no slot passed the similarity filter so `f_sim_best` is 0. The expression is therefore `0.0f / 0.0f`, which is NaN.

`NaN < 0.5f` is false, so `update_cache` stays false and `prompt_load()` is never reached.

The LRU branch that would otherwise set `update_cache = true` is also skipped, because it is guarded by `ret == nullptr` and `ret` was already assigned in the `id_slot` branch above.

**Suggested fix**

```cpp
const float f_keep = ret->prompt.tokens.size() > 0
    ? (f_sim_best*task.tokens.size()) / ret->prompt.tokens.size()
    : 0.0f;
```

An empty slot has no context to lose, so `f_keep = 0` is the correct value, and `update_cache` becomes true as intended.

**Impact**

Any setup that routes requests with `id_slot`. All slots are empty after a server restart, so the first request on each slot pays a full prefill even when the prompt cache holds an exact match.

**Reproduction script**

Runs against the project's own test harness, from `tools/server/tests`:

```python
import os, sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
os.environ["LLAMA_SERVER_BIN_PATH"] = "<path to llama-server>"
from utils import ServerPreset

A = ("Once upon a time in a land far away, there lived a brave knight "
     "who traveled across mountains and rivers to find the legendary "
     "golden sword hidden deep within the enchanted forest of whispers. ") * 8
B = ("Completely unrelated technical content about compiler optimization "
     "passes, register allocation, and instruction scheduling heuristics. ") * 8

def run(pin_to):
    s = ServerPreset.tinygemma3()
    s.no_mmproj = True; s.n_predict = 4; s.temperature = 0.0
    s.server_slots = True; s.kv_unified = True
    s.n_slots = 2; s.cache_ram = 4096
    s.start(timeout_seconds=120)
    def go(p, slot):
        d = {"prompt": p, "cache_prompt": True}
        if slot is not None:
            d["id_slot"] = slot
        return s.make_request("POST", "/completion", data=d).body["timings"]
    go(A, 0)   # slot 0 <- A
    go(B, 0)   # slot 0 <- B; A moves into the prompt cache; slot 1 stays empty
    t = go(A, pin_to)
    s.stop()
    return t

for pin_to, label in ((None, "UNPINNED (server picks)"),
                      (1,    "PINNED to EMPTY slot 1"),
                      (0,    "PINNED to slot 0 (holds B)")):
    t = run(pin_to)
    print(f"{label:<28} cache_n={t.get('cache_n')}  prompt_n={t.get('prompt_n')}")
```

**AI usage disclosure**

The reproduction, measurements and root-cause analysis were done with Claude assisting. I verified the results on my own hardware.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. The logic is unchanged between d7a207411 and 9723942ad.

### Relevant log output

_No response_

items.title: Compile bug: ggml_backend_sycl_device_get_memory aborts with "failed to get device memory size" on Intel Arc Pro B60 (Battlemage)
items.author: dgv21
items.body_excerpt:
### Git commit

Environment
GPU: Sparkle Arc Pro B60 24GB (Battlemage G21, PCI device 8086:e211)
OS: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS (Resolute), fresh install
Kernel: 7.0.0-31-generic
Kernel GPU driver: xe (confirmed correct driver for Battlemage — i915 does NOT support Battlemage compute, only basic display)
GuC firmware: xe/bmg_guc_70.bin version 70.58.0 (loaded successfully, confirmed via dmesg)
HuC firmware: xe/bmg_huc.bin version 8.2.10 (loaded successfully)
Compute stack: libze-intel-gpu1 / intel-opencl-icd 26.31.39395.13-1~26.04~ppa1 (kobuk-team/intel-graphics PPA)
oneAPI: 2026.1 (intel-oneapi-compiler-dpcpp-cpp, intel-oneapi-mkl-devel)
llama.cpp: built from master branch, same-day checkout, SYCL backend (-DGGML_SYCL=ON -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON, icx/icpx compilers)

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

SYCL

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

sycl-ls confirms the device is correctly detected before running llama.cpp:   [level_zero:gpu][level_zero:0] Intel(R) oneAPI Unified Runtime over Level-Zero V2, Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics 20.1.0 [1.17.39395+13]
[opencl:gpu][opencl:1] Intel(R) OpenCL Graphics, Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics OpenCL 3.0 NEO [26.31.39395.13]

llama-server (and presumably llama-cli) aborts immediately on model load with:  /home/geo/llama.cpp/ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp:6101: [ggml_backend_sycl_device_get_memory] failed to get device memory size

Full backtrace:

/home/geo/llama.cpp/build/bin/libggml-base.so.0(+0x17d48) [0x7031cbe31d48]
/home/geo/llama.cpp/build/bin/libggml-base.so.0(ggml_print_backtrace+0x285) [0x7031cbe31d25]
/home/geo/llama.cpp/build/bin/libggml-base.so.0(ggml_abort+0x109) [0x7031cbe30d99]
/home/geo/llama.cpp/build/bin/libggml-sycl.so.0(+0x230c76) [0x7031c6c30c76]
/home/geo/llama.cpp/build/bin/libggml-sycl.so.0(+0x230d97) [0x7031c6c30d97]
/home/geo/llama.cpp/build/bin/libllama.so.0(+0xaf808) [0x7031cacaf808]
/home/geo/llama.cpp/build/bin/libllama.so.0(llama_model_load_from_file+0xfc) [0x7031cacb097c]
... (common_init_from_params / server_context_impl::load_model chain)

This reproduces on a completely fresh OS install with current drivers/firmware/oneAPI — ruling out stale config, leftover packages, or a driver mismatch as the cause. Also reproduces identically whether the system has one or two B60 cards installed, so it is not specific to multi-GPU configurations.


Root cause (best guess)

get_memory_size() in ggml-sycl.cpp calls into a Level-Zero/SYCL memory-query API that appears to return failure on this specific GPU/driver/firmware combination, even though the device is otherwise fully functional (confirmed by clinfo, sycl-ls, and xpu-smi all reporting the device correctly). The current code treats any query failure as fatal via GGML_ABORT, with no fallback path.

Fix / Workaround

Replacing the hard abort with a fallback value lets the model load and run normally. Confirmed working on this hardware:

File: ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp, ggml_backend_sycl_device_get_memory() (~line 6101 on current master; also a second occurrence a few lines later in a related function)

Before: cpp
if (!res) {
    GGML_ABORT("[%s] failed to get device memory size", __func__);
}

THE FIX!

if (!res) {
    GGML_LOG_WARN("[%s] failed to get device memory size, using fallback\n", __func__);
    *total = 25769803776ULL;
    *free  = 25769803776ULL;
}


(25769803776 = 24GB in bytes, matching this card's VRAM — should ideally be derived from actual card VRAM rather than hardcoded, but works as an immediate fallback since it's used consistently across both occurrences in the file.)

Applied via:   sed -i 's/GGML_ABORT("\[%s\] failed to get device memory size", __func__);/GGML_LOG_WARN("[%s] failed to get device memory size, using fallback\\n", __func__);\n        *total = 25769803776ULL;\n        *free  = 25769803776ULL;/' ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp

### First Bad Commit

cpp
if (!res) {
    GGML_ABORT("[%s] failed to get device memory size", __func__);
}

### Compile command

```shell
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force
cd llama.cpp
cmake -B build -DGGML_SYCL=ON -DGGML_SYCL_F16=ON \
  -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=icx -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=icpx \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS_RELEASE="-O3 -DNDEBUG" \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE="-O3 -DNDEBUG" -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF
cmake --build build --config Release -j4
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
0.00.121.120 I cmn  common_param: common_params_print_info: verbosity = 3 (adjust with the `-lv N` CLI arg)
0.00.121.365 W srv  llama_server: -----------------
0.00.121.366 W srv  llama_server: CORS is set to allow all origins ('*') and no API key is set
0.00.121.366 W srv  llama_server: this can be a security risk (cross-origin attacks)
0.00.121.367 W srv  llama_server: more info: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25655
0.00.121.367 W srv  llama_server: -----------------

items.author: srflaherty
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

`llama-bench` built from source at b10405 (`e79e4bf`), b11074 (`26394b4`) and b11425 (`e117148`), and at the two commits either side of #25773 for the bisect. Windows, MSVC + Ninja, `GGML_VULKAN=ON`, static, AVX2.

### Operating systems

Windows 11 Pro (build 26300)

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (driver 617.14), Intel Core i9-14900K. `ggml_vulkan` reports: `uma: 0 | fp16: 1 | bf16: 1 | fp4: 0 | warp size: 32 | shared memory: 49152 | int dot: 1 | matrix cores: NV_coopmat2`.

### Models

Qwen3-Embedding-8B Q8_0 (`Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B-GGUF`), Qwen3-Reranker-8B Q8_0, IBM granite-4.2-8b Q8_0.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Prompt processing on this card is **16–18% slower since #25773** ("vulkan: use spec constant for matrix matrix multiplication A-type", `91f6a6cf3`) on all three Q8_0 models. Token generation is unchanged. It is still present at b11425.

Command — only the build differs between arms; A·B·B·A order, 5 repetitions each, nothing else on the card (the second Vulkan device here is an Intel UHD 770, hence `-dev Vulkan0 -sm none`):

```
llama-bench -m granite-4.2-8b-Q8_0.gguf -dev Vulkan0 -sm none -ngl 99 -fa 1 -ub 512 -b 512 -r 5 -p 512 -n 128
llama-bench -m Qwen3-Embedding-8B-Q8_0.gguf -dev Vulkan0 -sm none -ngl 99 -fa 1 -ub 512 -b 512 -r 5 -embd 1 -p 128,512 -n 0
```

**The commit before (`6d9c82ea2`) vs #25773 (`91f6a6cf3`)**, pp512, tokens/s:

| model | 6d9c82ea2 | 91f6a6cf3 | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3-Embedding-8B Q8_0 | 2,798 | 2,348 | −16% |

We found it with `git bisect run` between b10405 and b11074, where the whole difference is this one commit (two A·B·B·A passes, pp512): embedding 2,895 / 2,901 → 2,411 / 2,400 · reranker 2,909 / 2,881 → 2,421 / 2,416 · granite 3,062 / 3,062 → 2,497 / 2,489.

**Today, b10405 vs b11425** (A·B·B·A, pp512):

| model | b10405 | b11425 | |

granite tg128: 43.4 / 43.5 → 43.5 / 43.5 t/s (unchanged).

Happy to run a test build, try a patch, or collect `GGML_VK_PERF_LOGGER` output on this card.

91f6a6cf3 (#25773)

items.title: Misc. bug: Qwen3.6 tool calls leak into content when the model omits <tool_call> (fallback scoped out in #27679)
items.author: tibernero
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

version: 0.5.0-dev (build 11382, commit 11fe02151), llama-swap v262 CUDA image
Also checked: build 10433 (commit 9b05354ec), which does not show the problem.

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_XS.gguf --jinja -ngl 999 -fa on \
  --ctx-size 163840 --parallel 1 -n 8192 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 \
  --reasoning-budget 6000 --chat-template-file qwen-fixed-v21.3-terse.jinja
```

The template is froggeric's Qwen fixed template (v21.3); it contains `<think>`.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With tools in the request and tool_choice auto, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B sometimes writes a tool call without the opening `<tool_call>` token. The rest of the call is well formed:

```
<function=web_search>
<parameter=query>
Brooklyn Bridge opening year date
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
```

On b11382 that whole block comes back in `message.content` with `finish_reason: stop` and no `tool_calls`. Requesting with `"parse_tool_calls": false, "reasoning_format": "none"` shows the raw output goes straight from `</think>\n\n` to `<function=`, so the model really does skip the opener.

The payload below (one system prompt, one user question, two web tools) reproduces it. 100 non-streaming requests each, same GGUF, same template:

| build | tool calls parsed | leaked into content |
|---|---|---|
| b11382 (Linux, RTX 3090) | 15 | 9 |
| b10433 (Windows, RTX 5090) | 13 | 0 |

The two builds ran on different machines, so this is not a clean bisect, but the parser difference below accounts for it.

`python3 repro.py http://HOST:PORT/v1/chat/completions 100 MODEL payload.json`

<details><summary>repro.py</summary>

```python
import json, sys, urllib.request
url, n, model = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]
body = json.load(open(sys.argv[4])); body["model"] = model
c = {"tool_calls": 0, "leaked_as_content": 0, "plain_answer": 0}; ex = None
for _ in range(n):
    r = urllib.request.Request(url, json.dumps(body).encode(), {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    m = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(r, timeout=180))["choices"][0]["message"]
    t = m.get("content") or ""
    if m.get("tool_calls"): c["tool_calls"] += 1
    elif "<function=" in t: c["leaked_as_content"] += 1; ex = ex or t
    else: c["plain_answer"] += 1
print(n, c); print("example leaked content:", repr(ex))
```

</details>

items.title: Nepheral: a P2P AI network using llama.cpp (Rust bindings, CPU/Vulkan/CUDA, one model copy per GPU)
items.author: JEHR037
items.body_excerpt: Hi everyone! For the last five or six months I've been building **Nepheral**, a peer-to-peer network where people's machines answer each other's questions with local models. llama.cpp is the engine that makes it possible, so I wanted to share how it's used here. ### How llama.cpp is used - **In-process, from Rust**, through the [`llama-cpp-2`](https://crates.io/crates/llama-cpp-2) bindings (0.1.157). No sidecar server: the node loads the GGUF directly. - **Three backends from one codebase**: CPU, Vulkan and CUDA builds, plus an "auto" build that detects CUDA or Vulkan at runtime and falls back to CPU. - **Multi-GPU rigs**: besides llama.cpp's own split across cards, a node can load **one copy of the model per GPU** and run one worker per card, so a rig answers several questions at once. - **Any GGUF from Hugging Face**, checked against the publisher's SHA-256 before loading. Vision projectors (`mmproj`) are skipped for now. - **Answers for the network are stateless**: each question carries its own context, and reasoning/"thinking" is turned off for those answers so small models reply straight away. ### What Nepheral does around it - Every install is a node. Nodes with a model enter a draw for each question; phones and machines without a GPU can still ask. - Questions are encrypted for the drawn nodes and split into pieces held by other nodes; the winner gathers them, answers with llama.cpp, and seals the answer back to the asker. The answering node does read the question (it runs the model), so the app masks emails, phone numbers and similar first. - Conversation memory is decided on the asker's device with a small multilingual embedding model, so the network only gets the context it needs. ### Honest limits - Most nodes today run small models and answers take about 4 to 20 seconds. - The code isn't public yet; it will be released under BUSL 1.1. ### Try it / help If you have a GPU that sits idle, you can join as a node (Windows, Linux, or a headless Linux server), and I'd love feedback on how it detects and loads models on your hardware: https://nepheral.net/download Thanks to everyone working on llama.cpp. None of this would exist without it.

items.title: [RFC]: End-to-End Transfer Tracing for Mooncake
items.author: llfl
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

  This RFC proposes a unified tracing architecture for Mooncake transfer execution.

  The design introduces a reusable tracing subsystem and applies it across the transfer path so a single
  logical transfer can be observed across:

  - store-facing orchestration
  - transfer-engine batch management
  - multi-transport task submission
  - per-slice data-plane execution
  - terminal completion / failure / timeout reporting

  The result is a structurally consistent trace tree that supports both live debugging and offline postmortem
  analysis.

  ---

  ## Motivation

  Mooncake transfer workflows cross several layers, but observability has historically been fragmented. Logs
  and metrics can show symptoms, but they do not preserve causality.

  This creates recurring problems:

  - latency attribution is ambiguous
  - control-plane and data-plane delays are hard to separate
  - timeout root cause is difficult to localize
  - store-level operations and transfer-engine execution are not naturally correlated
  - external systems cannot reliably ingest or reconstruct transfer timelines

  We need tracing that preserves parent-child relationships across the full transfer lifecycle, not just
  isolated spans emitted by individual modules.

  ---

  ## Goals

  - Provide a common tracing substrate for Mooncake components
  - Preserve trace continuity across store, transfer engine, and transport layers
  - Model transfer execution with stable, explicit span hierarchy
  - Export traces to local files and OTLP collectors
  - Support async export with retry and spool behavior
  - Improve trace completeness for failure and timeout cases
  - Make offline investigation possible from raw JSONL outputs

  ## Non-goals

  - Redesign transfer scheduling or transport selection
  - Replace existing metrics or logs
  - Guarantee zero-overhead tracing on hot paths
  - Fully redesign all observability ownership boundaries in one patch
  - Solve every TENT-specific tracing gap in this RFC

  ---

  ## Background

  A Mooncake transfer is not a single function call. It is a lifecycle:

  1. a store-side operation decides how to move data
  2. transfer-engine allocates and manages a batch
  3. multi-transport selects concrete transports
  4. transports submit slice-level work
  5. status polling eventually determines terminal state

  Without explicit trace propagation, each stage can emit useful local signals while the global story remains
  invisible.

  The core design principle of this RFC is:

  **Make the lifecycle first-class.**
  Do not infer it from logs after the fact.

  ---

  ## Proposal

  ### 1. Introduce `mooncake-tracing`

  Add a dedicated tracing module that provides:

  - `TraceContext`
  - `TraceCarrier`
  - `TraceRecord`
  - `TracingFacade`
  - RAII-style `Span`
  - configurable sampling
  - pluggable exporters

  This module becomes the single place where trace creation, parenting, export, and sampling behavior live.

  ### 2. Define a stable transfer span hierarchy

  The proposed hierarchy is:

  - `mooncake.transfer.operation`
    - `mooncake.transfer.submit_gap`
    - `te.batch`
      - `te.batch.submit`
        - `te.task.submit`
          - slice events
      - `te.batch.execute`
      - `te.task.status`
      - `te.batch.status`
    - `mooncake.transfer.wait_completion`
    - `mooncake.transfer.complete`

  This hierarchy captures both:
  - the user-visible transfer operation lifecycle
  - the internal execution lifecycle inside the transfer engine

  ### 3. Support parent context propagation

  When an upstream trace context exists, Mooncake should attach to it.
  When no parent exists, Mooncake should create its own operation root.

  This allows Mooncake transfers to participate in larger distributed traces while still remaining self-
  contained when invoked directly.

  ### 4. Keep batch-level tracing alive until terminal state

  A short-lived submit-only span is insufficient because a transfer can spend most of its time after
  submission.

  The batch root span must survive until terminal completion, failure, cancellation, or timeout.
  A separate persistent execution span (`te.batch.execute`) captures the data-plane lifetime.

  ### 5. Add explicit task and slice tracing state

  `MultiTransport` maintains trace registry state for:

  - batch context
  - task context
  - transport name
  - slice queue state
  - slice terminal state
  - deduplicated terminal markers

  This avoids duplicate terminal events and lets status polling produce complete traces even when terminal
  evidence appears asynchronously.

  ### 6. Export traces through configurable backends

  Supported paths include:

  - in-memory exporter for tests
  - JSONL exporter for local/debug workflows
