items.title: [RFC] [Feature] Intra-Device Heterogeneous Memory Allocation Support
items.author: jackbondpreston-arm
items.body_excerpt:
# 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Terminology: Inter- vs Intra-Device Heterogeneous Memory
We define **intra**-device heterogeneous memory as memory which is heterogeneous (has different properties), *within the same device*.
PyTorch currently supports **inter**-device heterogeneous memory by enabling applications to allocate Tensors on different devices, ie. through the `device` parameter on `Tensor` constructors:

```python^Q
torch.zeros(..., device="cuda") # allocate Tensor in CUDA memory, using CUDA allocator
```

but not for intra-device heterogeneous memory.

### Motivation
Heterogeneous host-side memory is becoming more common. Some example implementations that existed previously, are available today, or are coming soon include:

- Intel's [Sapphire Rapids HBM/Xeon Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapphire_Rapids#Sapphire_Rapids-HBM_(High_Bandwidth_Memory/Xeon_Max_Series)): 64GB on-chip HBM, with "flat mode" supporting putting HBM and DRAM on different NUMA nodes.
- SiPearl's [Rhea](https://sipearl.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/PR_SiPearl_Rhea1_EN.pdf) and [Rhea-2](https://www.anandtech.com/show/21295/sipearls-rhea2-cpu-added-to-roadmap-second-gen-european-cpu-for-hpc): On-chip HBM and off-chip DDR.
- In the future, expected increasing prevalence of CXL.mem - adding another tier of heterogeneous memory to systems utilising it.
- A future trend towards more DDR + [Non-volatile Memory (NVM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-volatile_memory) platforms.

Making the most of these platforms with multiple types of host-memory will likely include application programmers making choices about which memory type they want certain allocations to be on. In PyTorch, this means allowing applications to specify which memory backing a Tensor will use - as this is the main unit of storage within PyTorch. An application may wish to place Tensors on HBM in order to maximise bandwidth when performing ML operations, or to place on DRAM to make use of capacity in cases of oversubscription. 
Currently PyTorch has no way to allow applications to place tensors on specific memory types within a device, so application programmers can't maximise performance and usage on these heterogeneous systems.

### Feature: Support for intra-device heterogeneous memory support
The proposal is to implement support for another layer of memory heterogeneity - *intra-device* heterogeneity on top of *inter-device* heterogeneity. 
For example, in a case where a CPU has multiple types of memory, a PyTorch application can choose which of these their Tensor will be backed by, when using the CPU device. 
The same could also be applicable to other devices (e.g. CUDA, XPU, etc.) - if they have multiple types of memory, some application programmers in the future may want finer-grained control of the Tensors' backing.

## Design

### Extra (Default) Parameter for `Device`s
An extra optional parameter will be added to the `torch.device`/`c10::Device` constructors, allowing the specification of a memory type within that device. This can then be provided to Tensor constructors, to specify that the Tensor should be allocated on this device, *and* on a specific memory type within this device:

```python
cpu_hbm = torch.device("cpu", 0, memory_type="hbm")

x = torch.zeros(1000, device=cpu_hbm)
```

Also supported will be the string representation of devices:

```python
# type[:[index][:[memory_type]]]

torch.device('cpu:0:hbm') == torch.device(type='cpu', index=0, memory_type='hbm')
torch.device('cpu::hbm') == torch.device(type='cpu', memory_type='hbm')
torch.device('cuda:1:') == torch.device('cuda:1') = torch.device(type='cuda', index=1)
```

The parameter will be of an enum type, containing all the memory types supported by any devices in PyTorch. For example:

```cpp
/* New enum - MemoryType */
enum class MemoryType {
    DEFAULT,
    DDR,
    HBM,
    CXL,
    PMEM,
    DISK,
    // ...
}
```

The default value for MemoryType, if not specified, is `DEFAULT`. This will use the default memory type, which must be whichever memory type PyTorch used before this change, for backwards compatibility.

The heterogeneous allocation support will be implemented *by the device allocator*. The MemoryType from the `torch.device` used for the Tensor allocation will be passed through to the allocator's `allocate` method:

```
/* c10/core/Allocator.h                           */
/* Example change for demonstration purposes only */

struct C10_API Allocator {
  virtual ~Allocator() = default;

  virtual DataPtr allocate(size_t n) = 0;

  virtual DataPtr allocate(size_t n, MemoryType memType = MemoryType::DEFAULT) {
    // default is to ignore memType, devices can provide implementations using this parameter where necessary
    return allocate(n);
  }

  // ...
```

Currently the `StorageImpl` constructors do not take any information about the `device` argument provided to the Tensor constructor functions, only a pointer to the dispatched Allocator. Thus, the `MemoryType` (or the whole `Device`) will have to be passed down through e.g. `empty_generic` as an extra argument, through `StorageImpl` and down to the `Allocator::allocate()` function.

The `DataPtr`'s `device_` member will record the `MemoryType` *actually used* for the allocation, in cases where it differs from the user's request.


### API to query supported heterogeneous memory devices
Additionally, we propose adding an API to allow users to check the heterogeneous memory currently available for use on each device. This would have different implementations per-device, but would return an enumeration of the types of memory.

```python
# Equivalent - can accept a device or string, like Tensor constructors
>>> torch.get_device_memory_types("cpu")
>>> torch.get_device_memory_types(torch.device("cpu")) 
[ "ddr", "hbm", "cxl" ]

# Example implementation for CUDA, if it did not support heterogeneous memory types
>>> torch.get_device_memory_types("cuda:1")
[ ]
```

A device can return nothi

items.title: [inductor] Rebuild async-compile pools that have died instead of returning a closed pool
items.author: zm0794
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I prepared the report below with AI assistance (Kimi Code); the root cause was verified against 2.15.0.dev and the minimal repro run locally. Quoting it in full:

> **Describe the bug**
>
> `AsyncCompile.pool()` and `AsyncCompile.process_pool()` are memoized with `@functools.lru_cache(1)`. The cache is never invalidated when the pool goes away, so once a pool has been shut down — or has died on its own because its worker sidecar crashed — the same dead object is handed out forever. Every later compile then fails with `RuntimeError: Attempting to use a closed pool` (`torch/_inductor/compile_worker/subproc_pool.py`), which turns a transient failure into a permanent one for the rest of the process.
>
> This is easy to hit in any long-lived process — a pytest session, a service, or a training job that keeps compiling: a single sidecar crash poisons every subsequent `torch.compile` call in that process.
>
> **Observed on a real workload (out-of-tree backend)**
>
> We hit this in a long pytest session, after an upstream upgrade made our backend's Triton compilation actually go through `AsyncCompile` (`worker_start_method="subprocess"`). A stale `typing` backport (`3.7.4.3`) installed in the test venv shadowed the stdlib `typing` module inside the sidecar process, so the sidecar died during its own startup — `from typing import TypeVar` in `compile_worker/__main__.py` raised `AttributeError` — before it served a single job. The parent only saw the result-pipe EOF and set `running = False`; the dead pool stayed cached, and every later async Triton compile in that session failed with *Attempting to use a closed pool*: roughly 1640 test failures cascading from one root cause. (The sidecar's stdout/stderr go to `/dev/null` by default — `worker_suppress_logging=True` — so nothing was logged at the crash site.)
>
> **Root cause**
>
> These pools are process-wide singletons that must be created lazily, and `lru_cache(1)` is the shortest way to express that. But `lru_cache` has no invalidation rule for "the cached object died": `shutdown_compile_workers()` shuts the pools down without clearing the cache, and a sidecar death only flips `SubprocPool.running` to `False` (via `_on_sidecar_death()`, or the EOF path in `_read_thread()`). The only invalidation that exists today is `after_fork()`.
>
> The design assumption behind that: a pool's lifetime equals the process lifetime — teardown happens through `atexit.register(shutdown_compile_workers())`, so the only reset anyone needed was at a process boundary (fork).
>
> **Timeline — why this stayed latent, and what changed**
>
> The cache bug is trigger-agnostic: any death of the pool while the process keeps running exposes it. The individual death paths have very different version availability:
>
> - **Explicit `pool.shutdown()`** — present since the caching was introduced (May/June 2024). But in normal flow the only production caller of `shutdown_compile_workers()` is `atexit.register(...)`, i.e. pools die exactly when the process dies, so the dead-pool-reuse path was never exercised in production (tests do call it, but don't compile again in the same process afterwards).
> - **Sidecar startup death → result-pipe EOF → `running = False`** (the old `_read_thread` code) — present in 2.13; this is the path our CI hit.
> - **Sidecar mid-compile death in fork mode** — the pipe never EOFs (fd inheritance across a bare `os.fork()`, per #189290's root cause), so pre-#189290 this wedged the job in a hang instead of raising: a different failure mode that points nowhere near the pool cache.
> - **Detection of mid-compile death** (`_health_monitor` / `_on_sidecar_death`, the #189290 stack, July 2026) — made sidecar death *detectable* (hang → `running = False`) but did not touch the pool cache, so a natural pool death now surfaces as the permanent "closed pool" cascade.
>
> So the bug has been reproducible on every version since 2024 through the explicit-shutdown trigger (the minimal repro above runs unchanged on 2.13; verbatim output in Versions). What was missing until recently was a realistic *natural* trigger in long-lived processes. Our exposure came from an upgrade making our backend's Triton compiles actually go through `SubprocPool`, plus a broken `typing` backport killing the sidecar at startup. A tracker search for the exact error string returns no genuine prior report.
>
> **Minimal repro (pure PyTorch, no third-party backend)**
>
> ```python
> import torch
> from torch._inductor import async_compile

items.title: [PrivateUse1] set_data cross-device fails: has_compatible_shallow_copy_type dense_backends lacks PrivateUse1Bit
items.author: zm0794
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I prepared the report below with AI assistance; the repro and root-cause analysis were verified locally against v2.14.0 and main. Quoting it in full:

> **Describe the bug**
>
> `Tensor.set_data()` / `aten.shallow_copy_data_` raises "incompatible tensor type" when copying between a CPU tensor and a PrivateUse1 tensor. The root cause is that `TensorImpl::has_compatible_shallow_copy_type` hardcodes the dense backend set **without `PrivateUse1Bit`**, and `VariableHooks::set_data` calls `_has_compatible_shallow_copy_type` unqualified (resolving to the **native** function), so a `PrivateUse1` override of this operator is bypassed.
>
> **Repro (pure PyTorch, no third-party backend)**
>
> ```python
> import types
> import torch
> from torch._subclasses.fake_tensor import FakeTensorMode
> torch.utils.rename_privateuse1_backend("foo")
> m = types.ModuleType("torch.foo")
> m.is_initialized = lambda: True
> m.current_device = lambda: 0
> torch._register_device_module("foo", m)
> with FakeTensorMode():
>     cpu_t = torch.empty(2, device="cpu")
>     foo_t = torch.empty(2, device="foo")  # privateuse1 tensor
>     print(torch.ops.aten._has_compatible_shallow_copy_type(cpu_t, foo_t))  # False
>     torch.ops.aten.shallow_copy_data_(cpu_t, foo_t)
>     # RuntimeError: Attempted to call variable.set_data(tensor), but variable and
>     # tensor have incompatible tensor type.
> ```
>
> Note: `aten.shallow_copy_data_` is only exposed as a public op since 2.14, so the script above requires PyTorch 2.14+. On 2.13 the same root cause is visible one level down: `torch.ops.aten._has_compatible_shallow_copy_type(cpu_t, foo_t)` returns False for a PrivateUse1 `from` tensor (verified on 2.13.0+cpu).
>
> **Root cause**
>
> 1. `c10/core/TensorImpl.h` — `has_compatible_shallow_copy_type`: `dense_backends = {CPUBit, CUDABit, MPSBit, HIPBit, XPUBit, HPUBit, MTIABit}`, i.e. **no `PrivateUse1Bit`**, so any PrivateUse1 `from` tensor returns false.
> 2. `torch/csrc/autograd/variable.cpp` — `VariableHooks::set_data` calls `_has_compatible_shallow_copy_type(self, new_data)` **unqualified**, resolving to `at::native::_has_compatible_shallow_copy_type` and bypassing op dispatch.
>
> ### Versions
>
> Reproduced on PyTorch 2.14.0 (also reproduced on main; at the operator level `aten._has_compatible_shallow_copy_type(cpu_t, foo_t)` also returns False on 2.13.0). Local environment used for verification:

> OS: Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64)
> Python version: 3.12.3
> GCC version: 13.3.0

items.title: [Inductor] torch.mvlgamma silently returns zeros for p=0 instead of raising the eager p>=1 check
items.author: tinywisdom
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.mvlgamma(x, p)` validates `p` in eager (`TORCH_CHECK(p >= 1, "p has to be greater than or equal to 1")`,
`aten/src/ATen/native/UnaryOps.cpp`), but under `torch.compile` (Inductor) this check is lost: the op decomposes
through `torch.special.multigammaln`, which has no `p >= 1` guard, so an invalid `p=0` **silently returns zeros**
instead of raising. This is a validation-lost case (cf. the ☂️ #197554 tracker).

```python
import torch
x = torch.tensor([1.5, 2.5, 3.5], device='cuda')
f = lambda x: torch.mvlgamma(x, 0)
f(x)                                       # eager:    RuntimeError: p has to be greater than or equal to 1
torch.compile(f, backend="inductor")(x)    # inductor:  tensor([0., 0., 0.])  -- check dropped, silent
```
**Expected:** the compiled function raises the same `p >= 1` error as eager (or otherwise rejects), rather than
silently returning zeros. Related umbrella: #197554. (Distinct from #198155, which concerns dtype rejection, not
the `p` parameter check.)

items.title: `[Inductor] nll_loss silently computes a loss for a shape-mismatched target that eager and aot_eager reject`
items.author: tinywisdom
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.nn.functional.nll_loss` with a target whose spatial dimensions do not match the input raises a `RuntimeError: size mismatch` in eager **and** under `torch.compile(backend="aot_eager")`, but `backend="inductor"` **silently computes a (meaningless) loss** instead of raising. Because `aot_eager` (which also traces and runs an AOT graph) still raises, the lost check is specific to Inductor's lowering/decomposition, not a general "compile does not validate" behavior.

```python
import torch
def fn(inp, tgt): return torch.nn.functional.nll_loss(inp, tgt)
inp = torch.randn(2, 3, 2, 2)          # N=2, C=3, spatial (2,2)
tgt = torch.randint(0, 3, (2, 2, 1))   # spatial (2,1) -- mismatched

fn(inp, tgt)                                      # RuntimeError: size mismatch (input [2,3,2,2], target [2,2,1])
torch.compile(fn, backend="aot_eager")(inp, tgt)  # RuntimeError: size mismatch
torch.compile(fn, backend="inductor")(inp, tgt)   # tensor(-0.7886)  <- silently wrong
```

**Expected:** compiled `nll_loss` (Inductor) rejects the shape-mismatched target like eager and aot_eager, rather
than silently returning a loss computed from mismatched shapes. Related to the validation-lost umbrella #197554, but distinct in that aot_eager still raises and Inductor additionally produces a wrong numeric result.

items.title: [Bug] Sync prefix indexer hashes every block of a BlockStored event against the first block's parent
items.author: ankit373
items.body_excerpt:
### What's wrong

`SyncPrefixHashTable.ProcessBlockStored` (`pkg/utils/syncprefixcacheindexer/sync_hash.go`) computes the AIBrix hash of every block in a `BlockStored` event from the same parent:

```go
for i, engineBlockHash := range event.BlockHashes {
    ...
    var parentAibrixHash = s.seed
    if event.ParentBlockHash != nil {
        if ph, exists := hashMapping.engineToAibrix[*event.ParentBlockHash]; exists {
            parentAibrixHash = ph
        }
    }
    aibrixHash := s.computeHash(parentAibrixHash, s.getBlockTokens(event, i))
```

`ParentBlockHash` is the parent of the first block only. Block `i > 0` should chain from block `i-1` of the same event. On the request path `GetPrefixHashes` builds a proper chain (`H(seed, b0)`, `H(h0, b1)`, ...), so every block after the first in a multi-block event gets a hash the gateway never produces.

vLLM emits one `BlockStored` per batch of newly full blocks, so a long prefill arrives as a single event with many blocks (the decoder splits the tokens per block in `convertTokenIDs`). In practice prefix matching from KV events stops after the first block of each event.

### Repro

Table with block size `bs`, three blocks `b0 b1 b2`:

```go
table.ProcessBlockStored(BlockStored{BlockHashes: []int64{1, 2, 3}, Tokens: [][]byte{b0, b1, b2}, ...})
table.MatchPrefix(model, -1, b0+b1+b2, {pod})
```

Expected 100, got 33. Same for an event whose first block was already known (33), and an event continuing from a parent block (66 instead of 100).

The existing `TestProcessBlockStored` only counts mappings, so it passes either way.

### Fix

Look up the parent once, then carry the previous block's AIBrix hash through the loop, including the already-mapped branch.

items.title: [RFC]: Autoscaler-driven elastic EP: observe-first staging, membership semantics, and failure rules
items.author: bolubo
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix's PodAutoscaler scales replicas, and for MoE serving that unit is coarse: one replica can span dozens of GPUs, and traffic rarely varies in whole-replica quanta. vLLM can now resize DP/EP membership at runtime (`enable_elastic_ep`, `POST /scale_elastic_ep`, `POST /is_scaling_elastic_ep`, plus the DP-coordinator wave protocol), and #2288 asks AIBrix to drive it, starting observe-only. This RFC proposes how that drive should work, staged as observe, act, and graceful draining, and focuses on the platform-side semantics that are missing today: aligning three divergent states (Kubernetes resources, engine-committed membership, routable capacity), treating an engine resize as a transaction inside a reconcile loop, and writing down failure rules before production discovers them. The proposal is deliberately conservative: default off, hold rather than auto-recover, never act on unverified state. The observe stage is already in flight (#2812); we are asking for feedback on the act-side semantics before implementing them.

### Motivation

Whole-replica scaling is coarse and expensive for MoE: one replica may span dozens of GPUs, and traffic variation is rarely a whole-replica quantum. The engine now exposes the levers to resize DP/EP membership at runtime, but nothing in AIBrix drives them. Existing platform attempts in this space are either heavy (new CRDs, gated off) or still exploratory, and the upstream external-orchestration contract is not frozen yet (vllm/vllm#42515, vllm/vllm#43202).

**Benefit hypothesis (to be measured).** Two effects decide whether elastic EP is worth enabling. Sub-replica demand changes can be absorbed inside a footprint instead of moving whole replicas, which makes capacity quantization finer and avoids provisioning for step peaks; and ramps can be served as soon as the engine commits new ranks, without waiting for new pods. The cost side is the commit window (the engine answers 503 while resizing) and the added control complexity this RFC addresses. Enabling is least attractive when demand is stable at whole-replica quanta or when the window is not acceptable for the served workload. We plan to measure the deciding axes on one node first (time to add capacity for a width move versus a replica move, GPU-hours per unit of served traffic under bursty load, and error budget consumed during commit windows); multi-footprint economics need a larger setup and remain future work.

Three properties make this harder than an HPA-style target:

1. **Three states, not one.** Kubernetes knows which pods and processes exist; the engine knows which ranks are committed; the router knows which endpoints can take traffic. These states move at different speeds and in different orders: during a scale-up, capacity exists before the engine accepts it; during scale-down, the engine stops first and capacity is reclaimed after; after a rank failure, the desired state is unchanged while the engine serves degraded. "Replica count" cannot express any of this.

2. **A transaction inside a control loop.** An engine resize is a one-shot operation that takes tens of seconds, has intermediate states, and has no generic rollback. Today's known upstream bugs include a cancel path that corrupts engine state without rollback (vllm/vllm#57691) and a scale-up crash under EAGLE3 + CUDA graphs (vllm/vllm#58479). Kubernetes reconciliation, by contrast, assumes idempotent, replayable steps with eventual convergence; it has no word for "commit or hold". That gap has to be designed rather than coded ad hoc.

3. **No failure vocabulary.** Every step can fail quietly: partial joins, a controller restarting mid-commit, outcomes that cannot be verified after a timeout. Writing down the required behavior for these cases is the core of this RFC.

### Proposed Change

| Stage | What it adds | State |
|---|---|---|
| 0: observe | record engine scaling state in PodAutoscaler status; no decisions | in flight (#2812) |
| 1: act | opt-in width changes with transaction discipline and gates | this RFC |
| 2: draining | gateway policy for the engine's 503 window | this RFC (design) |

**Stage 0: observe (in flight: #2812).** PodAutoscaler records whether a scaling commit is in progress on the target's elastic-EP engines in `status.elasticEPScaling` (`inProgress`, `observedEngines`, `scalingEngines`, `lastTransitionTime`; no width read exists yet). No replica decisions change. This gives operators visibility and gives the controller a trustworthy read path for Stage 1.

**Stage 1: act with guardrails (opt-in, default off).** For deployments that enable elastic EP and opt in:

1. Read the **committed** width from the engine; never trust the last requested value.
2. Use target semantics: ask the engine to *be N* (the engine call takes `new_data_parallel_size` and a `drain_timeout`, default 120s), not to add one, so retries and re-ordering are harmless.
3. Treat each call as a transaction inside reconcile: one bounded operation per attempt (call, wait for commit up to a bound, verify, record the outcome, continue).
4. Gate every operation: never act while the engine reports scaling; never act on degraded or partially committed membership; enforce a settle window and hysteresis so a tens-of-seconds operation cannot oscillate.
5. Re-read state every reconcile; the controller never trusts its own last command (level-triggered).
6. Single writer for width: while act mode is on, the controller is the intended single writer for width; other writers are outside this contract and are surfaced as drift (F7).

**Stage 2: graceful draining.** While a commit is in flight, the engine answers 503 to all requests, including readiness probes. In our single-node test (4 x RTX 4090 48G, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, DP 2 to 4) the window lasted 37.2s on scale-up and 15.3s on scale-down; the raw evidence is recorded in #2812. The window affects the data plane of the deployment as a whole, not only the resized ranks. AIBrix holds the autoscal

aibrix/metadata-service:nightly  970MB
```

This appears unusually large for the runtime and metadata-service processes and is worth investigating.

Both images are built from `build/container/Dockerfile.python`, which installs the dependencies declared by the AIBrix Python wheel. The largest image layer is the `pip install` layer at approximately 814 MB.

## Measurements

| Component | Approximate size |
|---|---:|
| Debian + Python base layers | 156 MB |
| Final `pip install` layer | 814 MB |
| `site-packages` | 844 MiB |

The largest installed distributions are:

| Distribution | Size |
|---|---:|
| scipy | 142 MiB |
| pandas | 74 MiB |
| numpy | 59 MiB |
| plotly | 58 MiB |
| scikit-learn | 55 MiB |
| PuLP | 38 MiB |
| matplotlib | 37 MiB |
| dash | 32 MiB |
| kubernetes | 30 MiB |

Most of the scientific-computing and visualization imports appear under `aibrix.gpu_optimizer`, rather than the runtime or metadata-service entry points. Their installed dependency closure accounts for approximately 584 MiB.

There is also a mismatch between the Dockerfile comment and the package metadata: the Dockerfile says the profiling group is excluded to avoid packages such as pandas and matplotlib, but those packages are currently declared as main dependencies in `python/aibrix/pyproject.toml`. Therefore, `--without profiling` does not exclude them.

The two image names are also built independently from the same Dockerfile. In the inspected nightly builds, their large dependency layers have different digests, so those layers are not shared even though their installed contents and sizes are nearly identical.

## Impact

- Longer image pull and node startup times
- More registry and node storage usage
- Slower scale-out and cold starts for runtime workers
- Longer CI image builds and duplicate uploads
- Larger dependency and vulnerability-scanning surface

## Possible Changes

The exact implementation should be decided after confirming the dependency requirements of every published entry point. Possible changes include:

- Audit direct and transitive dependencies for `aibrix_runtime`, `aibrix_metadata`, `aibrix_batch_worker`, downloader, and GPU Optimizer.
- Adjust Python package metadata and container build targets so each published image installs only the dependencies required by the processes it runs.
- Preserve the storage backends and Kubernetes integrations currently supported by each entry point.
- If two published images remain identical, build the image once and apply both tags so their layers have the same digest.
- Correct the stale Dockerfile comment about excluded dependencies.
- Add image-size reporting or a regression threshold to CI, together with container smoke tests for the affected entry points.

The GPU Optimizer currently runs from `aibrix/metadata-service:nightly`, so any dependency changes must also update or preserve that deployment path.

## Environment

- Architecture: ARM64
- Tags: `nightly`
- Observed image sizes: approximately 970 MB each

items.title: [PyTorch backend][encoder-decoder] KvCacheConfig(dtype="fp8") overruns the cross-attention KV pool: illegal memory access or silently wrong output unless the pool is 2x the required size
items.author: lminer
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With an encoder-decoder model on the PyTorch backend, setting the KV cache dtype to `fp8` makes
the cross-attention cache access memory beyond its pool. A request only succeeds when the
cross-attention pool holds at least **twice** the blocks the in-flight requests need. Below that
the process either dies with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` or, when the
stray access lands in other mapped memory, returns wrong tokens with no error. The same pool
sizes work with the default cache dtype.

## Environment

- Images: `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29` and
  `nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.4.0rc0.dev202610040000` (both reproduce)
- GPU: NVIDIA L4 (24 GB), driver 595.91.07; AWS g6.2xlarge
- Model: `google/flan-t5-base`, weights loaded as bf16
- `LLM(backend="pytorch", ...)`, block reuse off, no CUDA graphs

## Reproduction

The prompt is 483 tokens, i.e. 16 blocks of 32 tokens in the cross-attention pool. With
`cross_kv_cache_fraction=0.5`, `max_tokens=768` gives a 24-block pool and `max_tokens=1024` a
32-block pool (the log line `Max KV cache blocks per sequence: 16 [window size=512], tokens per
block=32, primary blocks=24` confirms the sizes).

```bash
docker run --rm --gpus all --ipc=host -v $PWD:/w nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorrt-llm/release:1.3.0rc29 \
  python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py fp8 768     # crashes on the first request
docker run ... python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py fp8 1024    # decodes
docker run ... python3 /w/fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py auto 768    # decodes (default cache dtype, same pool)
```

| KV dtype | `max_tokens` | cross pool blocks | blocks needed | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp8 | 768 | 24 | 16 | `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` |
| fp8 | 1024 | 32 | 16 | OK |
| auto | 768 | 24 | 16 | OK |

After the error the process does not exit by itself; it has to be killed.

`fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py`:

```python
"""Encoder-decoder model on the PyTorch backend: an FP8 KV cache overruns the cross-attention pool.

    python3 fp8_cross_kv_repro_t5.py <kv dtype: fp8|auto> <kv max_tokens>

The prompt is ~480 tokens, i.e. 16 blocks of 32 tokens in the cross-attention pool.
"""
import json
import os
import sys

from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

from tensorrt_llm import LLM, SamplingParams
from tensorrt_llm.llmapi import KvCacheConfig


def main():
    kv_dtype, kv_tokens = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2])
    # The backend takes the weight dtype from the checkpoint's config.json, so write a bf16 copy.
    src = snapshot_download("google/flan-t5-base", allow_patterns=["*.json", "*.model", "model.safetensors"])
    ckpt = "/tmp/flan-t5-base-bf16"
    os.makedirs(ckpt, exist_ok=True)
    for name in os.listdir(src):
        if name != "config.json" and not os.path.exists(f"{ckpt}/{name}"):
            os.symlink(os.path.realpath(f"{src}/{name}"), f"{ckpt}/{name}")
    config = json.load(open(f"{src}/config.json"))
    config["torch_dtype"] = config["dtype"] = "bfloat16"
    json.dump(config, open(f"{ckpt}/config.json", "w"))

    llm = LLM(
        model=ckpt,
        backend="pytorch",
        max_batch_size=1,
        max_beam_width=1,
        max_input_len=512,
        max_seq_len=2048,
        kv_cache_config=KvCacheConfig(
            enable_block_reuse=False, max_tokens=kv_tokens, cross_kv_cache_fraction=0.5, dtype=kv_dtype
        ),
        cuda_graph_config=None,
    )
    prompt = "summarize: " + "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog near the river bank. " * 30
    print("prompt tokens:", len(llm.tokenizer.encode(prompt)), flush=True)
    params = SamplingParams(max_tokens=32)
    for i in range(3):
        out = llm.generate(prompt, params)
        print(f"request {i}: {list(out.outputs[0].token_ids)[:12]} {out.outputs[0].text[:60]!r}", flush=True)
    print("OK", kv_dtype, kv_tokens)
    llm.shutdown()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## More than one request in flight

The same rule holds with several requests submitted together. Measured on rc29 with a second,
larger encoder-decoder model, a batch of requests that needs 752 blocks in total:

| cross pool blocks | result |
|---|---|
| 768 | illegal memory access (also on the 1.4.0 nightly) |
| 896 | illegal memory access |
| 1,024 | **no error, wrong output**: every request runs to `max_tokens`, none matches the same request decoded alone |
| 1,280 | illegal memory access |
| 1,536 | OK |

So the threshold is 2 x 752 = 1,504 blocks. With the default cache dtype, 768 blocks are enough.
Admitting the requests one at a time only helps because fewer are then in flight together.

With `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` that run reports the failure in the cross-attention context pass:

```
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/cross_attention.py", line 268, in forward
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/trtllm.py", line 2330, in forward
  File ".../tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention/backends/fmha/fallback.py", line 122, in forward
    thop.attention(
RuntimeError: [TensorRT-LLM][ERROR] CUDA runtime error in cudaStreamIsCapturing(stream, &status): an illegal memory access was encountered (../include/tensorrt_llm/common/cudaUtils.h:157)
  tensorrt_llm::common::op::AttentionOp::enqueueContext<__half, tensorrt_llm::kernels::KVBlockArray>(...)
```

## Expected

Either the FP8 cross-attention cache stays inside a pool sized for the requests (as the default
dtype does), or the configuration is rejected for encoder-decoder models. An out-of-range access
should not be able to return wrong tokens silently.

## Guess at the cause

The 2x factor suggests the cross-attention pool is allocated at one byte per element (FP8) while
the cross-attention kernel addresses it with a two-byte element size. Not verified in the source.

## Also seen

With the FP8 cache and a large enough pool, on the larger model the first request after start-up
returns different tokens from the identical request sent again (every run). This does not happen
wit

If I can reproduce or confirm the root cause, I’ll work on a regression test and a focused fix.

items.title: [BUG | QST] CPU overhead regression with TVM-FFI
items.author: kainzhong
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
In v4.6 update, the following is changed in `python/CuTeDSL/cutlass/cutlass_dsl/cutlass.py`:
```
-                if kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults:
+                # Route through the kwargs-capable compiled class whenever
+                # the signature has kwonly/defaults OR any positional arg
+                # carries a dataclass instance (detected by the spec
+                # converter, including Union[...] over dataclasses). The
+                # kwargs wrapper is the only place tvm-ffi's
+                # ``map_dataclass_to_tuple`` unpack hook fires.
+                if (
+                    kwargs_wrapper_spec.kwonly_names
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_defaults
+                    or kwargs_wrapper_spec.arg_names
+                    or map_dataclass_to_tuple
+                ):
```
So basically if a @cute.jit function satisfies one of the following:
- `kwonly_names`: have keyword only arguments (indicated by *)
- `arg_defaults`: have default arguments
- `arg_names`: have any argument that is not a keyword only argument
- `map_dataclass_to_tuple`: have dataclass arguments

With these restrictions (especially `kwonly_names` and `arg_names`), basically only a CuTeDSL function with no arguments can go to the else branch and become a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` which is a subclass of `tvm_ffi.Function` so they get to be called in C++ and bypass python completely. For CuTeDSL functions with arguments, they now have to go through the `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs` path.

This will slightly slow down calling a CuTeDSL function from python due to extra python layers from in `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs`, which isn't a big deal since python is slow anyway. However, if you register the CuTeDSL function via tvm-ffi and call it from C++, the overhead becomes obvious because you will leave C++ and enter python (`TVMFFIJitCompiledFunctionWithKwargs.__call__`) and then enter the compiled CuTeDSL function. This makes the CPU overhead regress compared to pre-4.6 version since there wasn't going through python with GIL and argument wrapper stuff.

I also wonder what's the motivation behind this. My guess is this makes a @cute.jit function behave more like a python function where it can use kwargs instead of can only be called using positional args, but meanwhile when we do want to call it with positional args (in C++) this only makes it slower.

Currently there is a hack to fix this, which is instead of registering the compiled CuTeDSL function, we can register its `__tvm_ffi_object__` which would be a `tvm_ffi.Function` object, and we need to guarantee the args order is exactly the same in C++. I feel it's a bit hacky and fragile as cutlass evolves. 

Another proposition of mine is we can tell users (probably in docs) that if they define CuTeDSL functions in this format: `def func(a, b, c, /)` with nothing after / and no default values, then we can optimize this case into a `TVMFFIJitCompiledFunction` because we know nobody will use kwargs in this case. I think if this fix is OK I can open a PR on it.

Not sure what's the opinion of the CUTLASS people?

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**
I think my explanation should be clear enough so I don't think I need an example to reproduce.
You can just follow the example in https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/pull/3289 and measure the CPU time to notice the difference.

**Expected behavior**
Should be faster?

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
This regressed after v4.6 update

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

Hi @kainzhong, thanks for reaching out! This is a known issue for us. Your understanding is correct - the condition you mention is generally `true`, except the trivial functions without any args. But per our benchmark, the overhead it introduces is < 1us, while the overall launch overhead is typically <10 us. We think it is fine to keep this overhead for compatibility of diversed inputs. And we agree to have more documents here. Any PR is appreciated.

items.title: `tt.scan`/`tl.cumsum` hits an internal `AddPartialReduce` assert when `num_ctas > 1`
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
Launching a kernel that runs `tl.cumsum` (any `tt.scan`) under a multi-CTA layout (`num_ctas >= 2`) triggers an internal consistency assertion in the scan lowering:

```
triton-opt: .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157:
void AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
```

**Expected**: either a clean diagnostic telling the user that scan is not supported under multi-CTA layouts, or correct codegen.
**Actual**: the internal assert fires. On a bare `triton-opt` run this is a `SIGABRT`; through the Python frontend the same assertion is surfaced as an opaque `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed` after the assert text is printed, rather than a user-facing diagnostic.

The assert exists to catch a block-count mismatch, and it does — but the failure mode gives the user no hint that `num_ctas` is the problem.

This is **not** the same defect as the batched-dot `num_ctas` crash fixed by #11811 / reported in #11808. That bug lived in `TritonNvidiaGPUAssignCGALayoutsPass` (a rank mismatch while *assigning* the CGA layout). The IR reproducer below never runs that pass — the `CGALayout` is already written into the encoding and it crashes later, inside `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM`'s scan lowering. On the Python frontend the same kernel does go through `AssignCGALayouts` successfully and only aborts at lowering. So this survives the #11811 fix; I have not rebuilt past that commit to confirm on current `main`, but the failing code path (`ScanOpToLLVM`, not `AssignCGALayouts`) is untouched by it.

## Reproducer 1 — `tl.cumsum` + `num_ctas=2`

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def scan_k(x_ptr, o_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, AX: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :])
    r = tl.cumsum(x, axis=AX)
    tl.store(o_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], r)

x = torch.randn(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
o = torch.empty(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
scan_k[(1,)](x, o, 32, 32, 0, num_ctas=2)   # <- num_ctas=2 triggers it
```

Output (the assert message is emitted, then the pipeline reports a generic failure):

```text
python: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

`num_ctas=1` compiles and runs correctly. The crash is independent of the scan axis and of which tensor dimension the CGA layout splits.

## Reproducer 2 — `triton-opt` (offline, no GPU)

`repro.mlir`:

```mlir
#b = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,1],threadsPerWarp=[1,32],warpsPerCTA=[4,1],
                  order=[1,0], CGALayout=[[1,0]]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas"=2:i32,"ttg.num-warps"=4:i32,
                   "ttg.threads-per-warp"=32:i32} {
  tt.func @p(%v:tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) {
    %r = "tt.scan"(%v) <{axis = 0 : i32, reverse = false}> ({
    ^bb0(%a:f32,%b:f32):
      %s = arith.addf %a, %b : f32
      "tt.scan.return"(%s) : (f32) -> ()
    }) : (tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) -> tensor<32x32xf32,#b>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```text
$ triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv \
    --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90 -o /dev/null
triton-opt: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
(SIGABRT, exit 134)
```

## Controls

- **`num_ctas=1`** (drop the `CGALayout`): compiles cleanly (rc 0).
- **`tt.reduce` with the same 2-CTA `CGALayout`**: compiles cleanly **and produces numerically correct output** (`tl.sum` + `num_ctas=2` matches the reference). Reduction lowering accounts for the CTA dimension; scan lowering does not.
- The assert fires for every scan configuration I tried: any scan axis, 2D or 3D tensors, `num_ctas=2` or `4`, and CGA splits on either dimension. The gap is systemic to `tt.scan` under multi-CTA, not tied to one config.
  - The **same assertion text is reached at two sites**, chosen by how many warps carry unique data along the scan axis (`axisNumWarps`). With the layouts Triton picks for the Python reproducer, `axis=0` goes through `AddPartialReduce` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`, while `axis=1` on a 2D tensor (and the scan axis of a 3D tensor) takes the `axisNumWarps==1` fast path and fires the identical assert inside `AddPartialReduceOneWarp` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:263`. A hand-written layout that puts several warps on the scan axis hits `:157` instead — so the site is decided by `axisNumWarps`, not by rank. Both come from the same `ScanLoweringHelper` block-count math, so the suggested fix below covers both.

<details>
<summary>Relevant native stack frames (triton-opt)</summary>

```text
#17 AddPartialReduce(...)
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:184:63
#21 (anonymous namespace)::ScanOpConversion::emitFastScan(
      mlir::triton::ScanOp, ..., mlir::triton::TargetInfoBase const&) const
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:522:3
#22 ConvertOpToLLVMPattern<mlir::triton::ScanOp>::matchAndRewrite(...)
#27 (anonymous namespace)::OperationLegalizer::legalize(mlir::Operation*)
```
</details>

Note on the two line numbers: the assert that fails is at **`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`** (the `numScanBlocks * ... == srcValues.size()` check). The `#17` frame prints `184:63` because `-O2` attributes the inlined cold `__assert_fail` block to the next source line — the `__assert_fail` call is preceded by `mov $0x9d, %edx` (`0x9d = 157`), confirming the assert's own line argument is 157. The `#18–#20` frames are inlined `SmallVector` destructors on the same PC, not real calls.

## Root cause

`AddPartialReduce` (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`) asserts:

```cpp
assert(numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelE

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Verified against current main (`aad2a60d9`, local `triton-opt` built with `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`, pinned LLVM 24.0.0git): this is fixed by #11990.

Running the exact pipeline from the report (`--allocate-shared-memory-nv --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90`):

| config | result |
|---|---|
| repro as posted (scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[1,0]]`, split along the scan axis) | clean `error: TODO: unsupported scan layout`, exit 1, no assert |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 1 | same clean error |
| scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[0,1]]` (split along the non-scan axis) | compiles, exit 0 |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 0 | compiles, exit 0 |
| `num_ctas=1` control | compiles, exit 0 |

No SIGABRT anywhere. The two assert sites (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157` and `:263`) are still in the tree but no longer reachable from these inputs. The mechanism matches the #11990 description: scan-axis CTA splits now fail `ScanLoweringHelper::isSupported()` via `getCTASplitNum(...)[axis] != 1`, and non-scan-axis partitions use the per-CTA shape in `getNonAxisNumBlocks()` / `getAxisBlockStride()`, which is what the assert's block-count product needed.

One observation in case anyone touches this code: the rejection text is the pre-existing placeholder `TODO: unsupported scan layout`, which does not tell the user that `num_ctas` is the trigger. Not worth a PR on its own, but if the scan-axis case is meant to stay unsupported, naming the cause there would save the next person a source build.

Suggest closing this as fixed by #11990.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL >= 4.6: FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward with block-sparse masks spills registers, up to 1.8x slower than 4.5.3 (same kernel source)
items.author: janhuenermann
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

With the same kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.6.0.dev0 and later generate PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 backward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_bwd_sm100.FlashAttentionBackwardSm100`) that spills registers. The spills appear when the kernel is specialized for block-sparse attention with a `mask_mod`. That is the path `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention(..., kernel_options={"BACKEND": "FLASH"})` takes. With CuTe DSL 4.5.3, the same source compiles to PTX with no spills, or almost none. The kernel is at the 128-register cap (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory traffic. On B200 the backward kernel is 22% slower with a sliding-window mask and 82% slower with a document mask. The dense, causal, GQA and native `window_size` specializations of the same kernel are not affected.

This looks like the backward counterpart of #3701 (forward kernel, 4.7/4.8 vs 4.5.1), and it narrows down where the regression landed. 4.5.3 is fine. 4.6.0.dev0 already regresses, and it is the first release whose PTX header says `Based on NVVM 23.0.0` (4.5.3: `NVVM 20.0.0`).

| native sliding window 1024 (`window_size`), 2 × 16384 | 0.714 | 0.713 (0%) | 0.756 |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: sliding window 1024**, 2 × 16384 | 0.858 | **1.045 (+22%)** | **1.027 (+20%)** |
| **block-sparse `mask_mod`: document mask** (causal within random-length documents), 1 × 32768 | 1.279 | **2.329 (+82%)** | **2.209 (+73%)** |

The 4.5.3 and 4.6.0.dev0 columns run the same FA4 source (b20, see "Same source" below).
¹ The 4.8.0 column runs FA4 4.0.0b32, the latest release at the time of testing (b33 has a byte-identical backward kernel). FA4 changed between b20 and b32, so this column shows that the regression persists; it is not a clean A/B.

items.title: [Bug] mm_mxfp8 silently writes wrong results for a non-contiguous out (cutlass, cute-dsl, auto)
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`mm_mxfp8` silently returns wrong results when `out` is not contiguous, for the `cutlass`, `cute-dsl` and default `auto` backends. The kernels write a compact row-major `M x N` block starting at `out`'s data pointer and ignore its real strides. The result in `out` is garbage, and the write also overwrites memory just outside it (for example, the neighbouring columns of a larger buffer that `out` was sliced from). Nothing in `mm_mxfp8` checks the layout of `out`.

### Measured behavior

`M, N, K = 256, 1536, 1024`, bf16 output, inputs quantized with `mxfp8_quantize(..., sf_swizzle_layout=SfLayout.layout_128x4)`. "Correct" means cosine similarity 0.9993 against a bf16 `torch.mm` reference; "wrong" means about 0.001.

| `out` layout | `cute-dsl` | `cutlass` | `auto` | `cudnn` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| row-major, strides `(N, 1)` | correct | correct | correct | correct |
| row slice of a taller buffer, `buf[:M]` (still contiguous) | correct | correct | correct | correct |
| column slice of a wider buffer, `buf[:, :N]` (row stride > N) | **wrong**, neighbouring columns overwritten | **wrong**, neighbouring columns overwritten | **wrong** | correct |
| column-major view, `buf.T` (strides `(1, M)`) | raises `ValueError: Mismatched mC.strides[1] ...` from the compiled kernel | **wrong** | **wrong** | correct |

`cudnn` honors arbitrary output strides. `auto` resolves to `cutlass` here, so the default path is affected. Not tested: `trtllm`, `cutedsl_low_latency`, `b12x`.

### Reproduction

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
from flashinfer import SfLayout, mm_mxfp8
from flashinfer.fp8_quantization import mxfp8_quantize

m, n, k = 256, 1536, 1024
a = torch.randn(m, k, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
w = torch.randn(n, k, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
a8, a_sf = mxfp8_quantize(a, sf_swizzle_layout=SfLayout.layout_128x4)
w8, w_sf = mxfp8_quantize(w, sf_swizzle_layout=SfLayout.layout_128x4)

buf = torch.full((m, n + 64), 7.0, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
out = buf[:, :n]  # non-contiguous: row stride n + 64
mm_mxfp8(a8, w8.T, a_sf, w_sf, out=out, out_dtype=torch.bfloat16, backend="cutlass")

ref = a @ w.T
print(F.cosine_similarity(out.float().flatten(), ref.float().flatten(), dim=0))  # ~0.001
print((buf[:, n:] == 7.0).all())  # False: columns outside `out` were overwritten
```

### Expected

Either honor `out`'s strides, as `cudnn` does, or reject a non-contiguous `out` with a clear error. Silently writing a wrong result, and writing outside the given view, should not happen.

### Notes

- **Checks:** no check on `out`'s layout exists in `mm_mxfp8`, `_check_mm_mxfp8_problem_size`, or the `cutlass` / `cute-dsl` backend requirement functions. The only stride check on this path, in the `cutedsl_low_latency` requirement, covers the inputs `a` and `b`. The docstring does not state a layout requirement for `out`.
- **`cute-dsl` error:** its error for the column-major case is incidental. It comes from the compiled kernel's stride check on the last dimension, which does not catch a padded row stride.
- **Possible fixes:** raise `ValueError` for a non-contiguous `out` in the affected backends, or compute into a temporary contiguous buffer and copy into `out`.

### Environment

- FlashInfer main `125c989e0` (2026-10-05)
- Measured on SM107 (cc 10.7), nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8. The affected code paths are not architecture-specific, but other architectures were not measured.

items.title: [Feature Request]: Hierarchical Eviction with Assign / Evict / Fallback
items.author: kanceler
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe your feature request

# Discussion Draft: Hierarchical Eviction with Assign / Evict / Fallback

## Background

The current [type-aware eviction PR](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/pull/2746) shows that Mooncake Store needs a way to distinguish eviction semantics across object data types. For example, Hidden State and KV Cache differ in cache granularity, reuse interval, recomputation cost, and serving impact. They should not always be ranked by the same global lease-time ordering.

However, if each new policy is implemented directly inside `MasterService`, the master service will become increasingly complex as we add tenant-aware, type-aware, cost-aware, or other future eviction policies.

One possible direction is to model eviction policy as a small set of composable operations rather than as policy-specific branches embedded in `MasterService`.

## Core Idea

The policy layer can be expressed using three basic operations:

```text
Assign
Evict
Fallback
```

These operations are policy-side planning operations. They do not directly mutate metadata or remove replicas. `MasterService` remains responsible for safe execution.

### Assign

`Assign` partitions a candidate set by some dimension and assigns an eviction target to each child scope.

The partition dimension can be tenant, object data type, model, priority, namespace, or another future policy dimension.

For example:

```text
global_scope
-> Assign(by tenant)
   -> tenant A scope + A_evict_ratio + A_evict_ratio_lowerbound
   -> tenant B scope + B_evict_ratio + B_evict_ratio_lowerbound
```

Inside each tenant, the policy can continue partitioning by object data type:

```text
tenant B scope
-> Assign(by type)
   -> tenant B / KV Cache scope + KV_evict_ratio + KV_evict_ratio_lowerbound
   -> tenant B / Hidden State scope + Hidden_evict_ratio + Hidden_evict_ratio_lowerbound
```

In this model, tenant and type are not hard-coded hierarchy levels in the framework. They are just different ways to use `Assign`.

The assigned target can be represented as a ratio or as bytes. For memory pressure, bytes are often the more natural responsibility unit, while ratios are useful for compatibility with the current `BatchEvict` semantics.

### Evict

`Evict` selects victims within the current scope according to that scope's ranking policy.

It does not cross the scope boundary. For example, when running inside `tenant B / Hidden State`, it only selects victims from Hidden State candidates belonging to tenant B.

Different scopes can use different ranking policies:

- KV Cache can use a lease/LRU-like policy.
- Hidden State can use a policy that accounts for longer reuse intervals and higher recomputation cost.
- Unknown or general types can use the default lease-based policy.

`Evict` only produces a planned victim list. It does not modify metadata, release quota, remove replicas, or interact with offload state.

### Fallback

`Fallback` is used when child scopes fail to satisfy the lowerbound target of their parent scope. It selects additional victims inside the parent scope while relaxing the child partition boundaries.

For example, if type-scoped eviction inside a tenant cannot satisfy that tenant's lowerbound target, the policy should first fall back within that tenant rather than immediately shifting pressure to other tenants:

```text
tenant B scope
-> Fallback(tenant scope)
```

This means the policy can select from all remaining candidates in tenant B, without strictly preserving the original type-level split.

If all tenant scopes together still cannot satisfy the global lowerbound target, the policy can then use a global fallback:

```text
global_scope
-> Fallback(global scope)
```

Global fallback should not degenerate into raw lease-time ordering. It should still be able to consider tenant pressure and type pressure, so that fallback does not systematically punish scopes that are not the main source of memory pressure.

Fallback only relaxes policy partition boundaries. It does not relax execution safety boundaries. Hard pin, soft pin, group semantics, offload behavior, replica refcount, quota accounting, and metadata correctness are still enforced by `MasterService` during execution.

## Composed Flow

Using these three operations, a hierarchical eviction policy can be expressed as:

```text
global_scope
-> Assign(by tenant)
-> for each tenant_scope:
     -> Assign(by type)
     -> for each type_scope:
          -> Evict(type policy)
     -> Fallback(tenant scope)
-> Fallback(global scope)
```

This flow expresses several principles:

1. Assign responsibility before selecting victims.
2. Prefer eviction inside more specific scopes first.
3. If child scopes cannot satisfy the parent target, fall back within the parent scope first.
4. Only when the parent scope still cannot satisfy the target should the policy fall back to a higher-level scope.

## Relationship With MasterService

`MasterService` does not need to understand each policy's internal rules. It only needs to provide the mechanism around policy planning:

1. Build a lightweight candidate view.
2. Execute the policy's plan with revalidation.
3. Report actual eviction progress back to the policy flow.

The candidate view can be produced by the existing metadata scan. It should contain object identity and a small set of policy-relevant attributes, such as tenant, data type, memory footprint, lease state, and pin state.

The candidate view should not be a full metadata snapshot. It should not copy complete `ObjectMetadata`, replica lists, group membership, or segment state.

When executing eviction, `MasterService` uses the candidate reference to locate the real metadata again, revalidates whether the object is still evictable, and then handles group eviction, offload-on-evict, quota release, replica removal, metrics, and metadata erase.

Therefore, the policy layer owns decision-making, while `MasterService` owns mutation and correctness.

items.author: gilfree
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.fx.Tracer` has a `record_stack_traces` member. It does not give the correct stack trace, starting with torch  2.4 RC.

I am not sure it is part of the external API, but it was nice to have. The following is working in 2.3, but broken in 2.4RC


```python
import torch.fx
class M1(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.linear(x)
class M2(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.m1 = M1()
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.m1(x)
m = M2()
tracer = torch.fx.Tracer()
tracer.record_stack_traces=True
graph = tracer.trace(m)
sym=torch.fx.GraphModule(m,graph)
print(sym.print_readable())
assert 'code: return x + self.linear(x)' in sym.print_readable()
assert 'code: return x + self.m1(x)' in sym.print_readable()
```

It was broken in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121449/ where you stopped using the find_user_frame (or an equivalent function) to filter non user stack traces.

Something along these lines can be probably used as a fix:

```python
    def create_proxy(self, kind, target,args, kwargs, name, type_expr = None, proxy_factory_fn = None):
....
     if self.record_stack_traces and not proxy.node.stack_trace:
            proxy.node.stack_trace = _find_user_frame2_4(''.join(CapturedTraceback.extract().format()))


    def _find_user_frame2_4(self, stack_trace):
        stack_trace=stack_trace.split('\n')
        if 'torch/fx/proxy.py' in stack_trace[-3]:
            stack_trace=stack_trace[:-1]
            while len(stack_trace)>2 and '/fx/' in stack_trace[-2]:
                stack_trace=stack_trace[:-2]
        return '\n'.join(stack_trace)
```

Notes:
- I am not sure why you don't see the effect in `torch.export.export`.
- `torch.export.unflatten` looses stack trace for collapsed modules.

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected op` in backward-slice when `tl.gather` feeds `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
A `tl.gather` result used as a `tl.dot` operand inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts the `NVGPUWarpSpecialization` pass at `WSDataPartition.cpp:330` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected op")`) during backward-slice partitioning — `tt.gather` is not in the op whitelist. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        idx = tl.full([M, K], 1, tl.int32)
        a = tl.gather(a, idx, axis=1)          # gather result feeds tl.dot
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:330!
```

## Root cause
`getBackwardSliceToPartition`'s op whitelist does not include `tt.gather`; reaching it hits `llvm_unreachable` rather than a graceful "unsupported" diagnostic. The identical kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()` with `tl.atomic_add` after `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
`tl.atomic_add` on the dot accumulator written **after** `acc += tl.dot` inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts at `WSDataPartition.cpp:775` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected asyncTaskIds.size()")`) — the atomic carries a task-id count the sliceOp dispatch does not handle. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
        tl.atomic_add(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)   # atomic AFTER dot, on acc
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:775!
```

## Root cause
Inside `WSDataPartition.cpp`'s `sliceOp`, the per-task-id dispatch assumes a fixed set of `asyncTaskIds.size()` values; the atomic-on-accumulator produces a count outside the handled set and hits `llvm_unreachable`. The kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [AMD] CoalesceAsyncCopy produces a layout the direct-to-LDS lowering cannot coalesce when a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension
items.author: bogdan-petkovic
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

### Describe the bug

`TritonAMDGPUCoalesceAsyncCopy` can rewrite an async copy into a src layout that the direct-to-LDS lowering then rejects on GFX9. It happens when the blocked order and the shared order differ and a warp has more lanes than the fastest shared dimension has elements.

For a swizzled shared encoding the pass distributes the lanes and warps along the shared order and then rebuilds the blocked encoding with the original blocked order (added in #10928). The order of a blocked encoding also decides how the lanes are linearized, so once the lanes span more than one dimension, the first lanes walk along the dimension that is strided in LDS and the writes are no longer coalesced. This only works while all lanes of a warp fall in the fastest shared dimension, like the 64x2 tile in the tests of #10928.

The existing test `async_copy_different_order` in `test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir` already shows it. Its expected layout, `threadsPerWarp = [32, 2], warpsPerCTA = [1, 4], order = [1, 0]` for an `order = [0, 1]` shared layout, fails the same way when it is lowered.

### Reproducer

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad. No GPU needed, this is a compile failure.

`repro.mlir`, a 16x4 f32 copy with 2 warps on gfx950:

```mlir
#blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [2, 1], order = [1, 0]}>
#shared = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 1, maxPhase = 1, order = [0, 1]}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 2 : i32, "ttg.target" = "hip:gfx950", "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 64 : i32} {
  tt.func @copy(%input: tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> {tt.contiguity = dense<[1, 4]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.divisibility = dense<[16, 16]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.constancy = dense<[1, 1]> : tensor<2xi32>},
                %view: !ttg.memdesc<16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>) {
    %token = ttg.async_copy_global_to_local %input, %view : tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> -> <16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```
triton-opt repro.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx950 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

```
repro.mlir:7:14: error: cannot lower 'ttg.async_copy_global_to_local' to a direct-to-LDS copy: the resulting writes into shared memory are not coalesced for a vectorization of 1 element(s). Adjust the blocked or shared encoding so each warp writes a contiguous range.
```

CoalesceAsyncCopy rewrites the src to `#ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [1, 0]}>`. Lanes 1 to 3 then take the next columns, 16 elements apart in LDS. The same tile with `order = [0, 1]` lowers to a single buffer load to LDS:

```
sed 's/warpsPerCTA = \[2, 1\], order = \[1, 0\]/warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [0, 1]/' repro.mlir > shared-order.mlir
triton-opt shared-order.mlir --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

And the existing test case:

```
awk 'BEGIN{RS="// -----\n"} /async_copy_different_order/' test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir > different-order.mlir
triton-opt different-order.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx942 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx942
```

fails with the same error.

### How we hit it

In rocmlirTriton (https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton) a non-power-of-two K tile is split into power-of-two segments, so a K tile of 36 has a last segment of 4. For f32 convolutions on gfx950 with an M tile of 16 or 32 the copy of that segment is a 16x4, 32x2 or 16x8 tile, which is exactly this case. Our weekly tuning ran into it on 677 configs. We disabled those tile sizes on gfx950 for now.

In our tree, falling back to the shared order when the rebuilt encoding cannot be lowered fixed all of them and left the code of every config that already compiled unchanged. We did not send that as a PR because it calls `canLoadDirectToLDS` from the pass, and a fix that builds the right layout up front seems preferable. Happy to test any fix.


### Environment details

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad, built from source with CMake (TritonRelBuildWithAsserts, nvidia and amd backends, only the triton-opt target) against the prebuilt LLVM from cmake/llvm-info.json (b010a18d2b648cab83c83967ff26b8fde11acdc6). Ubuntu 22.04.5 on x86_64, GCC 11.4.

No GPU is needed, this is a compile failure in triton-opt and the target comes from gfx-arch (gfx950 for the reproducer, gfx942 for the existing test case). We first hit it compiling f32 convolutions for gfx950 in rocmlirTriton, whose vendored Triton has the same CoalesceAsyncCopy code.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Picking this up. I read the pass and the mechanism checks out: the swizzled branch distributes lanes along the shared order and then stamps the original blocked order back on, which re-linearizes the lanes. Once a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension, consecutive lanes walk a dim that is strided in LDS, and the rewritten copy is exactly what the direct-to-LDS lowering rejects.

Fix I am testing: after building the blocked-order candidate, check it with canLoadDirectToLDS (the same predicate the lowering uses, already called from this pass) and keep the shared-order distribution when the candidate would not lower. That matches what you validated in rocmlirTriton, and leaves every config whose rewritten layout already lowers byte-identical. Will add lit coverage for both the pass output and the end-to-end lowering of your 16x4 repro.

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body: PR up: #12159. The pass now checks the re-stamped encoding with `canLoadDirectToLDS` and keeps the shared-order distribution when the src order cannot lower. Your 16x4 reproducer lowers cleanly with it, and `async_copy_different_order` turned out to have the same latent problem, its expected layout changes to the shared order as well.

items.title: [RFC]: Control-plane orchestration of vLLM sleep mode and kvcached for warm standby and multi-model GPU pooling
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

AIBrix scales replicas as 0-or-N and only *observes* engine memory state; it never drives it. Two engine-side mechanisms now make GPU memory reclaimable at runtime — vLLM **sleep mode** (park a whole idle model's weights+KV) and **kvcached** (elastically shrink/grow a model's KV so several models share one GPU) — but both are mechanism-only, with no control plane. This RFC proposes AIBrix own the *policy*: a control-plane-driven "warm/asleep" tier between one replica and zero, plus KV-budget arbitration across co-resident models. The result: multi-minute cold starts become second-scale wakes, and one GPU can densely host many long-tail models.

### Motivation

Scaling is binary today. To reclaim a GPU we either keep a replica running (burning HBM while idle) or delete the pod and pay a multi-minute cold start (weight load + CUDA graph capture) when traffic returns. Neither fits bursty or long-tail traffic.

The engine now exposes the levers, but not the policy:

| | vLLM sleep mode | kvcached (github.com/ovg-project/kvcached) |
|---|---|---|
| Scope | whole model (weights + KV) | KV cache only (weights allocated outside it) |
| Granularity | all-or-nothing, single process | page-level elastic, cross-process co-residency |
| Target | a fully **idle** model | several **active** models sharing a GPU |
| Mechanism | CUDA VMM; `/sleep` `/wake_up`; level 1 weights→CPU, level 2 discard | CUDA VMM; per-process `cudaMemGetInfo` headroom + `/dev/shm` budget via `kvctl` |
| Control | manual API only; `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`-gated; no autoscaling | decentralized by design; no scheduler/admission/cross-node; `controller/` is a demo |

They are complementary: kvcached handles elastic KV among active co-resident models; sleep parks idle models' weights. Both are VMM actuators that enforce/observe — neither *decides*. The missing piece is a control plane that decides **which** model sleeps/wakes and **when**, **how much** KV budget each co-resident model gets, **admission** when a GPU is oversubscribed, and **routing/readiness** as models move between awake / warm / asleep. AIBrix already scrapes `vllm:engine_sleep_state` but never acts on it, and has no notion of co-resident KV budget — so it is the natural owner.

### Proposed Change

(Sketch only; full design — CRD, state machine, budget algorithm, agent protocol — to follow in a complete doc.)

1. A **warm/asleep lifecycle state** between `minReplicas` and zero: low traffic → `POST /sleep?level=1&mode=wait` (graceful drain); traffic returns → `/wake_up` (seconds). Pod/IP/endpoint persist.
2. A **KV-budget arbiter** across co-resident models, driving `kvctl` limits by policy (per-model min/max/share, priority) with cost-asymmetric reclaim — shrink KV first (cheap), sleep weights only when protected floors don't fit (expensive).
3. A **decide/execute split**: a Go controller (placement, admission, sleep/wake & budget policy, status) over a pod-side agent (kvcached engine, `kvctl`, sleep).
4. **Required couplings:** invalidate the prefix index on sleep (KV is wiped — see the sleep/prefix-index bug), exclude asleep pods from routing/readiness, and document the `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE` requirement.

### Alternatives Considered

- **HPA scale-to-zero** (`minReplicas=0`): already supported, but pays the full cold start and has no warm tier.
- **Leave it to kvcached's decentralized scheme:** works on a single node but has no admission/priority/cross-node policy and no sleep orchestration — precisely the demo `controller/` AIBrix would replace.
- **Token-level time-sharing** (swap at request granularity): higher utilization ceiling but far more complex/intrusive; this RFC targets model-granularity pooling.

items.title: [Bug]: Helix all-to-all receive path: restored payload words reach the outgoing bulk copy without a proxy fence
items.author: builtin-pb
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

Source analysis of `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/` (`helixAllToAll.cu`, `ll128Proto.cuh`, `cudaAsyncOps.cuh`) at main `b031dbe`; these files are unchanged since `a1f562a`. Hopper or later (bulk async copies); no runtime environment involved.

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [ ] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

Found by checking a slice from the restore to the bulk store (a one-warp kernel that calls the shipped `protoUnpack`) against the PTX memory model with our own PTX-level checker; not reproduced on hardware.

On the receive path of the Helix all-to-all (`helixAllToAll.cu`):
1. after the incoming copy completes (`smemBarWait`, line 534), `LL128Proto::protoUnpack` (539–540) has the lanes with `halfLaneId < 15` restore the payload word displaced by each 128-byte block's flag, with an ordinary shared-memory store (`ll128Proto.cuh:140`);
2. `s2gAllFields` (543) then has lane 0 issue `cp.async.bulk.global.shared::cta` (`cudaAsyncOps.cuh:166`) to copy the fields out, and this bulk copy reads those bytes.

No proxy fence lies between the restoring stores and the bulk copy's read. The `__syncwarp()` at `ll128Proto.cuh:144` is a warp barrier, and the `cp_async_bulk_wait_group_read` at 545 follows the issue.

### Expected behavior

The bulk copy reads the restored payload words. PTX requires a proxy fence for that. PTX ISA 9.4 §8.6: "A proxy fence is required to synchronize memory operations across different proxies." §9.7.10.28.2: bulk copies are performed in the async proxy, and "Accessing the same memory location across multiple proxies needs a cross-proxy fence." The completion of the incoming copy makes its data visible to the generic proxy; it does not publish later generic stores to the async proxy.

### actual behavior

Without the fence, PTX allows the outgoing bulk copy to read a block's flag word instead of its restored payload word, so the received field would carry a stale value at that position, with no error. Field 0 is always bulk-copied, so block 0's restored word is read whenever field 0 has at least 128 bytes; field 1 is affected only with `USE_BULK_FIELD1` (variable field 1 allowed and 16-byte aligned). Lane 0's own restore is also unordered with its own bulk read, so this is not only a cross-lane issue. We have not observed a failure on hardware.

### additional notes

Suggested fix: every restoring lane, including the issuing lane, executes `fence.proxy.async.shared::cta` after its restore and before the bulk copy. It can go just before the `__syncwarp()` at `ll128Proto.cuh:144` (a shared header), or in `helixAllToAll.cu` right after the `protoUnpack` call (line 540), executed by all lanes and followed by a `__syncwarp()`, so that lane 0's copy is ordered after every lane's fence. With a fence in every lane, the same slice passes the check.

A related site not covered by that check: the next entry's incoming bulk load into the same shared bytes also follows these generic stores without a proxy fence.
